title: Linear Algebra Review Guide
text: CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide Linear Algebra Review Guide CS 135: Computational Semantics -- From Logic to Geometry · Fall 2026 James Pustejovsky Companion to the Session 1 Self-Assessment · Posted with the answer key How to use this guide The self-assessment was a map, and this is the legend. It is organized by section (A through F) so that you can go directly to whatever came out weakest and skip the rest. For each section it tells you why that material shows up in the course and when, what you need to know (which is narrower than a full linear algebra course), what the common errors on the assessment were, where to review, and how to check whether the review worked. Two points before you start. • Trust the gap, not just the score. If you scored well on a section but circled a low confidence, you probably know the mechanics and not the picture; read the "why it matters" paragraph and do the self-check, and you are likely done. If you scored low but circled a high confidence, that is the section to spend real time on -- it usually means a specific misconception, and the "common mistakes" list is aimed at exactly that. • The window is Weeks 2 through 5. Sessions 4 through 6 are logic and composition and make no use of linear algebra at all. The embedding sessions (7 through 9) start to lean on Sections C and D, and the geometric algebra unit from Week 7 onward leans on everything, Section E above all. A few hours spread across the next four weeks will close any gap on this list; the same hours spent during Week 8 will not. Priority order If more than one section came out low, review in this order. It is ordered by how much the course depends on the section and how soon. Priority Section Reason 1 E -- Determinants, area, orientation The geometric algebra unit is built on this. The outer product is a determinant that remembers its orientation. Nothing in Sessions 12 and 13 makes sense without it. 2 C -- Inner products, projection Needed twice: for embedding similarity in Sessions 7 through 9, then again for contraction and projection in Session 14. 3 B -- Span, independence, basis Blades represent subspaces; a subspace is a span; a blade is zero exactly when its factors are dependent. Sessions 13 and 17. 4 F -- Rotations, orthogonal maps Rotors (Session 15) are the geometric algebra version of rotation. You need to know what a rotation is before you see it rebuilt. 1 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide Priority Section Reason 5 D -- Matrices as linear maps Embedding matrices and attention weights (Sessions 8 and 9); tensor products (Session 11). 6 A -- Vectors and vector spaces Foundation for everything, but most students have it. Review only if A2 or A3 went wrong. Section G (SVD, eigenvectors) is not on this list. It is taught in the course, not assumed, and there is nothing to review for it. What you do not need The course uses a narrow slice of linear algebra. You do not need fluency with Gaussian elimination as an algorithm, row-reduced echelon form, LU factorization, the rank--nullity theorem in its general form, Cramer's rule, or anything about eigenvalues beyond what Session 16 introduces. If a review resource spends a chapter on solving systems of equations, skip it. The emphasis here is on the geometry: what vectors, subspaces, inner products, determinants, and rotations mean as pictures, and how the algebra tracks the picture. The resources this guide points to Four sources are used throughout. All are free or in the library; none requires purchasing anything. • 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra. A series of short videos (roughly ten to fifteen minutes each) built entirely around geometric intuition. For this course it is the single best resource, because its point of view -- matrices are transformations, determinants are scale factors, dot products are projections -- is exactly the point of view geometric algebra generalizes. Cited below by chapter number. • Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, and the MIT OCW 18.06 lectures. The standard undergraduate treatment. Cited by book section; the OCW lectures follow the book and are useful if you learn better from a lecture. • Hefferon, Linear Algebra. A free, open textbook with full solutions, good for doing exercises. Its "Geometry of Determinants" and "Geometry of Linear Maps" topics are particularly well matched to this course. • Immersive Linear Algebra (immersivemath.com). A free online text with interactive figures. Good for Sections C, E, and F, where being able to drag a vector and watch a projection, area, or rotation change is worth more than a page of text. Chapter and section numbers below are for the current editions as of this writing. If a number does not match what you have, use the topic name; the topics have not moved. Section A -- Vectors and Vector Spaces Where it is used: Throughout; Session 12 in particular. Suggested review time if this section came out low: 1 to 2 hours. Most students only need A2 and A3. 2 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide Why it matters in this course Session 12 introduces the geometric product, and the first thing it asks of you is to stop thinking of a vector as a list of numbers. The list is a description of the vector relative to a basis; the vector is the arrow. Geometric algebra is built to work with the arrow directly, and much of its payoff comes from expressions that never mention coordinates. Question A3 was on the assessment specifically to see who already draws that distinction. The subspace test (A2) matters for a similar reason. Blades in geometric algebra represent subspaces, and a subspace has to pass through the origin and be closed under the vector operations. The plane x + y + z = 1 is not one, and neither is the positive octant. If you answered (d), it is worth understanding why (a) is the only correct answer. What you need to know • Vector addition and scalar multiplication, componentwise, and what they look like as arrows (parallelogram rule, stretching). • The definition of a vector space, and the three-part test for whether a subset is a subspace: contains the zero vector, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiples. • The distinction between a vector and its coordinate representation in a basis. The same arrow has different coordinates in different bases. Common mistakes on the assessment • A2: choosing (d) because (b) "looks like" (a). The plane x + y + z = 1 does not contain the origin, so it fails immediately. Choosing (c) because the set is closed under addition; it is, but it is not closed under multiplication by negative scalars. • A3: answering "true" without qualification. The intended answer is that this is true only relative to a choice of basis; a vector is an element of the space, and the three numbers are its coordinates. Where to review • 3Blue1Brown, Chapter 1 ("Vectors, what even are they?") and Chapter 16 ("Abstract vector spaces"). The second one is the direct answer to A3. • Strang, Sections 1.1 and 3.1 (vector spaces and subspaces). The subspace examples in 3.1 cover A2 exactly. • Hefferon, Chapter Two, Section I (Definition of Vector Space), particularly the subspace examples and exercises. Self-check Do these without looking anything up. Answers are in the Appendix. A1. Let u = (1, −2, 0) and v = (3, 1, 1). Compute 2u + v. A2. Is the set of all (x, y) in R² with xy = 0 a subspace of R²? Give a one-line reason. A3. The vector (1, 1) in R² has coordinates (1, 1) in the standard basis. What are its coordinates in the basis {(1, 1), (1, −1)}? 3 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide Section B -- Span, Independence, Basis Where it is used: Sessions 13 and 17. Suggested review time if this section came out low: 2 to 3 hours. Why it matters in this course In Session 13 you will meet the outer product of two vectors, a ∧ b, which represents the plane spanned by a and b, together with an orientation and an area. It is zero exactly when a and b are linearly dependent. The outer product of three vectors represents the volume they span and is zero exactly when they are dependent. So the concept of independence is not background here: it is the condition for a blade to be nonzero, and "dimension of the span" becomes "grade of the blade". Session 17 goes further and uses blades to represent subspaces of a semantic space directly. If you are not comfortable with what it means for a set of vectors to span a subspace, or with the fact that a basis for an n-dimensional space has exactly n vectors, Session 17 will be harder than it needs to be. What you need to know • The span of a set of vectors, as the set of all linear combinations, and as a picture: a line, a plane, all of space. • Linear independence, both as a definition (the only combination giving zero is the trivial one) and as a picture (no vector in the set lies in the span of the others). • Basis: a linearly independent spanning set. Dimension: the number of vectors in any basis. Every basis of Rn has exactly n vectors. • The consequences: more than n vectors in Rn are always dependent; fewer than n never span; a spanning set can be thinned to a basis and an independent set can be extended to one. Common mistakes on the assessment • B1: computing something and concluding the vectors are independent without noticing that w = u + v. Whenever one vector is the sum of two others, the set is dependent. A quick test in R³ is the determinant of the matrix with the three vectors as columns; here it is zero. • B2: answering 3 because there are three vectors. All three lie on the same line through the origin; the span is a line and the dimension is 1. • B4: concluding only "S spans R⁴" or nothing. Seven vectors in R⁴ must be dependent (seven exceeds four). Since S spans, some four of them form a basis. The set is not itself a basis. Where to review • 3Blue1Brown, Chapter 2 ("Linear combinations, span, and basis vectors"). Watch this one even if you scored well; the way it draws span is the way blades will be drawn in Session 13. 4 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide • Strang, Section 3.4 (Independence, basis, and dimension). This is the definitive statement of everything above, with the counting arguments for B4. • Hefferon, Chapter Two, Sections II and III (Linear Independence; Basis and Dimension). The exercises with solutions are the best place to practice deciding independence by hand. • OCW 18.06, Lecture 9 (Independence, basis, and dimension), if you prefer a lecture. Self-check Do these without looking anything up. Answers are in the Appendix. B1. Are (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6) linearly independent? What is the dimension of their span? B2. What is the dimension of span{(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0)} in R³? Describe the span geometrically. B3. Five vectors are given in R³. Without computing anything, what can you say about their independence? Can they span R³? B4. Give a basis for the plane x + y + z = 0 in R³. How many vectors does it need? Section C -- Inner Products, Norms, Orthogonality, Projection Where it is used: Sessions 7 through 9 (embedding similarity) and Session 14 (contraction and projection). Suggested review time if this section came out low: 2 to 3 hours. Why it matters in this course This is the section the course uses first. In Sessions 7 through 9, word and sentence embeddings are vectors, and almost every question about them -- how similar are two words, which context does a word best fit, what does an attention weight measure -- is answered by an inner product. Cosine similarity (C5) is an inner product divided by two norms, and you will compute it constantly. It returns in Session 14 with the geometric product, which splits into a symmetric part (the inner product) and an antisymmetric part (the outer product from Section B). Projection of a vector onto a subspace, which you did in C4 for a line, is done there with a single algebraic expression that works for planes and higher-dimensional subspaces without change. That expression only makes sense if you already know what projection onto a line is doing. What you need to know • The dot product, computed componentwise, and its geometric meaning: u · v = ǁuǁ ǁvǁ cos θ. • The norm ǁuǁ = √(u · u), and the unit vector u / ǁuǁ. • Orthogonality: u · v = 0 means the vectors are perpendicular (for nonzero u and v). The sign of the dot product tells you whether the angle is acute, right, or obtuse. 5 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide • Projection of u onto v: projv u = (u · v / v · v) v. The result is a vector along v, and u minus that projection is orthogonal to v. • Cosine similarity: (u · v) / (ǁuǁ ǁvǁ), which ranges over [−1, 1] and is 1 for parallel, 0 for orthogonal, −1 for opposite vectors. Common mistakes on the assessment • C2: computing u · v = 0 correctly but not saying what it means. The point of the question is the interpretation: the vectors are orthogonal. • C4: returning the scalar 3 rather than the vector (3, 0). A projection onto a line is a vector on that line. The scalar 3 is its length (the scalar projection); the question asked for the vector. • C5: stopping at 1/√2 without naming the angle, or naming it as 90°. Since cos θ = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, θ = 45°. Where to review • 3Blue1Brown, Chapter 9 ("Dot products and duality"). The duality half is optional, but the first half is the cleanest picture of why the dot product measures projection. • Strang, Sections 1.2 (Lengths and dot products) and 4.2 (Projections). Section 4.2 starts with projection onto a line, which is what you need, before moving to subspaces. • Immersive Linear Algebra, the chapter on the dot product. Drag the vectors and watch the projection. • OCW 18.06, Lecture 15 (Projections onto subspaces), first twenty minutes. Self-check Do these without looking anything up. Answers are in the Appendix. C1. Compute ǁ(1, 2, 2)ǁ. C2. Compute the vector projection of u = (2, 3) onto v = (1, 1). Check that u minus your answer is orthogonal to v. C3. What is the cosine similarity of (1, 0) and (0, 1)? Of (1, 0) and (−1, 0)? C4. Two embedding vectors have cosine similarity 0.95. What does this say about the angle between them? What does it not say about their lengths? Section D -- Matrices as Linear Maps Where it is used: Sessions 8 and 9 (embeddings, attention) and Session 11 (tensor products). Suggested review time if this section came out low: 1 to 2 hours. Why it matters in this course Everything in Sessions 8 and 9 is matrix multiplication: an embedding matrix takes a one-hot word vector to a dense vector; the query, key, and value matrices in attention are linear maps applied to every token; the attention weights form a matrix that mixes the value vectors. You do 6 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide not need to be fast at multiplying matrices by hand, but you need to know what a matrix does -it sends each basis vector to a column -- and how shapes have to line up (D3). Session 11 introduces tensor products as one route to compositional semantics, and the argument there compares tensor products with geometric products. The comparison needs D4: that matrix multiplication is not commutative, that AB and BA are different maps. Geometric algebra also has a noncommutative product, but its noncommutativity is controlled and meaningful. That contrast is easier to appreciate once you are used to the matrix case. What you need to know • A matrix as a linear map: Ax is a linear combination of the columns of A with coefficients from x. The columns are the images of the basis vectors. • Shape rules: an m × n matrix maps Rn to Rm. The product AB is defined when the column count of A matches the row count of B, and (m × n)(n × k) = m × k. • Composition: AB means "apply B, then A". This is why AB ≠ BA in general. • Diagonal matrices scale each axis independently; this is the picture behind D1. Common mistakes on the assessment • D2: "the coefficients" or "the equations". The columns are the images of the standard basis vectors under T. If you know where the basis goes, you know everything about the map, and the matrix is just that information written down. • D3: 2 × 2 (taking the inner dimensions) or 3 × 4 with the reasoning reversed. The inner dimensions must match and then vanish; the outer ones remain: 3 × 4. • D4: "true". It is false. Rotating and then reflecting is not the same as reflecting and then rotating. Where to review • 3Blue1Brown, Chapter 3 ("Linear transformations and matrices") and Chapter 4 ("Matrix multiplication as composition"). Chapter 4 is the picture behind D4. • Strang, Sections 2.3 and 2.4 (Matrix operations; Rules for matrix operations). Section 2.4 has the noncommutativity examples. • Hefferon, Chapter Three, Section III (Computing Linear Maps), which develops "the columns are the images of the basis" carefully. Self-check Do these without looking anything up. Answers are in the Appendix. D1. Let A = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]. Compute A(1, 0) and A(0, 1). What does A do to the plane? D2. A is 4 × 3. What is the shape of x if Ax is defined, and what is the shape of Ax? D3. Let R be rotation by 90° counterclockwise and F be reflection across the x-axis, both in R². Is RF = FR? Test on the vector (1, 0). Section E -- Determinants, Area, and Orientation 7 CS 135 · Linear Algebra Review Guide Where it is used: Sessions 12 and 13 build directly on it; used through the end of the course. Suggested review time if this section came out low: 3 to 4 hours. This is the section to prioritize. Why it matters in this course The outer product of two vectors, a ∧ b, is the central new object in Session 13. It has a magnitude, which is the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b, and an orientation, which is the sense (counterclockwise or clockwise) in which a is swept toward b. In two dimensions, a ∧ b is exactly the 2 × 2 determinant with a and b as columns, multiplied by the unit bivector. The determinant's magnitude is the area (E2); its sign is the orientation (E3); it vanishes when a and b are parallel (E4). Every one of the assessment questions in this section is a fact about the outer product in disguise. The same holds in three dimensions: a ∧ b ∧ c is the 3 × 3 determinant times the unit trivector, and its magnitude is a volume (E5). Once you see determinants this way, the geometric algebra unit is a matter of making the determinant into an algebraic object you can add, multiply, and take products with, rather than a number you compute and throw away. If you see determinants only as a formula, the unit will look like it is inventing things. The one idea students most often lack is that orientation is information. Swapping two columns negates the determinant (E3) and that sign is not a bookkeeping accident; it records which way around the parallelogram you went. Geometric algebra keeps that sign throughout, and it is what lets rotations, reflections, and the difference between "a then b" and "b then a" all live in one algebra. Spend your review time on E3, not E1. What you need to know • The 2 × 2 determinant formula ad − bc, and the 3 × 3 formula by cofactor expansion (you do not need a general n × n algorithm). • |det| of a 2 × 2 matrix is the area of the parallelogram spanned by its columns; for a 3 × 3 matrix it is the volume of the parallelepiped. Equivalently, |det A| is the factor by which A scales all areas (or volumes). • The sign of the determinant is the orientation: positive means the columns, in order, have the same handedness as the standard basis; negative means the map flips orientation (it includes a reflection). • det = 0 exactly when the columns are linearly dependent; the parallelogram is flattened to a line (or point) and has no area. • Swapping two columns negates the determinant. Scaling one column by c scales the determinant by c. The determinant is linear in each column separately (this is the property the outer product inherits). • det(AB) = det(A) det(B): scale factors compose by multiplying. Common mistakes on the assessment 8 CS 135 · Lin

title: Haskell Review Companion
text: CS 135 — Haskell Notation Reference Fall 2026 Haskell Notation Reference Every construct you need for Problem Set 1, and its semantic counterpart CS 135: Computational Semantics | James Pustejovsky | Brandeis | Fall 2026 How to use this. Keep it open beside the scaffold. Section 1 is the one-page summary; Sections 2–5 explain each construct; Section 6 lists the mistakes that cost people the most time. Nothing here is Haskell for its own sake — every entry exists because it implements something from the semantics. 1. The Correspondence, at a Glance Semantics Haskell Where it appears type e Entity entities in the domain type t Bool, aliased T sentence denotations type ⟨e, t⟩ Entity -> T, aliased ET nouns, intransitive verbs type ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ Entity -> Entity -> T, aliased TV transitive verbs type ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ ET -> T, aliased GQ quantified NPs determiner type ET -> GQ, aliased DET every, some, no domain D domain :: what quantifiers range over interpretation I the ...Set lists and likePairs the model characteristic function inSet, inRel sets → functions λx. φ \x -> ... every denotation you write function application juxtaposition: f x the composition rule ∀x all p domain universal quantification ∃x any p domain existential quantification P →Q not p || q inside every P ∧Q p && q inside some, and PM ¬P not p inside no [Entity] 2. Declaring Things Type signature :: Read :: as “has type”. Always write one; it is the semantic type of the expression, and it is what the compiler checks your definition against. student :: ET likes :: TV -- student has type <e,t> -- likes has type <e,<e,t>> New type data Creates a genuinely new type by listing its values. The values are the type — there is nothing underneath. data Entity = Alice | Bob | Carol | Fido 1 CS 135 — Haskell Notation Reference Fall 2026 deriving (Eq, Ord, Show, Enum, Bounded) Read | as “or”. Semantically this is the domain D: declaring the type declares what exists in the model. deriving asks the compiler to generate boilerplate: Eq gives == (needed by elem), Enum and Bounded give minBound, maxBound, and range notation (needed by domain), Show gives printing. Synonym type Creates a nickname, not a new type. T and Bool are interchangeable everywhere, and GHC may report errors using either name. type T type ET type TV = Bool = Entity -> T = Entity -> Entity -> T -- t -- <e,t> -- <e,<e,t>> The synonyms exist so signatures read like semantics rather than like plumbing. 3. Functions The arrow -> a -> b is the type of functions from a to b. It associates to the right. So Entity -> Entity -> Bool means Entity -> (Entity -> Bool) Give me an entity, and I hand back a one-place predicate. That is currying, visible in the type — and it is why partial application yields a verb phrase. Lambda \x -> ... The backslash is λ. \x -> e is λx. e. sleeps = \x -> x ‘elem‘ sleepSet sleeps x = x ‘elem‘ sleepSet -- lambda style -- equation style; identical \x y -> ... abbreviates \x -> \y -> ... — two nested lambdas. Application Juxtaposition. No parentheses, no commas. It associates to the left: f x y means (f x) y. sleeps Alice likes Bob likes Bob Alice -- one argument -- partial! -- both arguments : Bool : Entity -> Bool : Bool The middle line is the important one: applying a TV to one argument gives an ET — the type of a verb phrase. Partial application is phrase structure. Point-free definitions A definition need not mention its argument, if the right-hand side is already a function: student = inSet studentSet student x = x ‘elem‘ studentSet -- point-free -- equivalent, argument named Both define the same ET. The first makes visible that a predicate is an object you can build and pass around. 2 CS 135 — Haskell Notation Reference Fall 2026 4. Data and Lookup Lists [ ] [Entity] is the type of lists of entities; [Alice, Bob] is such a list. domain :: [Entity] domain = [minBound .. maxBound] -- range notation: [Alice, Bob, Carol, Fido] Writing domain this way rather than by hand means it stays correct when you add to the data declaration. Tuples ( , ) (Entity, Entity) is an ordered pair, so [(Entity, Entity)] is a list of pairs — a binary relation. likePairs = [(Alice,Bob), (Alice,Fido), (Bob,Fido)] Order matters: (Alice,Bob) is present, (Bob,Alice) is not. elem and backticks elem tests list membership. Backticks put a two-argument function between its arguments: elem x xs x ‘elem‘ xs -- prefix -- infix; identical, and reads like x an element of xs inSet and inRel These are given in the scaffold. They convert the model from sets into functions. inSet :: [Entity] -> ET inSet xs = \x -> x ‘elem‘ xs inRel :: [(Entity,Entity)] -> TV inRel ps = \obj subj -> (subj, obj) ‘elem‘ ps inSet is the characteristic function χS (x) = 1 ⇐⇒ x ∈ S — the set/function isomorphism, in four words. inRel takes the object first but stores pairs subject-first. It is the adapter between the two conventions. See the trap in §6. 5. Logic Booleans Logic Haskell Note P ∧Q P ∨Q ¬P P →Q p && q p || q not p not p || q not is a function; parenthesize its argument no arrow operator exists all :: (a -> Bool) -> [a] -> Bool any :: (a -> Bool) -> [a] -> Bool -- every element passes -- at least one passes forAll p = all p domain exists p = any p domain -- the clause for -- the clause for 3 forall x exists x CS 135 — Haskell Notation Reference Fall 2026 These are the satisfaction clauses of Session 3, transcribed. The assignment update g[x 7→ d] is Haskell’s function application p d: because p is a function of x, applying it to d is evaluating φ under the modified assignment. This works because domain is finite. An infinite domain would make all diverge. every :: DET every restrictor scope = all (\x -> not (restrictor x) || scope x) domain some’ :: DET some’ restrictor scope = any (\x -> restrictor x && scope x) domain Note the asymmetry, and do not swap it. every pairs with implication; some and no pair with conjunction. Swapping produces no type error and the wrong truth conditions — see §6. Primes on some’ and no’ avoid clashing with Prelude names. Same for read’. 6. Traps Determiners 1. Argument order on transitive verbs. likes Bob Alice means Alice likes Bob. Object first. This typechecks either way, so the compiler will not save you — you will simply get FAIL on the test. Check: likes obj subj looks up (subj, obj) in the pair list. 2. Wrong connective in a determiner. all (\x -> q x && p x) domain for every claims that everything in the domain is a Q that is P — not that every Q is P . Typechecks; wrong. Likewise implication inside some makes some dog sleeps true whenever anything fails to be a dog. 3. Missing parentheses after not. Application binds tightest, so not student x parses as (not student) x — applying not to a function. Write not (student x). 4. Bypassing the composition rules. s3 = likes bob alice may give the right answer, but Part D asks for spName alice (vpName likes bob). The rules are the point of the assignment; shortcuts receive partial credit. 5. Applying an entity to something. alice sleeps is a type error: alice :: not a function. The predicate applies to the individual, so write sleeps alice. 7. Reading a Type Error GHC error messages have a fixed shape. Find these two lines and compare them: * Couldn’t match expected type: Entity with actual type: Entity -> Bool * In the first argument of ‘tall’, namely ‘student’ 4 Entity is CS 135 — Haskell Notation Reference Fall 2026 Expected is what the position demands. Actual is what you supplied. The gap between them names the failing composition step — here, an ⟨e, t⟩ where an e was required, which is exactly the mismatch that motivates predicate modification. Message Usually means applied to one value argument, but its type has none you applied a non-function, e.g. an Entity expected Entity, actual Entity -> Bool you passed a predicate where an individual was wanted expected Bool, actual Entity -> Bool you forgot to apply a predicate to anything Variable not in scope typo, or a Prelude clash (try a prime) Read the first error only. Later ones are usually cascade damage from the first. 8. Working in GHCi $ runghc Fragment.hs $ ghci Fragment.hs -- run the test suite -- load interactively Inside GHCi: :t expr show the type of an expression — the most useful command :r reload after editing the file :q quit > :t likes Bob likes Bob :: Entity -> Bool > student Alice True > every student sleeps False -- confirms partial application gives an ET Ask the compiler when you are stuck. Put a hole where you cannot see what belongs: myDenotation = _ GHC will report the type it expects there, which is often enough to finish the line. If a hole is taking you more than three or four lines, stop — in the reference solution every hole is a single line, and you are probably fighting the language rather than doing the semantics. Bring it to lab or office hours. 5

title: Lecture 1 — Introduction & Lambda Calculus
text: Session 1: Introduction; the Lambda Calculus What Structure Does Meaning Composition Require? James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics August 28, 2026 1 / 49 Today 1 A question to start with 2 What this course is, how it is assessed, what you need 3 The arc – five bodies of material, and why each one forces the next 4 The lambda calculus – as far as the clock allows At the end: a paper handout, a linear algebra self-assessment. Not graded. Please take one on your way out. 2 / 49 Two Sentences The dog bit the man. The man bit the dog. Same words. Same word frequencies. Same bag of tokens. 3 / 49 Two Sentences The dog bit the man. The man bit the dog. Same words. Same word frequencies. Same bag of tokens. Radically different meanings. One of them is news. 3 / 49 Two Sentences The dog bit the man. The man bit the dog. Same words. Same word frequencies. Same bag of tokens. Radically different meanings. One of them is news. The question for this course: what does a representation of meaning have to be in order to tell these apart – and to keep telling them apart when the sentences get complicated? 3 / 49 Why This Is Harder Than It Looks Suppose meanings are vectors – as they are in essentially every modern NLP system. How do we combine the vectors for dog, bit, and man? Operation Problem u+v commutative – both sentences get the same vector u⊙v also commutative – same problem [u; v] order-sensitive, but dimension grows with sentence length u⊗v order-sensitive, but dimension grows exponentially 4 / 49 Why This Is Harder Than It Looks Suppose meanings are vectors – as they are in essentially every modern NLP system. How do we combine the vectors for dog, bit, and man? Operation Problem u+v commutative – both sentences get the same vector u⊙v also commutative – same problem [u; v] order-sensitive, but dimension grows with sentence length u⊗v order-sensitive, but dimension grows exponentially Meanwhile the logical tradition solves ordering immediately and completely – but has no notion of similarity at all. In it, dog and wolf are simply different symbols. 4 / 49 Why This Is Harder Than It Looks Suppose meanings are vectors – as they are in essentially every modern NLP system. How do we combine the vectors for dog, bit, and man? Operation Problem u+v commutative – both sentences get the same vector u⊙v also commutative – same problem [u; v] order-sensitive, but dimension grows with sentence length u⊗v order-sensitive, but dimension grows exponentially Meanwhile the logical tradition solves ordering immediately and completely – but has no notion of similarity at all. In it, dog and wolf are simply different symbols. Each tradition solves exactly what the other cannot. That is the situation this course is about. 4 / 49 What This Course Is One question, pursued across five bodies of material: Theme The idea 1 Meaning as logic composition is function application 2 Meaning as distribution meaning is position in a space 3 Linear algebra, revisited the geometry we already half-know 4 Geometric algebra one product that keeps what the others lose 5 Functional geometric algebra semantics on that substrate This is not a survey of five topics. It is one argument in five movements, and each movement exists because the previous one ran out of road. 5 / 49 Learning Goals By the end of the course you will be able to: represent and compute meaning in both logical and distributional frameworks, and articulate the strengths and limits of each; carry out type-driven semantic derivations, including quantification and scope, and evaluate them against models; implement a compositional fragment of English and test it computationally; work with the core constructions of geometric algebra and apply them to semantic representation; carry out and evaluate mappings between model-theoretic artifacts and vectorial encodings; read and evaluate contemporary research in computational semantics – including work whose central questions are still open; integrate these skills in a substantial final project. 6 / 49 Prerequisites – and a Reassurance Formally: introductory programming (any language), plus LING 130a or COSI 121b, or permission of the instructor. In practice, two things matter: No prior Haskell or functional programming is assumed. Problem Set 1 gives you a working file with holes in it; you write the semantics, not the infrastructure. Nearly every answer is one line. Labs 1–3 cover the language. Some linear algebra helps in the second half – not the computational kind, but you should be comfortable with vectors, inner products, and what a determinant means geometrically. Hence today’s handout. Students arrive here from computer science, from linguistics, and from elsewhere. One of the five themes will probably be much harder for you than the others. That is expected, and it is not a signal that you are in the wrong room. It is a signal to come to office hours early. 7 / 49 Resources No textbook to buy. Everything is on Moodle or freely available online. Key Text Used in EU JM LS W D M P van Eijck & Unger, Comp. Semantics with Functional Programming Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed.) Lenci & Sahlgren, Distributional Semantics Widdows, Geometry and Meaning Dorst, Fontijne & Mann, Geometric Algebra for Computer Science Macdonald, Linear and Geometric Algebra (optional, gentler) Papers packet – Smolensky, Plate, Coecke et al., FGA papers Theme 1 Themes 1–2 Theme 2 Themes 2–3 Theme 4 Themes 3–4 Themes 4–5 Course site: www.cs-135.org – schedule, slides, assignments, announcements. Moodle: readings and submissions. 8 / 49 Assessment The three problem sets are one argument: Component Weight Problem Set 1 15% Problem Set 2 15% Problem Set 3 15% Quiz 1 (take-home) 10% Quiz 2 (take-home) 10% Final project 30% Participation and lab 5% 1. Build a fragment of English in the logical tradition. 2. Build distributional representations – and demonstrate for yourself where they fail to compose. 3. Rebuild the fragment from PS 1 on a geometric substrate; evaluate the comparison. PS 3’s writeup asks what the geometric version cannot do. A well-argued negative result earns full credit. 9 / 49 The Semester at a Glance Sessions Part 1–6 7–10 11 12–16 17–24 25–27 Meaning as Logic Meaning as Distribution The algebraic thread in NLP Geometric Algebra (+ flex) Functional Geometric Algebra Projects Theme Assessment 1 2 2–3 3–4 5 — PS 1 Quiz 1, PS 2 Quiz 2 PS 3 Final project Session 16 is a deliberate flex session. Sessions 12–15 build a lot of mathematics quickly. If it is not landing, tell me before we get there and we slow down. Session 24 is the research frontier. Some of what we discuss there has no published answer. Final projects may take those questions on, and are graded on the quality of the investigation, not on whether the approach works. 10 / 49 Administration over. The Arc Five themes. Each one exists because the last ran out of road. 11 / 49 The Arc in One Picture no similarity 1. Logic exact composition no composition 2. Distribution similarity, learning not closed 3. Linear algebra the geometry underneath no semantics 4. Geometric alg. one invertible product 5. FGA semantics on that substrate Red labels are what is missing – the gap that forces the next move. We now walk this arc once, quickly, so you know where we are going. Then we go back to the start and do it properly. 12 / 49 Theme 1: Meaning as Logic Frege’s Principle (compositionality) The meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined. Take this seriously and two questions follow: 1 What are the meanings of the parts? 2 What is the combination operation? 13 / 49 Theme 1: Meaning as Logic Frege’s Principle (compositionality) The meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined. Take this seriously and two questions follow: 1 What are the meanings of the parts? 2 What is the combination operation? Montague’s answer (1970), which has organized formal semantics ever since: The parts are functions. The combination operation is function application. 13 / 49 Theme 1: How It Works Every expression gets a semantic type recording what it combines with. Expression Type Alice sleeps likes Alice sleeps e ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ t Denotation an individual individuals to truth values individuals to predicates a truth value Composition is application, and the types say which way round: [[likes Bob]] = (λx.λy. like(y, x))(b) ⇝ λy. like(y, b) [[Alice likes Bob]] = (λy. like(y, b))(a) ⇝ like(a, b) And Bob likes Alice gives like(b, a) – a different formula. The opening problem, solved exactly, in two steps. 14 / 49 Theme 1: What It Buys Exact structure. Argument positions are never confused. β-reduction loses nothing. Unbounded recursion. Embedding is free: Alice thinks Bob said Carol left. Truth conditions. A sentence’s meaning connects to a model – so we can ask whether it is true, and what follows from it. Entailment and inference. Every student sleeps ⇒ Alice sleeps, if Alice is a student. This falls out of the semantics rather than being stipulated. A theory of what cannot combine. Type mismatch is not falsehood; it is undefinedness. Sixty years of results, and everything we build later is measured against this. 15 / 49 Theme 1: Where It Runs Out What the logical tradition cannot say: dog and wolf are similar. Here they are just distinct constants; there is no notion of degree. How to get [[dog]] from data. The lexicon is written by hand. What a word means in context – bank by the river vs. bank with the money. Anything graded: typicality, vagueness, gradient acceptability. The gap Meaning here is structural but not substantive. We know how dog composes; we know nothing about what dog is like. This forces Theme 2. If you want similarity and learnability, meanings must live in a space with a metric – not be symbols in a lexicon. 16 / 49 Theme 2: Meaning as Distribution The distributional hypothesis Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. (Harris 1954; Firth 1957) A radical proposal: stop writing lexical entries by hand. Read meaning off the corpus. dog cat driver barked purred drove ate 42 2 0 0 51 0 1 0 63 38 44 12 Each row is a vector. dog and cat are now close – and nobody had to say so. 17 / 49 Theme 2: The Machinery 1 Raw counts are dominated by frequency. Reweight – pointwise mutual information, then PPMI: P (w, c) PMI(w, c) = log P (w)P (c) 2 The matrix is huge and sparse. Reduce it – singular value decomposition, or learn a low-dimensional embedding directly (word2vec, GloVe). 3 Similarity is geometry. The cosine of the angle between two vectors: cos(u, v) = 4 u·v ∥u∥ ∥v∥ Context can be built in. A word’s vector need not be fixed – transformers compute it from the sentence it appears in. Notice that step 3 is already linear algebra doing semantic work. Hold that thought until Theme 3. 18 / 49 Theme 2: What It Buys Similarity, for free. Nearest neighbors of dog: cat, puppy, pet, hound. Learnability. No hand-written lexicon. Point it at a corpus and it improves. Graded structure. Typicality, vagueness, and degree come out naturally, because the space has a metric. Context sensitivity. Contextual embeddings give bank different vectors in different sentences. It works. Every deployed NLP system in the world is built on this. Everything Theme 1 could not do, Theme 2 does easily. 19 / 49 Theme 2: Where It Runs Out Return to the opening problem. We have dog, bit, man. Combine them. Operation Keeps Loses u+v u⊙v [u; v] u⊗v topic shared features order order, roles order, roles order, roles; sparse overlap fixed dimension; no recursion fixed dimension – d2 , then d3 . . . The gap – the hinge of this course Vector operations either forget structure or explode in dimension. Nothing on the standard toolkit binds two meanings, keeps their roles distinct, allows the binding to be undone, and returns something the same size as what went in. This forces Theme 3. If the problem is which operations we have on vectors, the honest 20 / 49 response is to ask what operations vectors actually admit. Theme 3: Linear Algebra, Revisited You have met most of this before. We revisit it because the standard presentation hides the parts we need. Object Usually taught as What it really is vector a directed magnitude, basis-independent inner product a list of numbers P a formula, ui vi determinant a computation an oriented area or volume matrix a grid a record of where the basis went how much of u lies along v The right-hand column is what Themes 4 and 5 are built on. The left-hand column is why the connection is invisible to most people who have taken linear algebra. This is also why today’s handout weights determinants and orientation more heavily than a normal review would. 21 / 49 Theme 3: The Inner Product Loses Information u · v = ∥u∥ ∥v∥ cos θ The inner product takes two vectors and returns one number. It measures alignment. It is symmetric: u · v = v · u. Order information is destroyed. It is not invertible: from u · v = 5 you cannot recover v. It lowers dimension: two vectors in, a scalar out. This is the diagnosis from Theme 2 again – now stated about the operation rather than about the application. So: is there an operation on vectors that is not symmetric, and that can be undone? 22 / 49 Theme 3: The Determinant Knows About Order Here is the piece of linear algebra that matters most for this course – and it is usually taught as a computation.   a b det = ad − bc c d Its absolute value is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns. Its sign records orientation – swap the columns and the sign flips. It is zero exactly when the columns are dependent. An antisymmetric operation on two vectors returning an oriented magnitude. That is order information, living inside linear algebra, in plain sight. Grassmann (1844) took this seriously and built an algebra from it: the outer product a ∧ b. 23 / 49 Theme 3: What We Have, and What Is Missing Symmetric? Invertible? Grade Inner product u · v yes no lowers Outer product u ∧ v no no raises The outer product keeps order. But it still cannot be undone – from u ∧ v you cannot recover v knowing u, because a plane does not determine its factors. The gap Two operations, each throwing away half of what we need, neither invertible. And the system is not closed: the outer product of two vectors is not a vector, so there is no single space in which we can keep working. This forces Theme 4. 24 / 49 Theme 4: Geometric Algebra Clifford’s move (1878): do not choose between them. Take the sum. The geometric product ab = a ·b |{z} + symmetric, scalar a ∧ b} | {z antisymmetric, bivector An object of mixed kind – a scalar plus an oriented area. That looks strange, and it is the entire point: a a−1 = 1 where a−1 = a ∥a∥2 The geometric product is invertible. Neither of its parts is. Keeping both is exactly what makes division possible. 25 / 49 Theme 4: Grades Close the vector space under this product and you get objects of every grade: Grade Name Geometry Example in R3 0 1 2 3 scalar vector bivector trivector magnitude directed length oriented area oriented volume 3 2e1 − e3 5e12 e123 All of them live in one algebra, Cl(Rn ), and can be added and multiplied freely. The two old products become grade operations: wedge a ∧ b – raises grade: builds structure up contraction a ⌟ B – lowers grade: takes structure apart And these two are adjoint. Whatever the wedge builds, contraction is the canonical way to undo. 26 / 49 Theme 4: What It Buys Return to the requirements the composition problem left us with: Need Theme 2’s attempts Geometric algebra bind two meanings ⊗ (explodes) wedge ∧ undo a binding approximate, noisy contraction ⌟ preserve order only via ⊗ or [ ; ] antisymmetry of ∧ one carrier space — transform continuously — Cl(Rn ), all grades at once e rotors, R □ R exact Rotors deserve a note: R = e−Bθ/2 applies a rotation by multiplication, preserves grade, composes, and is differentiable in θ. A transformation you can differentiate is a transformation you can learn – which is how Theme 4 reconnects to Theme 2. 27 / 49 Theme 4: Where It Runs Out Geometric algebra is a mathematical theory. It says nothing whatever about language. Nothing in Clifford’s work tells us: which multivector should represent dog; whether grade corresponds to anything linguistic; how quantification, negation, or coercion are supposed to work; what a model is in this setting, or what makes a sentence true. The gap We have an algebra with exactly the operations the composition problem demanded – and no interpretation. A substrate without a semantics. This forces Theme 5 – and note that we are now back to the question Theme 1 answered, asked again over a different substrate. 28 / 49 Theme 5: Functional Geometric Algebra The proposal: read the operations of the algebra as the operations of a semantics. Semantics (Theme 1) Geometric algebra (Theme 4) arity of a predicate ←→ grade of a multivector argument binding ←→ wedge product ∧ function application ←→ type coercion ←→ left contraction ⌟ e rotor action R □ R individuals ←→ vectors (grade 1) n-place predicates ←→ grade-n structures If this correspondence holds up, we get Theme 1’s exact composition on Theme 2’s graded, learnable substrate. That is the whole bet. 29 / 49 Theme 5: Grade as Arity The central claim in one line: a predicate’s arity is the grade of the multivector representing it. Alice sleeps likes Type (Theme 1) Grade (Theme 5) e ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ 1 2 3 And application lowers grade, exactly as it lowers type: 3 ⌟ |{z} 1 −→ |{z} likes Bob 2 |{z} likes Bob ⌟ |{z} 1 −→ |{z} 1 Alice truth The same derivation you saw in Theme 1 – two applications, same order – but every object is now geometric, living in a metric space where similarity means something. 30 / 49 Theme 5: Coercion as Rotation A place where the geometric picture offers something the logical one does not. Type coercion in natural language: Mary began the book. (began reading it? writing it?) An object of one type is used where another is required, and the semantics repairs it. In the logical tradition this needs a type-shifting rule: a discrete, stipulated operation. In geometric algebra there is a natural candidate – a rotor: e M 7−→ R M R, R = e−Bθ/2 preserves grade – arity is unchanged ✓ continuous in θ – coercion by degree, not by fiat composable and invertible Whether this is the right analysis of coercion is exactly the sort of question this course leaves open. 31 / 49 Theme 5: What Is Actually Open I want to be straightforward about the status of this material. Settled Geometric algebra itself – 150 years old, standard mathematics Established Distributional semantics; the composition problem Proposed The FGA correspondence: grade/arity, wedge/binding, contraction/application Open Does grade give full typing, or only arity? Is contraction-based derivation confluent? How is variable binding handled – reflexives, anaphora? What is a learning objective over graded representations? Session 24 is about the last four rows, and final projects may attack any of them. You are not being asked to accept this framework – you are being asked to acquire the tools to evaluate it. Problem Set 3 explicitly asks you what it cannot do. 32 / 49 The Arc, Restated Theme Gives us Cannot give us 1 Logic exact composition, truth, inference similarity, learning 2 Distribution similarity, learning, gradedness composition 3 Linear algebra the geometry underneath a closed, invertible product 4 Geometric algebra one invertible product; grades any interpretation 5 FGA a candidate semantics on that substrate – still being worked out Each row’s last column is the next row’s reason for existing. We now go back to the top and start properly. Theme 1 begins with the machinery Montague borrowed from Church. 33 / 49 The L

title: Details of Lambda Calculus Syntax & de Bruijn Indexing
text: Conversions and de Bruijn Indexing α, β, η — and Life Without Variable Names James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 (Session 1A — supplement to Session 1) 1 / 31 Why This Supplement Session 1 introduced α, β, and η quickly, because the goal was to reach a semantic derivation before the hour ended. They deserve more care, for two reasons: They are easy to confuse. All three are written with a squiggle and relate two terms. They do quite different work, and knowing which is which will matter on Quiz 1. α is a genuine engineering problem. Renaming bound variables sounds trivial. It is the single most common source of bugs in implementations of binding, and there is a standard fix worth knowing: de Bruijn indexing. Today: the three conversions, properly distinguished and practiced; then variable names removed entirely. 2 / 31 Today 1 The three conversions, side by side 2 α: renaming, and the side condition 3 β: substitution, defined carefully 4 η: extensionality, and when it matters 5 Practice 6 Reduction strategies, and a term that never stops 7 de Bruijn indexing: variables as distances 8 β-reduction without names: shifting and substitution 9 What implementations actually do 3 / 31 The Three, Side by Side Rule Changes Reading α λx.M ≡α λy.M [x := y] the name of a bound variable renaming β (λx.M ) N ⇝ M [x := N ] performs an application computation η λx.(M x) ≡η M removes a redundant wrapper extensionality The one-line distinction: α says two terms were already the same; nothing happens. β does something – it is the computation step. η says a function that only forwards its argument is that function. Note the arrows: β is usually written as a directed reduction because it makes progress. α and η are usually written as equivalences. 4 / 31 α: Renaming α-conversion λx.M ≡α λy.M [x := y] provided y does not occur free in M Valid. λx.x ≡α λy.y λx.λy. x y ≡α λa.λb. a b λx. f x ≡α λz. f z Invalid. λx.λy. x ̸≡α λy.λy. y λx. x y ̸≡α λy. y y In the first, renaming x to y lets the inner binder capture it. In the second, y was free and has now been captured. The side condition is the whole rule. Renaming is only safe when the new name is not already in use free inside the body. 5 / 31 β: Substitution, Carefully β-reduction (λx.M ) N ⇝ M [x := N ] The subterm (λx.M ) N is called a redex (reducible expression). Substitution is defined by recursion on the term: x[x := N ] = N y[x := N ] = y (y ̸= x) (P Q)[x := N ] = (P [x := N ]) (Q[x := N ]) (λx.P )[x := N ] = λx.P (x is rebound – stop) (λy.P )[x := N ] = λy. P [x := N ] if y not free in N (λy.P )[x := N ] = λz. (P [y := z])[x := N ] otherwise, z fresh The last two lines are where α hides inside β: substitution has to rename on the fly to avoid capture. This is why the two rules cannot be separated in practice. 6 / 31 Why (λx.P )[x := N ] = λx.P This clause surprises people. Two things it is not saying. It does not give N [x := N ] replaces free occurrences of the variable x. Only the clause x[x := N ] = N ever produces N , and it fires only when the term is the variable x. Here the term is an abstraction, so a different clause applies. It does not give λx. (P [x := N ]) x has no free occurrences in λx.P . Every x inside P is bound by that very λx. Substitution touches only free occurrences, so there is nothing to replace. This is variable shadowing, and you already rely on it: let x = 1 in (\x -> x) 5 -- evaluates to 5, not 1 The inner binder wins. The outer x is invisible inside the lambda. 7 / 31 The Wrong Rule Gives the Wrong Answer Reduce (λx.λx. x) a b two ways. Correct – the inner λx rebinds, so substitution stops: (λx.λx. x) a ⇝ (λx. x)[x := a] = λx. x (λx. x) b ⇝ b Wrong – recursing into the body anyway: (λx.λx. x) a ⇝ λx. a (λx. a) b ⇝ a The two rules disagree on the final answer: b versus a. Only the first is right, because the x in the body is bound by the inner binder and therefore refers to the second argument, not the first. 8 / 31 The Three Abstraction Clauses, Reorganized All three ask the same question – what happened to x? Situation Action Clause x rebound by this binder stop (λx.P )[x := N ] = λx.P different binder, safe recurse (λy.P )[x := N ] = λy. P [x := N ] different binder, would capture rename, then recurse (λy.P )[x := N ] = λz. (P [y := z])[x := N ] The first row is the only case where substitution does no work at all. A notational aside: some presentations define substitution directly in terms of FV(M ) rather than by cases on the term’s shape. Under that definition this clause is not stipulated – it follows, since x ∈ / FV(λx.P ) by construction. 9 / 31 Capture, Once More, Slowly Reduce (λx.λy. x y) y. Wrong. Substitute blindly: (λy. x y)[x := y] = λy. y y × The argument y was a free variable – some particular thing. Now it is bound by λy and means something else entirely. Right. The final substitution clause applies, because y is free in the argument. Rename first: (λy. x y) ≡α (λz. x z) then (λz. x z)[x := y] = λz. y z ✓ The result λz. y z is a function that applies the external y to its argument. The wrong answer λy. y y is self-application. These are not remotely the same function. 10 / 31 η: Extensionality η-conversion λx.(M x) ≡η M provided x does not occur free in M Read it right to left: wrapping M in a lambda that immediately hands its argument to M changes nothing. Examples. λx. f x ≡η f λx. sleep(x) ≡η sleep Side condition needed: λx. x x ̸≡η x because x is free in the body M = x. The rule does not apply. What η asserts. Two functions that agree on every argument are the same function. That is a substantive claim – it says functions are determined by their behaviour, not their definition. 11 / 31 Does η Matter for Semantics? Usually not, and occasionally a lot. In our fragment, these are η-equivalent: sleeps = \x -> sleep x sleeps = sleep Both are fine, and you will see both styles in the Problem Set 1 scaffold. Where it does matter: Normal forms. Whether λx.f x counts as “already reduced” depends on whether η is in your calculus. Comparing denotations. Asking whether two lexical entries mean the same thing is asking whether they are βη-equivalent. Type-directed reasoning. Some type systems use η-expansion to put terms into a canonical form before comparison. An extensional theory of meaning is committed to η. An intensional one – Session 6 – may not be, since two functions can agree extensionally and differ in ways that matter for belief. 12 / 31 Which Conversion Is This? Name the conversion relating each pair. Two minutes. 1 2 3 4 5 λa. a b and λc. c b (λx. x + 1) 5 and 5 + 1 λy. g y and g λx.λy. x and λp.λq. p (λf. f a)(λz. z) and (λz. z) a 13 / 31 Which Conversion Is This? Name the conversion relating each pair. Two minutes. 1 2 3 4 5 λa. a b and λc. c b (λx. x + 1) 5 and 5 + 1 λy. g y and g λx.λy. x and λp.λq. p (λf. f a)(λz. z) and (λz. z) a Answers. 1 α – bound variable renamed; the free b untouched. 2 β – an application was performed. 3 η – redundant wrapper removed. 4 α – both binders renamed consistently. 5 β – the outer redex was reduced. The test: did anything get computed (β)? Was only a name changed (α)? Did a layer disappear (η)? 13 / 31 Practice: Reduce to Normal Form 1 (λx.λy. y x) a b 2 3 (λf.λx. f (f x)) (λy. y) c  (λx. x) (λy. y) (λz. z) 4 (λx.λy. x y) (λw. w) d 14 / 31 Practice: Reduce to Normal Form 1 (λx.λy. y x) a b 2 3 (λf.λx. f (f x)) (λy. y) c  (λx. x) (λy. y) (λz. z) 4 (λx.λy. x y) (λw. w) d Answers. 1 (λy. y a) b ⇝ b a 2 (λx. (λy.y)((λy.y) x)) c ⇝ (λy.y)((λy.y) c) ⇝ c 3 (λx.x)(λz.z) ⇝ λz. z 4 (λy. (λw.w) y) d ⇝ (λw.w) d ⇝ d Item 4 is worth a second look: the intermediate term λy. (λw.w) y is η-equivalent to λw. w, so you could have shortcut. Whether that is allowed depends on whether η is in your calculus. 14 / 31 A Term That Never Stops Ω = (λx. x x) (λx. x x) Reduce it: (λx. x x) (λx. x x) ⇝ (λx. x x) (λx. x x) ⇝ · · · It reduces to itself. There is no normal form. The untyped lambda calculus is Turing complete, so non-termination is unavoidable. The simply typed lambda calculus – the one we use for semantics – is strongly normalizing: every term reduces to a normal form, in finitely many steps, whatever order you choose. Try to type λx. x x. You need x : ⟨σ, τ ⟩ and x : σ simultaneously, so σ = ⟨σ, τ ⟩ – an infinite type. Types rule out exactly the terms that misbehave, which is one more reason semantics uses them. 15 / 31 Reduction Strategies When a term has several redexes, which do you reduce first? Strategy Reduces Analogue Normal order leftmost, outermost first lazy evaluation Applicative order leftmost, innermost first eager evaluation Example. (λx. a) Ω Normal order: reduce the outer redex, discarding Ω unevaluated ⇝ a. Terminates. Applicative order: evaluate the argument Ω first ⇝ never terminates. Church–Rosser guarantees that if two strategies both terminate, they agree. It does not guarantee both terminate. Normal order finds a normal form whenever one exists. Haskell is lazy, so it is closer to normal order – which is why undefined in an unused position does not crash the Problem Set 1 test harness. 16 / 31 The Trouble With Names Every implementation of the lambda calculus has to deal with α. That means: Equality is not syntactic. Deciding whether λx.λy. x and λp.λq. p are the same term requires an α-equivalence check, not a structural comparison. Substitution must generate fresh names. You need a supply of unused variables, and “unused” means unused anywhere relevant – a global condition inside a local operation. Capture bugs are silent. A missing freshness check does not crash. It produces a well-formed term with the wrong meaning. What if we simply did not have names? 17 / 31 de Bruijn’s Idea Replace each variable occurrence by a number: how many binders you must cross, going outward, to reach the one that binds it. Named de Bruijn Why λx. x λx.λy. x λx.λy. y λx.λy. x y λx. x (λy. x y) λ. 0 λ.λ. 1 λ.λ. 0 λ.λ. 1 0 λ. 0 (λ. 1 0) bound by the nearest binder cross one binder to reach λx bound by the nearest same x, two depths Note the last row. The same variable gets different indices depending on depth. The index is a distance, not a name. After N. G. de Bruijn, who introduced the notation in 1972 for Automath. 18 / 31 The Payoff λx.λy. x and λp.λq. p are α-equivalent but syntactically different. In de Bruijn notation, both are: λ.λ. 1 α-equivalence becomes syntactic identity. Two terms are α-equivalent exactly when their de Bruijn representations are the same string. The α rule disappears – not because it was solved, but because it can no longer be stated. This is the same design lesson we will meet again in Session 6A: choose a representation in which things that mean the same thing are the same thing. Canonical form eliminates a whole class of problems rather than managing it. 19 / 31 Free Variables Need a Context λx. x y has a free y. What index does it get? Free variables are numbered by continuing to count outward past the outermost binder, relative to a fixed naming context Γ. With Γ = [y, z] (so y is nearest, then z): Named de Bruijn Reading y z λx. x y λx.λw. y 0 1 λ. 0 1 λ.λ. 2 first in the context second in the context inside one binder, y shifts up by one inside two binders This is the price: the representation of a free variable depends on its depth. Closed terms – which is what our lexical entries are – avoid the issue entirely. 20 / 31 Practice: Translate Convert to de Bruijn notation. All are closed. 1 2 3 4 λx.λy.λz. x z (y z) λf.λx. f (f x) λx. (λy. y) x λa.λb. b (λc. a) 21 / 31 Practice: Translate Convert to de Bruijn notation. All are closed. 1 2 3 4 λx.λy.λz. x z (y z) λf.λx. f (f x) λx. (λy. y) x λa.λb. b (λc. a) Answers. 1 λ.λ.λ. 2 0 (1 0) 2 λ.λ. 1 (1 0) 3 λ. (λ. 0) 0 4 λ.λ. 0 (λ. 2) Item 4: inside three binders, a is two levels out from λc, so index 2. Count binders crossed, not variables. 21 / 31 β-Reduction Without Names Substitution now has to renumber, because removing a binder changes every distance beneath it. Shifting ↑dc – add d to every free index, with cutoff c ( k if k < c (bound below the cutoff) ↑dc (k) = k + d otherwise ↑dc (λ. t) = λ. ↑dc+1 (t) ↑dc (t1 t2 ) =↑dc (t1 ) (one more binder, raise the cutoff) ↑dc (t2 ) Intuition. The cutoff c separates indices that point inside the term being moved (leave alone) from those that point outside it (adjust). This is the bookkeeping that variable names were hiding. It has not gone away – it has become arithmetic, which is at least mechanical and testable. 22 / 31 Substitution and the β Rule Substitution [j 7→ s] t – replace index j by term s [j 7→ s] k = s if k = j, else k [j 7→ s] (λ. t) = λ. [j + 1 7→↑10 (s)] t   [j 7→ s] (t1 t2 ) = [j 7→ s] t1 [j 7→ s] t2 Going under a binder: the target index goes up by one, and the substituted term must be shifted, since it is now one level deeper. β-reduction   1 (λ. t1 ) t2 ⇝ ↑−1 [0 → 7 ↑ (t )] t 1 0 2 0 Shift the argument up (it is entering a binder), substitute for index 0, then shift the whole 23 / 31 result down (the binder is gone). A Worked Reduction Reduce (λ. 0 0) (λ. 0) – that is, (λx. x x)(λy. y). Here t1 = 0 0 and t2 = λ. 0. Step 1 – shift the argument up. ↑10 (λ. 0) = λ. ↑11 (0) = λ. 0 (index 0 is below the cutoff 1, so unchanged) Step 2 – substitute for index 0. [0 7→ λ.0] (0 0) = (λ. 0) (λ. 0) Step 3 – shift the result down.  (λ.0)(λ.0) = (λ. 0) (λ. 0) ↑−1 0 Result: (λ. 0)(λ. 0), which reduces again to λ. 0 – the identity. Matches (λx.x x)(λy.y) ⇝ λy. y. ✓ 24 / 31 What Have We Bought? Named de Bruijn α-equivalence a relation to check string equality Fresh name supply required not needed Capture avoidance a side condition to remember built into shifting Substitution rename-then-substitute arithmetic Readability good poor Error messages meaningful names numbers The trade is clear. Correctness and canonicity, at the cost of human legibility. So the standard engineering answer is: parse into de Bruijn, compute in de Bruijn, print back with names. The user never sees an index; the implementation never sees a name. 25 / 31 Variations You May Meet Scheme Idea Used because de Bruijn indices count binders from the inside out canonical, standard de Bruijn levels count from the outside in stable under weakening Locally nameless indices for bound, names for free best of both; common in proof assistants HOAS reuse the host language’s binders substitution comes free Locally nameless is worth knowing about: bound variables get indices (so α is trivial), free variables keep names (so error messages stay readable). Coq and many Agda developments use it. HOAS – higher-order abstract syntax – represents object-language binders using the implementation language’s lambda. You get capture-avoiding substitution for free, at the cost of no longer being able to inspect the body structurally. 26 / 31 Why You Will Not Do This in Problem Set 1 Reassuring news: the scaffold requires none of this machinery. likes :: TV likes = \obj subj -> (subj, obj) ‘elem‘ likePairs Haskell’s own binding does the work. When you write \x -> ..., GHC handles renaming, capture avoidance, and substitution. You are borrowing a correct implementation. That is precisely the argument for writing semantics in a functional language: the lambda calculus you are studying is the language you are writing in, so its metatheory is the compiler’s problem rather than yours. GHC does not use de Bruijn indices internally – it uses names paired with unique integers – but the problem it is solving is the one on the last several slides. 27 / 31 Forward: Binding Will Come Back Two threads from today run to the end of the course. 1 Canonical representations matter. de Bruijn eliminates α by making equivalent things identical. Session 6A shows the same move in λ-DCS, where implicit variables eliminate spurious ambiguity for a semantic parser. Same lesson, different century. 2 Variable binding is a real mechanism, not a triviality. It needs shifting, freshness, and capture avoidance – an entire apparatus. When Part IV proposes that the wedge product implements “binding”, the question to ask is: which binding? The wedge binds a role to a filler. λ binds a variable, with capture avoidance and the ability to be used twice. Those are different operations sharing a word, and whether the geometric one can do the work of the logical one is an open question – and a candidate final project. 28 / 31 Summary Concept Key point α β η Substitution Ω Normal order de Bruijn index Payoff Shifting β in de Bruijn Practice renaming a bound variable; nothing is computed the computation step; substitution with capture avoidance extensionality; a pure forwarder is the function recursive; the hard clause renames on the fly untyped terms may not normalize; typed ones always do outermost first; finds a normal form if one exists distance to the binder, counted in binders crossed α-equivalence becomes string equality renumbering when a term crosses a binder shift up, substitute at 0, shift down parse to indices, compute, print with names 29 / 31 Reading and Exercises Reading: EU Chapter 2, for the conversions in the semantic setting Pierce, Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 6 – the definitive short treatment of de Bruijn indices and shifting Barendregt, The Lambda Calculus – if you want the full metatheory Exercises (not collected, but Quiz 1 will resemble them): 1 2 3 Translate the Session 1 practice terms into de Bruijn notation and reduce them there. Check that the answers agree.  Show ↑−1 ↑10 (t) = t for any t. Why does the reverse order fail? 0 Give two terms that are β-equivalent but not η-equivalent, and two that are η-equivalent but not β-equivalent. 30 / 31 Questions? title: Lecture 2 — Semantic Types
text: Session 2: Semantic Types and Type-Driven Interpretation What Can Combine With What James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics September 1, 2026 1 / 36 Where We Were Last session. Meanings are functions; composition is β-reduction. We derived [[Alice likes Bob]] = like(a, b) in two steps, and the word-order problem from the opening slide dissolved. But nothing stopped us writing nonsense. [[Alice]]([[Bob]]) is a perfectly well-formed untyped term. The calculus has no opinion about it. Today’s move Assign every expression a type. Composition is licensed only when types fit. Ill-formed combination stops being wrong and becomes impossible. 2 / 36 Today 1 The type system: two basic types, one constructor 2 Types for lexical categories – and what the assignment commits us to 3 Composition: function application, and why types determine direction 4 Worked derivations, with trees 5 When application is not enough: predicate modification 6 Adjectives, and how they stress the system 7 Type mismatch, and type shifting 8 Models: what makes a sentence true 9 Where types break: quantification Throughout: watch for the two things a type records – arity and sort. Theme 5 recovers one of them geometrically and struggles with the other. 3 / 36 Two Basic Types Every expression of the language gets a semantic type. Two are basic: Type Denotes Domain e an individual (entity) De – the domain of discourse t a truth value Dt = {0, 1} Examples. Alice, Bob, the dog – type e Alice sleeps, Bob likes Alice – type t Proper names denote individuals. Sentences denote truth values. Everything else in the language is a function built out of these two. That is a strong claim, and the rest of this session is about how far it gets us. 4 / 36 The Type Constructor The type inventory, defined recursively 1 e and t are types. 2 If σ and τ are types, then ⟨σ, τ ⟩ is a type: the type of functions from Dσ to Dτ . 3 Nothing else is a type. One base case, one constructor, one closure clause – the same shape as the definition of lambda terms last session, and the same shape as most definitions you will meet this semester. The domains follow the types: D⟨σ,τ ⟩ = DτDσ = { f | f : Dσ → Dτ } Note how fast this grows. If |De | = 4, then |D⟨e,t⟩ | = 24 = 16, and |D⟨⟨e,t⟩,t⟩ | = 216 = 65,536. 5 / 36 Reading Type Notation Types are right-associative and the brackets are often dropped: ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ is often written e → (e → t) or just e→e→t Read it as a recipe. e → e → t says: give me an individual, then another individual, and I will give you a truth value. Montague notation Arrow notation Haskell (PS 1) e t ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ e t e→t e→e→t (e → t) → t Entity Bool Entity -> Bool Entity -> Entity -> Bool (Entity -> Bool) -> Bool The third column is not an analogy. In Problem Set 1 the Haskell type is the semantic type, and the compiler enforces it. 6 / 36 The Type Hierarchy Type Denotes Linguistic example e individuals Alice, the dog t truth values Alice sleeps ⟨e, t⟩ sets of individuals sleeps, dog, tall ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ binary relations likes, read ⟨e, ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩⟩ ternary relations gave sets of sets every student, someone predicate modifiers quickly, former determiners every, some, no truth-value operators not connectives and, or ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ ⟨t, t⟩ ⟨t, ⟨t, t⟩⟩ The bottom half is where things get interesting – and where the naive picture (“meanings are things and predicates apply to them”) breaks down. 7 / 36 Types for Lexical Categories Category Proper name Common noun Intransitive verb Transitive verb Ditransitive verb Adjective (intersective) Sentence Type e ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ t Denotation a λx. student(x) λx. sleep(x) λx.λy. like(y, x) λz.λx.λy. give(y, x, z) λx. tall(x) like(a, b) Two things to notice. Common nouns and intransitive verbs share a type. Semantically, dog and sleeps are the same kind of object: a one-place predicate. The transitive verb takes its object first. This is a choice, and the next slides show why it is the right one. 8 / 36 Aside: Semantic Type is Not Syntactic Category dog is a noun; sleeps is a verb. Syntactically they behave completely differently. Semantically, both are functions from individuals to truth values. dog sleeps tall asleep Syntactic category Semantic type N V A A ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ The map from categories to types is many-to-one. Semantics is coarser than syntax – it cares only about what an expression combines with, not how it is spelled or where it may occur. This is why a semantic theory needs a syntax alongside it, related by a homomorphism. 9 / 36 Compositionality, Stated Precisely Last session’s informal version: the meaning of the whole is determined by the meanings of the parts and how they are combined. The precise version: Compositionality as homomorphism There is a map [[·]] from syntactic structures to meanings such that for every syntactic rule combining α and β into γ, there is a semantic operation F with  [[γ]] = F [[α]], [[β]] Three consequences. Meaning attaches to structures, not strings. Ambiguous strings get several structures. F depends only on the rule, not on the particular words. List the rules and the lexicon, and you have specified infinitely many sentences. 10 / 36 The Composition Rule Function Application (FA) If α has type ⟨σ, τ ⟩ and β has type σ, then α(β) has type τ , and  [[α β]] = [[α]] [[β]] That is the whole composition rule for now. One rule. And here is the key property. Given two expressions with known types, there is generally only one way to combine them. The types determine which is the function and which is the argument. ⟨e, t⟩ applied to e ✓ e applied to ⟨e, t⟩ × We never have to say that the verb applies to the subject. The type assignment already said it. 11 / 36 Derivation Tree: Alice sleeps sleep(a) : t a:e Alice λx.sleep(x) : ⟨e, t⟩ sleeps Reading the tree bottom-up: 1 The lexicon supplies a of type e and λx.sleep(x) of type ⟨e, t⟩. 2 Only one application typechecks: ⟨e, t⟩ takes e. 3 (λx.sleep(x))(a) ⇝ sleep(a), of type t. ✓ We draw the subject on the left because that is the syntax. The semantics does not care – it reads the types. 12 / 36 Currying, and Why the Object Comes First Recall from last session: the calculus has only one-argument functions, so a two-place relation is a function returning a function. [[likes]] = λx.λy. like(y, x) : ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ The first argument x is the object; the second y is the subject. Why that order? Because English builds the verb phrase first: [S Alice [V P likes Bob ] ] Applying to the object first gives us a constituent of type ⟨e, t⟩ – exactly the type of an intransitive verb. The VP is a one-place predicate, and the rest of the derivation cannot tell whether it came from sleeps or from likes Bob. Partial application is phrase structure. This is not a coincidence – it is why the typed lambda calculus fits natural language as well as it does. 13 / 36 Derivation Tree: Alice likes Bob like(a, b) : t a:e Alice λy.like(y, b) : ⟨e, t⟩ λxλy.like(y, x) : ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ likes Step 1. (λx.λy. like(y, x))(b) ⇝ λy. like(y, b) Step 2. (λy. like(y, b))(a) ⇝ like(a, b) b:e Bob – type ⟨e, t⟩ – type t ✓ And Bob likes Alice gives like(b, a). The two argument positions are never confused, at any depth of embedding. 14 / 36 Structure Matters: Bracketing Compositionality assigns meaning to structures. Different bracketings give different meanings. Alice gave Bob a book. [[gave]] = λz.λx.λy. give(y, x, z) : ⟨e, ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩⟩ Three applications, in a fixed order: [[gave a book]] = λx.λy. give(y, x, bk) [[gave Bob a book]] = λy. give(y, b, bk) [[Alice gave Bob a book]] = give(a, b, bk) : ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ : ⟨e, t⟩ :t Each step strips one λ and lowers the type by one arrow. Keep this shape in mind. In Session 18 the same derivation runs with grades 4, 3, 2, 1 in place of these types, and contraction in place of application. 15 / 36 When Application Is Not Enough Consider tall student. [[tall]] : ⟨e, t⟩ [[student]] : ⟨e, t⟩ Neither can apply to the other. ⟨e, t⟩ applied to ⟨e, t⟩ does not typecheck – the function wants an e and is being handed a function. Two possible responses: 1 Change the type of tall to ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩, so it takes the noun as argument. 2 Keep both at ⟨e, t⟩ and add a second composition rule. Both are used in the literature. We take (2) for now, and return to (1) when we look at adjectives more carefully. 16 / 36 Predicate Modification Predicate Modification (PM) If α and β are both of type ⟨e, t⟩, then [[α β]] = λx. [[α]](x) ∧ [[β]](x) : ⟨e, t⟩ Set-theoretically this is intersection: tall student denotes the tall things intersected with the students. tall student tall student We now have two rules: FA and PM. You implement both in Problem Set 1. Keep them general – a composition rule that mentions a particular word is not a composition rule. 17 / 36 Adjectives Are Not All Alike Predicate modification works for tall student. It fails badly elsewhere. Class Example Entailment pattern Intersective Norwegian student is Norwegian ✓ and is a student ✓ Subsective skillful surgeon is skillful ? and is a surgeon ✓ Non-subsective former senator is former × and is a senator × Privative fake diamond is a diamond × Norwegian student = Norwegians ∩ students. PM is exactly right. Skillful surgeon is not skillful-things ∩ surgeons – skill is relative to the activity. A skillful surgeon may be a terrible violinist. Former senator is not in the set of senators at all. Intersection gives the wrong answer. For the last three, the adjective must take the noun as its argument: type ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩. 18 / 36 What the Adjective Data Tells Us Class Type Rule Intersective ⟨e, t⟩ PM Subsective ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ FA Non-subsective ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ FA An uncomfortable consequence. The same syntactic position – prenominal adjective – now corresponds to two different semantic types, and which applies depends on the word. This is a genuine tension in the framework, not a detail. Either we complicate the type assignment, or we complicate the composition rules, or we let the lexicon carry the distinction. All three moves appear in the literature. Generative Lexicon theory – which we return to in Session 10 – is one response: enrich what a lexical entry contains, so that the composition can be predicted rather than stipulated. 19 / 36 Type Mismatch Is Compositional Failure What happens if we try to combine things that do not fit? [[Alice]] [[Bob]]  — type e applied to type e There is no rule that licenses this. The derivation does not produce a wrong answer; it produces no answer at all. The point In a typed system, ill-formed combinations are not false – they are undefined. The type discipline is a theory of what can compose with what, and it is prior to any question of truth. When you write the fragment in Problem Set 1, the Haskell type checker enforces exactly this. A type error is not an obstacle to the exercise. It is the exercise telling you that you have combined two meanings that cannot combine. 20 / 36 Sometimes Mismatch Should Be Repaired Not every mismatch is an error. Consider: Alice and every student left. Alice is type e; every student is type ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩. Conjunction demands two things of the same type. Partee’s response (1987): allow expressions to shift type by general, meaning-preserving operations. LIFT lift : e −→ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ lift(x) = λP. P (x) Alice becomes the set of properties Alice has. Now both conjuncts are ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ and conjunction proceeds. Note that lift(x) applied to P β-reduces straight back to P (x). Nothing is lost – the shift is 21 / 36 a repackaging. The Type-Shifting Landscape ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ lift lower be e ident ⟨e, t⟩ Partee’s triangle: three types that noun phrases can occupy, with systematic maps between them. lift: x 7→ λP.P (x) – Alice as a generalized quantifier ident: x 7→ λy.(y = x) – Alice as a predicate, for That is Alice lower: the partial inverse of lift Hold onto this slide. These shifts are discrete, stipulated operations – a finite list of repairs. In Session 21 we ask whether a rotor could do this work continuously instead, with θ interpolating between the source and target readings. 22 / 36 What a Type Records Step back. The type ⟨σ, τ ⟩ encodes two independent things: Arity Sort What it records Example how many arguments, in what order what kind each must be likes takes 2 and takes truth values These come apart. ⟨e, t⟩ and ⟨t, t⟩ have the same arity and different sorts – and the type system keeps them apart. A pointer to the end of the course Theme 5 proposes that grade in a geometric algebra plays the role of type. But grade is a number: it records arity and nothing else. Whether sortal distinctions can be recovered geometrically – from basis structure, subspaces, or signature – is an open question, and a candidate final project. 23 / 36 From Formulas to Truth We can now derive like(a, b) from Alice likes Bob. But is it true? That question has no answer until we say what the symbols refer to.
