A model M = ⟨D, I⟩ D – a non-empty set, the domain of individuals I – an interpretation function assigning, to each constant, an object of the right type: constants of type e 7→ members of D constants of type ⟨e, t⟩ 7→ functions D → {0, 1} and so on, by type Denotation is always relative to a model: we write [[α]]M . Meaning, in this tradition, is a systematic relation between expressions and a structure. The lambda calculus builds the expressions; the model supplies the world. 24 / 36 A Small Model D = {Alice, Bob, Carol, Fido} Constant Interpretation a, b student dog sleep like Alice, Bob {Alice, Bob, Carol} {Fido} {Carol, Fido} {(Alice, Bob), (Alice, Fido), (Bob, Fido)} Now we can evaluate: [[Alice likes Bob]]M = like(a, b) = 1 true [[Alice sleeps]]M = sleep(a) = 0 false This is essentially the model you will work with in Problem Set 1, slightly extended. 25 / 36 Predicates: Sets or Functions? I have written sleep two ways – as a set {Carol, Fido} and as a function of type ⟨e, t⟩. These are the same thing. Characteristic function A subset S ⊆ D corresponds to χS : D → {0, 1} with χS (x) = 1 iff x ∈ S. Set talk Function talk Type S⊆D R⊆D×D S ∩ S′ S ⊆ S′ χS : D → {0, 1} curried D → (D → {0, 1}) λx. χS (x) ∧ χS ′ (x) ∀x. χS (x) → χS ′ (x) ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ t Sets are easier to write down; functions compose. In Problem Set 1 the model is given as sets and the denotations as functions, and a helper converts between them. 26 / 36 Variables and Assignments One loose end. What is the denotation of an expression containing a free variable? [[sleep(x)]]M = ? There is no answer – x does not refer to anything until we say what it refers to. Assignment function An assignment g maps variables to objects of the appropriate type. Denotation is relative to a model and an assignment: [[α]]M,g . [[x]]M,g = g(x) [[λx.α]]M,g = the function d 7→ [[α]]M,g[x7→d] Here g[x 7→ d] is g modified to send x to d. For closed terms – which is what our lexical entries are – the assignment makes no difference, and we suppress it. It becomes essential in Session 3, when quantifiers bind variables. 27 / 36 Practice Using the model from two slides back, compute: 1 2 3 4 5 [[Bob likes Fido]]M [[Carol sleeps]]M The denotation of sleeping student (as a set) What type does likes Alice have, and what is its denotation as a set? Is Alice likes Alice true? 28 / 36 Practice Using the model from two slides back, compute: 1 2 3 4 5 [[Bob likes Fido]]M [[Carol sleeps]]M The denotation of sleeping student (as a set) What type does likes Alice have, and what is its denotation as a set? Is Alice likes Alice true? Answers. 1 like(b, Fido) = 1 true 2 sleep(Carol) = 1 true 3 {Alice, Bob, Carol} ∩ {Carol, Fido} = {Carol} 4 Type ⟨e, t⟩; denotation {x : (x, Alice) ∈ like} = ∅ – nobody likes Alice here. 5 (Alice, Alice) ∈ / like, so false. 28 / 36 The Problem: Quantified Noun Phrases Everything so far has been smooth. Here is where it stops. Every student sleeps. Alice sleeps worked because Alice is type e. So let us try type e for every student. It fails, for at least three reasons: There is no single individual that every student refers to. Every student sleeps does not mean sleep(some particular person). No student sleeps would need to refer to a non-existent individual. 29 / 36 The Problem: Quantified Noun Phrases Everything so far has been smooth. Here is where it stops. Every student sleeps. Alice sleeps worked because Alice is type e. So let us try type e for every student. It fails, for at least three reasons: There is no single individual that every student refers to. Every student sleeps does not mean sleep(some particular person). No student sleeps would need to refer to a non-existent individual. And a fourth, decisive one: Every student sleeps and Alice sleeps have the same syntax. If the semantics is compositional, they must combine by the same rule. 29 / 36 Montague’s Resolution If every student cannot be the argument, make it the function. [[every student]] = λP. ∀x [ student(x) → P (x) ] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ A generalized quantifier: a function from predicates to truth values. Equivalently, a set of sets – the sets that contain all the students. Now composition runs the other way:  [[Every student sleeps]] = [[every student]] [[sleeps]] ⇝ ∀x [ student(x) → sleep(x) ] Type t. ✓ And the composition rule is still just FA. The type determined which expression is the function. That is the deepest lesson of this session: we do not stipulate the direction of application; the type assignment does it for us. 30 / 36 And the Determiner Itself If every student is ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ and student is ⟨e, t⟩, then every must be [[every]] = λQ.λP. ∀x [ Q(x) → P (x) ] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ A function from a predicate (the restrictor) to a generalized quantifier. Determiner Denotation every λQ.λP. ∀x [ Q(x) → P (x) ] some, a λQ.λP. ∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] no λQ.λP. ¬∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] You will implement all three in Problem Set 1. Note that no can be defined in terms of some – and that the pattern λQ.λP is the same in all three; only the logical skeleton changes. 31 / 36 What This Sets Up Generalized quantifiers are the price of compositionality – and they buy something expensive. Every student read a book. Two quantifiers in one sentence. Which takes scope over which? Surface (∀ > ∃): each student read some book, possibly different ones. Inverse (∃ > ∀): one particular book was read by every student. Two readings, same words, same syntax. The types alone do not tell us which derivation to run. Session 5 is about this – and it is the capstone of Theme 1, because scope is where composition stops being mechanical and starts requiring a theory. 32 / 36 Summary Concept Key point Basic types Type constructor What a type records Function application Predicate modification Adjective classes Type mismatch Type shifting Model ⟨D, I⟩ Assignment g Generalized quantifiers e (individuals), t (truth values) ⟨σ, τ ⟩, applied recursively; one rule builds all types arity and sort – and these come apart the composition rule; types determine its direction for two ⟨e, t⟩ meanings; set intersection intersective / subsective / non-subsective need different types not falsehood – undefinedness. Composition simply fails lift, ident, lower: discrete, stipulated repairs supplies the world; denotation is relative to it needed once variables are free; essential from Session 3 NPs of type ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩; the NP becomes the function 33 / 36 Three Threads to Carry Forward 1 Types determine direction. We never stipulate which expression applies to which. This is the property Theme 5 must reproduce if grade is to do the work of type. 2 Arity and sort are different. Grade is a number and records only arity. Whether sortal distinctions survive the move to geometry is open. 3 Coercion is currently a stipulation. Partee’s shifts are a finite list of repairs applied when composition fails. Session 21

title: Lecture 2 — Computational Semantics from the NLP Perspective
text: Compositional Semantics from an NLP Perspective Types, Lambdas, and Categorial Grammar (companion to Session 2) James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics September 1, 2026 1 / 42 About This Deck Session 2 developed semantic types the way a formal semanticist would: Frege, Montague, denotations, models. This companion deck covers the same machinery the way a computational linguist would: starting from a task, building toward a system, and using the notation that dominates the NLP literature. Starts from Syntax-semantics Motivation Extra material Session 2 This deck compositionality phrase structure + rules what meaning is — a database query task CCG categories what a system must compute events, semantic roles, learning Same lambda calculus. Same types. Different door into the building. Use whichever one makes the ideas stick. 2 / 42 Today 1 A task: answering questions against a database 2 Meaning representations, and what we want from them 3 Where do logical forms come from? The composition problem 4 Lambda calculus as glue 5 Types, and why they earn their keep 6 Combinatory Categorial Grammar 7 Events and semantic roles 8 Learning, and why any of this survives the LLM era 3 / 42 Start With a Task You have a database of US geography. A user types: What states border Texas? Your system has to turn that string into something executable. What states border Texas? parse λx. state(x) ∧ borders(x, tx) execute {NM, OK, AR, LA} The middle box is a meaning representation. Everything in this deck is about how to build it – systematically, for sentences nobody has seen before. 4 / 42 Why Not Just Pattern-Match? A first instinct: write templates. "What states border X?" "What states are in X?" -> -> state(?) & borders(?, X) state(?) & in(?, X) This works. Briefly. Query Problem What states border Texas and Oklahoma? conjunction inside the argument What is the largest state bordering Texas? superlative over a filtered set What states border states that border Texas? recursion The last row is fatal. Language nests without bound, so no finite template list can cover it. We need to build meanings out of parts – which is to say, we need compositionality, whether or not we call it that. 5 / 42 What We Want From a Meaning Representation 1 Unambiguous. One representation per reading. If a sentence has two readings, we should get two representations. 2 Executable. We can run it against a database, knowledge base, or model and get an answer. 3 Compositional. Built from the parts, so novel sentences work. 4 Inference-supporting. If Texas borders Oklahoma, we should be able to derive Some state borders Oklahoma. 5 Canonical. Paraphrases should ideally converge. First-order logic SQL AMR Raw embeddings Unambig. Exec. Comp. Infer. Canon. ✓ ✓ partial — ✓ ✓ — — ✓ partial partial — ✓ — partial — partial — ✓ — The last row is Part II of this course, and its empty middle column is the whole problem. 6 / 42 Other Meaning Representations You Will Meet Formalism Looks like Used for FOL / lambda calculus λx.state(x) ∧ borders(x, tx) QA, semantic parsing SQL SELECT ... database interfaces SPARQL triple patterns knowledge graphs Lambda-DCS State ⊓ Border.Texas Freebase QA AMR rooted labelled graph broad-coverage annotation Python / API calls get states(borders="TX") tool use, agents WHERE ... They differ in expressiveness and in what they can be executed against. They do not differ in the compositional problem: every one of them has to be built from a sentence, and the building is the hard part. Learn the lambda calculus version and the rest are notation. That is why this course spends its time there. 7 / 42 An AMR, for Comparison Alice read the book in the library. The corresponding logical form: read-01 ∃e [ read(e) ∧ arg0(e, alice) ARG0 Alice ARG1 book location library ∧ arg1(e, book) ∧ loc(e, library) ] An AMR is a neo-Davidsonian logical form, drawn as a graph. Nodes are the event and its participants; edges are the role predicates. AMR deliberately drops quantifier scope, tense, and articles – which makes it annotatable at scale, and unable to distinguish the two readings of Every student read a book. A real engineering tradeoff, and worth knowing about. 8 / 42 First-Order Logic as the Target Sentence Logical form Texas borders Oklahoma borders(tx, ok) Texas is a state state(tx) What states border Texas? λx. state(x) ∧ borders(x, tx) Every state borders a state ∀x[state(x) → ∃y[state(y) ∧ borders(x, y)]] No state borders Hawaii ¬∃x[state(x) ∧ borders(x, hi)] Constants (tx, ok) name entities in the database. Predicates (state, borders) name tables or columns. Variables (x, y) are what the query returns or quantifies over. Note row three: a question is a one-place predicate. Executing it means finding everything that satisfies it – exactly a SELECT ... WHERE. 9 / 42 The Database Is the Model Session 3 will define a model as a domain plus an interpretation function. In this setting, that is just your data. Logic Database Example domain D constant 1-place predicate 2-place predicate truth value the set of rows/entities a primary key a table, or a column filter a join table query returns rows or not all 50 states, cities, rivers tx 7→ row Texas state(x) borders(x,y) Model-theoretic semantics is not an abstraction here – it is the specification of what your query engine does. “Truth in a model” is “the row is present”. Historically this is GeoQuery (Zelle & Mooney 1996) and ATIS – the datasets that made semantic parsing a subfield. 10 / 42 The Problem: Where Do Logical Forms Come From? We know what we want: Texas borders Oklahoma −→ borders(tx, ok) We know the words contribute pieces: Texas tx Oklahoma ok borders borders( , ) But how does a piece with holes in it combine with a piece that fills a hole? We need notation for “a formula with a labelled gap”. That is exactly what lambda abstraction is. 11 / 42 Lambda Notation in Sixty Seconds λx. φ means “the function that takes x and returns φ” Application substitutes the argument for the variable: (λx. state(x))(tx) ⇝ state(tx) Two arguments means two nested lambdas: λy. λx. borders(x, y) and you apply them one at a time: (λy.λx. borders(x, y))(ok) ⇝ λx. borders(x, ok) That intermediate result – λx. borders(x, ok) – is the meaning of the verb phrase borders Oklahoma. It is a formula with one gap left. 12 / 42 Partial Application Is Phrase Structure Expression Lambda term Gaps left borders λy.λx. borders(x, y) 2 borders Oklahoma λx. borders(x, ok) 1 Texas borders Oklahoma borders(tx, ok) 0 Every application fills one gap, and each intermediate result corresponds to a real constituent of the sentence. The lambda calculus was not designed for language, but partial application lines up exactly with phrase structure – which is why it became the standard glue for semantic parsing. Note the object comes first in the lexical entry, so that applying it once gives you the VP. 13 / 42 A Full Derivation Texas borders Oklahoma. Lexicon. Texas ⇝ tx Oklahoma ⇝ ok borders ⇝ λy.λx. borders(x, y) Step 1 – verb + object. (λy.λx. borders(x, y))(ok) ⇝ λx. borders(x, ok) Step 2 – VP + subject. (λx. borders(x, ok))(tx) ⇝ borders(tx, ok) Executable. Two reductions. And Oklahoma borders Texas gives borders(ok, tx) – a different query, as it should be. 14 / 42 A Question, Derived What states border Texas? states ⇝ λx. state(x) border Texas ⇝ λx. borders(x, tx) what ⇝ conjoin two one-place predicates λx. state(x) ∧ borders(x, tx) Executing it means: iterate over the domain, keep the x that satisfy the body. SELECT s.name FROM states s JOIN borders b ON s.id = b.state1 WHERE b.state2 = ’Texas’; The logical form and the SQL are the same query. One is compositional and one is not – which is why we generate the first and compile to the second. 15 / 42 Practice: Build the Logical Form Give a lambda term for each. Assume predicates state, city, river, borders, in, large. 1 2 3 4 5 Oklahoma borders Texas large states cities in Texas states bordering Texas large cities in states bordering Texas 16 / 42 Practice: Build the Logical Form Give a lambda term for each. Assume predicates state, city, river, borders, in, large. 1 2 3 4 5 Oklahoma borders Texas large states cities in Texas states bordering Texas large cities in states bordering Texas Answers. 1 borders(ok, tx) 2 λx. state(x) ∧ large(x) 3 λx. city(x) ∧ in(x, tx) 4 λx. state(x) ∧ borders(x, tx) 5 λx. city(x) ∧ large(x) ∧ ∃y[state(y) ∧ borders(y, tx) ∧ in(x, y)] Item 5 is the point: a relative clause introduces a fresh variable and an existential. No template could have produced it, but composition does – one word at a time. 16 / 42 The Pattern in Items 2–4 Every one of those had the same shape: λx. noun(x) ∧ modifier(x) | {z } | {z } restrictor filter Two one-place predicates, conjoined. But recall the type rule: ⟨e, t⟩ cannot apply to ⟨e, t⟩. The second composition rule When two constituents are both of type ⟨e, t⟩, combine them by conjunction: λx. f (x) ∧ g(x). Formal semantics calls this predicate modification; in database terms it is a conjunctive WHERE clause. So the fragment needs two composition rules, not one: application, and conjunction of like-typed predicates. That is enough for a surprisingly large fragment of query language. 17 / 42 Why Bother With Types? Nothing so far stops us combining things nonsensically: tx(ok) (λx.state(x)) λy.river(y)  A parser that generates candidate derivations will produce garbage like this by the thousand. We need a cheap filter. Semantic types e – an entity (Texas, Oklahoma, a row in the database) t – a truth value (a query that returns yes/no) ⟨σ, τ ⟩ – a function from things of type σ to things of type τ Rule: you may apply α to β only if α : ⟨σ, τ ⟩ and β : σ. Everything else is rejected before it is ever scored. 18 / 42 The Type Table Word class Example Type Proper noun Common noun Intransitive verb Adjective Transitive verb Determiner Preposition Sentence Texas state flows large borders every in — e ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ t Lambda term tx λx. state(x) λx. flows(x) λx. large(x) λy.λx. borders(x, y) λP.λQ. ∀x[P (x) → Q(x)] λy.λx. in(x, y) borders(tx, ok) Two things worth noticing. Nouns, intransitive verbs, and adjectives share a type – all are one-place predicates, or table filters. Determiners take two predicates and return a truth value, which is why quantification is where semantic parsers usually break. 19 / 42 Types as a Parser Filter A CKY-style semantic parser builds constituents bottom-up. At each cell it asks: can these two combine? Left Right Result ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ e ⟨e, t⟩ e e ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ t ✓ ⟨e, t⟩ ✓ × – entities are not functions × by application (but see conjunction) The type system prunes the search space before any statistical model is consulted – for a lexicon with several entries per word, the difference between a tractable chart and an intractable one. This is also why type-driven parsing survived into the neural era: it is a hard constraint, and hard constraints are cheap. 20 / 42 Combinatory Categorial Grammar Types tell us what can combine. They do not tell us about word order. λy.λx. borders(x, y) says the verb takes two entities – but not that the object is on the right and the subject on the left. CCG’s idea Put the directionality in the category. A category is either atomic (S, N P , N ) or a slash category: X/Y – “an X, if you give me a Y on the right” X\Y – “an X, if you give me a Y on the left” The slash always leans toward the argument. So S\N P is a verb phrase: give it a noun phrase on its left and you get a sentence. CCG is the standard syntax-semantics interface in NLP – Steedman’s framework, and the basis of most semantic parsing work from Zettlemoyer & Collins (2005) onward. 21 / 42 Categories and Types, Side by Side Word CCG category Semantic type Match? Texas NP e ✓ state N ⟨e, t⟩ ✓ flows S\N P ⟨e, t⟩ ✓ borders (S\N P )/N P ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ✓ every (S/(S\N P ))/N ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ ✓ The category and the type carry the same arity information. The category adds direction; the type adds what kind of thing each argument is. Neither subsumes the other – which is why CCG lexical entries always list both. Strip the slashes and replace N P by e, S by t: you recover the semantic type exactly. 22 / 42 Two Combinatory Rules Forward application (>) X/Y : f Backward application Y :a =⇒ X : f (a) X\Y : f =⇒ X : f (a) (<) Y :a Two rules. In both cases the semantics is function application – the slash direction only says where to look for the argument. This is the rule-to-rule hypothesis in its cleanest form: syntax and semantics are the same derivation, read two ways. Full CCG adds composition (B), type-raising (T), and substitution (S). We need only the two application rules today; type-raising reappears when we get to quantifier scope. 23 / 42 A CCG Derivation Texas borders Oklahoma NP tx (S\N P )/N P λy.λx.borders(x, y) NP ok > S\N P : λx.borders(x, ok) < S 1 2 : borders(tx, ok) Forward application: (S\N P )/N P finds its N P on the right. Semantically, apply the verb to the object. Backward application: S\N P finds its N P on the left. Apply the VP to the subject. The syntactic derivation and the semantic derivation are the same object. Read the top line for structure, the bottom for meaning. 24 / 42 Two More Combinators Application alone cannot derive every constituent we need. CCG adds two more rules. Forward composition (B) X/Y : f Type-raising Y /Z : g =⇒ X/Z : λx. f (g(x)) (T) X:a =⇒ T /(T \X) : λf. f (a) Type-raising should look familiar. λf. f (a) turns an entity into “the set of properties it has” – this is Partee’s lift from Session 2, wearing a CCG hat. Together, B and T let CCG treat non-traditional word sequences as constituents, which is what makes coordination and extraction work. 25 / 42 Why You Need Them: Coordination Texas borders Oklahoma and New Mexico Fine – Oklahoma and New Mexico is a constituent. But now: Texas borders and Louisiana borders Oklahoma Texas borders is not a constituent in traditional phrase structure. With type-raising and composition, it is: T Texas N P −−→ S/(S\N P ) : λf. f (tx) borders (S\N P )/N P Texas borders S/N P by forward composition B Now it has a category and a meaning, so it can be coordinated with another S/N P . This flexibility about constituency is CCG’s main selling point. 26 / 42 Type-Raising Gives You Scope Recall the problem from the quantifier slide: with two quantifiers there are two readings. Every state borders a state. In CCG, type-raising is optional and can apply to either argument. Different choices give different derivations – and different scopes. Derivation Reading subject quantifier applied last object type-raised and applied last ∀ > ∃ (surface) ∃ > ∀ (inverse) Scope ambiguity becomes derivational ambiguity. One string, two well-formed derivations, two logical forms. Elegant – and a practical headache, since the number of derivations grows fast. Session 5 works the formal-semantics version of the same problem. 27 / 42 Why CCG Won in NLP Radically lexicalized. Almost all the grammar lives in the lexicon; there are only a handful of universal combinatory rules. So learning a grammar reduces to learning a lexicon – which is a much better-posed statistical problem. Transparent interface. Every syntactic category determines a semantic type. No separate mapping to maintain. Flexible constituency. Composition and type-raising let CCG derive non-standard constituents, which handles coordination and extraction gracefully – states that border Texas and flow into the Gulf. Parseable. CCGbank exists; the parsers are fast and accurate. Lineage worth knowing: Zettlemoyer & Collins (2005) learned CCG lexicons for GeoQuery; Kwiatkowski et al. generalized the lexical induction; Artzi & Zettlemoyer applied it to instructions and dialogue. 28 / 42 Quantifiers, Briefly Every state borders a state. every has category (S/(S\N P ))/N and denotation λP.λQ. ∀x[P (x) → Q(x)] 1 Combine with the noun: λQ. ∀x[state(x) → Q(x)] 2 That is a function looking for a VP on its right. Apply it to the VP. – category S/(S\N P ) Notice what happened: the subject is now the function and the verb phrase is the argument – the reverse of the proper-name case. The category S/(S\N P ) says so explicitly. And with two quantifiers there are two derivations, giving two scope readings. That is Session 5, and in CCG terms it is handled with type-raising and composition. 29 / 42 Ambiguity Is Not a Bug Report A semantic parser must produce several logical forms, not one, because sentences genuinely have several readings. Type Example Source Lexical bank one word, several entries Attachment cities in states with rivers where the PP attaches Scope every state borders a state quantifier order Coordination large cities and states what large modifies Design consequence. The grammar’s job is to enumerate the well-formed readings; a statistical model’s job is to rank them; and the execution engine can sometimes break the tie – if only one reading returns rows, that is a strong signal. Note that this division of labour requires the grammar to be complete about what is possible. That is again the fragment discipline: be exact about coverage. 30 / 42 Negation, and Where It Bites Texas does not border Maine ¬ borders(tx, me) No state borders Hawaii ¬∃x[state(x) ∧ borders(x, hi)] Every state does not border Texas two readings The third is ambiguous between ∀x[. . . → ¬ . . .] and ¬∀x[. . . → . . .] – negation and quantifiers scope over each other just as two quantifiers do. Practical warning. Negation is where executable semantics gets expensive: ¬P (x) over an open domain means everything in the database that is not P . Most systems use a closed-world assumption and hope. It is worth knowing that this is an assumption rather than a theorem. 31 / 42 A Problem: Adverbs and Adjuncts Alice read the book in the library on Tuesday. With a fixed-arity predicate we are stuck: read(alice, book) read(alice, book, library) read(alice, book, library, tuesday) Three problems. We need a different predicate for every number of modifiers – unboundedly many. The entailment Alice read the book in the library ⇒ Alice read the book does not fall out; we would have to stipulate it. Modifiers can be added freely and in any order, which arity-fixed predicates cannot model. This is the adverbial modification problem, and it has a classic solution. 32 / 42 Davidson’s Move: Quantify Over Events Davidson (1967) Verbs introduce an extra argument – an event variable. Modifiers are predicates of that event. ∃e [ read(e, alice, book) ∧ in(e, library) ∧ on(e, tuesday) ] Modifiers are now conjuncts, so they can be added freely and in any order. Dropping a conjunct is valid inference, so the entailment is automatic. ✓ The verb keeps a fixed arity. Conjunction is commutative and monotone – exactly the properties adjunct modification has. The representation now matches the phenomenon. 33 / 42 Neo-Davidsonian: Roles as Separate Predicates Go one step further and pull the arguments out too: ∃e [ read(e) ∧ agent(e, alice) ∧ theme(e, book) ∧ in(e, library) ] Davidsonian Neo-Davidsonian Verb arity fixed, n+1 always 1 Arguments positional named roles Optional arguments awkward trivial This is the representation NLP actually uses. PropBank, FrameNet, and AMR are all essentially neo-Davidsonian: an event node, plus labelled edges to its participants. And semantic role labelling – one of the standard NLP tasks – is exactly the job of recovering those agent, theme, location predicates from text. 34 / 42 Why This Matters for the Rest of the Course Look at the shape of the neo-Davidsonian representation: ∃e [ read(e) ∧ agent(e, alice) ∧ theme(e, book) ] It is a set of (role, filler) pairs attached to an event node. Here Later in the course role–filler binding event node conjunction of roles the binding problem of Part III the object roles

title: Lecture 3 — Predicate Logic
text: Session 3: Predicate Logic and Models What Makes a Sentence True James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics September 4, 2026 1 / 37 Where We Were Session 1. Meanings are functions; composition is β-reduction. Session 2. Every expression has a type; types license composition and determine its direction. We derived [[Alice likes Bob]] = like(a, b) But we have been sloppy about two things. What is like(a, b)? We have been treating it as a formula, without saying what formulas are. What makes it true? We sketched models in passing, but never defined satisfaction. Today we make both precise. The output of a semantic derivation is a formula of predicate logic, and truth is defined by a recursive satisfaction relation over a model. 2 / 37 Today 1 The two-level architecture: why an intermediate logical language 2 Syntax of first-order logic 3 Free and bound variables; scope 4 Models, and assignment functions 5 Satisfaction – the recursive definition 6 Truth, validity, entailment 7 Quantifier interaction – and a preview of Session 5 8 Model checking as computation 9 A model in Haskell – and Problem Set 1 Problem Set 1 goes out at the end of today. 3 / 37 Why an Intermediate Language? We could map English directly to model-theoretic objects. Montague largely did. In practice almost everyone goes through a logical form instead: English Alice likes Bob composition Logical form like(a, b) satisfaction Model truth value Three reasons this pays. Modularity. Composition and evaluation are separate problems, debugged separately. Inference. A logical form supports entailment reasoning without ever touching a model. Computability. Over a finite model, satisfaction is a program you can run. Problem Set 1 has exactly this shape: your denotations build formulas; the harness evaluates them. 4 / 37 Vocabulary A first-order language is fixed by its non-logical vocabulary: Category Notation Example Individual constants a, b, c, . . . a for Alice Variables x, y, z, . . . Predicate symbols (n-ary) P, Q, R, . . . student (1-ary), like (2-ary) And its logical vocabulary, which is the same for every first-order language: ¬ ∧ ∨ → ↔ ∀ ∃ ( ) We omit function symbols. They are standard, and nothing in this course needs them. 5 / 37 Terms and Atomic Formulas Terms 1 Every individual constant is a term. 2 Every variable is a term. 3 Nothing else is a term. Terms are the expressions that denote individuals – the object-language counterpart of type e. Atomic formulas If P is an n-ary predicate symbol and t1 , . . . , tn are terms, then P (t1 , . . . , tn ) is an atomic formula. Examples. student(a) like(x, b) sleep(y) Note the correspondence: an n-ary predicate symbol is the object-language version of a meaning of type ⟨e, ⟨e, · · · t⟩⟩ with n arrows. 6 / 37 Well-Formed Formulas The recursive definition 1 Every atomic formula is a formula. 2 If φ is a formula, so is ¬φ. 3 If φ and ψ are formulas, so are (φ ∧ ψ), (φ ∨ ψ), (φ → ψ), (φ ↔ ψ). 4 If φ is a formula and x a variable, then ∀x φ and ∃x φ are formulas. 5 Nothing else is a formula. The third such definition this week – lambda terms, semantic types, and now formulas. Base case, constructors, closure clause. It is worth noticing the pattern, because every proof about these objects is by induction on the same structure. Examples. ¬ sleep(a) ∀x [ student(x) → sleep(x) ] ∃x ∀y like(y, x) 7 / 37 Scope of a Quantifier In ∀x φ, the formula φ is the scope of the quantifier. ∀x [ student(x) → ∃y [ book(y) ∧ read(x, y) ] ] {z } | scope of ∃y | {z scope of ∀x } Brackets matter. Compare: ∀x [ student(x) → sleep(x) ] every student sleeps ∀x student(x) → sleep(x) if everything is a student, then it sleeps – x is free! The second is not a sentence at all. We will always bracket explicitly. 8 / 37 Free and Bound, Again An occurrence of x is bound if it lies in the scope of a quantifier ∀x or ∃x; otherwise it is free. Formula Free variables Sentence? sleep(a) none yes sleep(x) x no ∀x sleep(x) none yes ∀x like(x, y) y no ∃y ∀x like(x, y) none yes A formula with no free variables is a sentence (or closed formula). Only sentences have truth values. A formula with a free variable is true relative to an assignment – which is why the next section introduces assignment functions properly. 9 / 37 Two Notions of Binding, Side by Side You have now seen binding twice this week. They are related but not identical. λ-binding (Session 1) Quantifier binding (today) Form λx.φ ∀x φ, ∃x φ Creates a function a truth value Discharged by application (β) satisfaction over the domain α-equivalent? yes yes Both bind variables; both are subject to capture; both are α-equivalent under renaming. And both are things that Theme 5 has to reconstruct. The wedge product binds in a third sense entirely – role to filler – and whether it can do the work of either of these is one of the open questions from Session 1. 10 / 37 Models, Precisely A model M = ⟨D, I⟩ D – a non-empty set, the domain I – the interpretation function, with I(c) ∈ D for each individual constant c I(P ) ⊆ Dn for each n-ary predicate symbol P I(P ) is the extension of P : the set of things (or tuples of things) it is true of. For a 1-ary predicate: a subset of D. For a 2-ary predicate: a set of ordered pairs. Recall from Session 2: a subset of D and a function D → {0, 1} are the same object. We move between the two freely – sets are easier to write, functions are easier to compose. 11 / 37 Our Running Model D = {Alice, Bob, Carol, Fido} Symbol Interpretation a, b, c student dog sleep like Alice, Bob, Carol {Alice, Bob, Carol} {Fido} {Carol, Fido} {(Alice, Bob), (Alice, Fido), (Bob, Fido)} The same model as Session 2, and essentially the one in Problem Set 1. Convention: like contains (x, y) when x likes y. So Alice likes Bob, and nobody likes Alice. 12 / 37 Assignment Functions A model interprets constants. It says nothing about variables. Assignment An assignment g is a function from variables to elements of D. For d ∈ D, write g[x 7→ d] for the assignment that is like g everywhere except that it sends x to d. Denotation of terms, relative to M and g: [[c]]M,g = I(c) [[x]]M,g = g(x) The modified assignment g[x 7→ d] is the entire technical content of quantification. Everything else follows from it. 13 / 37 Satisfaction: The Definition M, g |= φ (“φ is satisfied in M under g”) M, g |= P (t1 , . . . , tn ) ⇐⇒  [[t1 ]]M,g , . . . , [[tn ]]M,g ∈ I(P ) M, g |= ¬φ ⇐⇒ M, g ⊭ φ M, g |= (φ ∧ ψ) ⇐⇒ M, g |= φ and M, g |= ψ M, g |= (φ ∨ ψ) ⇐⇒ M, g |= φ or M, g |= ψ M, g |= (φ → ψ) ⇐⇒ M, g ⊭ φ or M, g |= ψ M, g |= ∀x φ ⇐⇒ for every d ∈ D : M, g[x 7→ d] |= φ M, g |= ∃x φ ⇐⇒ for some d ∈ D : M, g[x 7→ d] |= φ The last two clauses are the heart of it. Note the recursion: satisfaction of a quantified formula is defined in terms of satisfaction of a simpler formula, under modified assignments. 14 / 37 Truth in a Model Satisfaction is relative to an assignment. Truth is not. Truth For a sentence φ (no free variables): M |= φ iff M, g |= φ for every assignment g Why this is well-behaved. If φ has no free variables, then satisfaction does not depend on g at all – one can prove by induction that changing g at a variable not free in φ never changes the outcome. So for sentences: every assignment works, or none does. This is the point of insisting that only sentences have truth values, and the reason our lexical entries are always closed terms. 15 / 37 Worked Evaluation I Evaluate ∀x [ student(x) → sleep(x) ] in our model. By the ∀ clause, check every d ∈ D: student(d) sleep(d) student(d) → sleep(d) Alice 1 0 0 Bob 1 0 0 Carol 1 1 1 Fido 0 1 1 d Not every row is 1, so M ⊭ ∀x [ student(x) → sleep(x) ] – Every student sleeps is false. Note the last row: Fido satisfies the conditional vacuously, because he is not a student. This is the standard behaviour of material implication, and it is why ∀ pairs with → while ∃ pairs with ∧. 16 / 37 Worked Evaluation II Evaluate ∃x [ dog(x) ∧ sleep(x) ]. By the ∃ clause, we need some d: dog(d) sleep(d) dog(d) ∧ sleep(d) Alice 0 0 0 Bob 0 0 0 d Carol 0 1 0 Fido 1 1 1 Fido works, so M |= ∃x [ dog(x) ∧ sleep(x) ] – Some dog sleeps is true. Why ∧ and not →? With →, the formula ∃x[dog(x) → sleep(x)] would be true whenever anything fails to be a dog – satisfied by Alice, vacuously. That is not what some dog sleeps means. 17 / 37 Practice Evaluate in the running model. Two minutes, with a neighbour. 1 2 3 4 like(a, b) ¬ ∃x like(x, a) ∀x [ dog(x) → sleep(x) ] ∃x [ student(x) ∧ ¬ sleep(x) ] 18 / 37 Practice Evaluate in the running model. Two minutes, with a neighbour. 1 2 3 4 like(a, b) ¬ ∃x like(x, a) ∀x [ dog(x) → sleep(x) ] ∃x [ student(x) ∧ ¬ sleep(x) ] Answers. 1 True – (Alice, Bob) ∈ I(like). 2 True – no pair in I(like) has Alice in second position. 3 True – Fido is the only dog, and he sleeps. 4 True – Alice is a student and does not sleep. Notice that (4) is the negation of Worked Evaluation I, and gets the opposite value. That is not an accident – see the next section. 18 / 37 Three Logical Notions Truth is relative to a model. The interesting notions quantify over models. Notion Notation Holds when Satisfiable — some model makes φ true Valid |= φ every model makes φ true Entailment Γ |= φ every model making all of Γ true makes φ true Entailment is the payoff. It is the formal counterpart of it follows that, and what a semantic theory is ultimately accountable to: Every student sleeps, Alice is a student ⇒ Alice sleeps No competent speaker of English needs to be told this. A semantic theory that cannot derive it is not a theory of meaning. 19 / 37 Entailment, Verified Show: { ∀x[student(x) → sleep(x)], student(a) } |= sleep(a) Proof sketch. Let M be any model satisfying both premises. 1 From the first premise and the ∀ clause: for every d ∈ D, if d ∈ I(student) then d ∈ I(sleep). 2 Instantiate at d = I(a). 3 From the second premise: I(a) ∈ I(student). 4 Therefore I(a) ∈ I(sleep), i.e. M |= sleep(a). □ Note what the argument did not use: any particular model. The reasoning goes through for all of them at once, which is exactly what entailment demands. This is also why the logical form is worth having. We reasoned entirely in the object language and never evaluated anything. 20 / 37 Logical Equivalence φ and ψ are logically equivalent (φ ≡ ψ) when they are satisfied in exactly the same models under the same assignments. Equivalence Name ¬¬φ ≡ φ double negation φ → ψ ≡ ¬φ ∨ ψ material implication ¬(φ ∧ ψ) ≡ ¬φ ∨ ¬ψ De Morgan ¬∀x φ ≡ ∃x ¬φ quantifier duality ¬∃x φ ≡ ∀x ¬φ quantifier duality ∀x∀y φ ≡ ∀y∀x φ like quantifiers commute ∃x∃y φ ≡ ∃y∃x φ like quantifiers commute Conspicuously absent from this list: ∀x∃y φ and ∃y∀x φ. 21 / 37 Unlike Quantifiers Do Not Commute ∀x ∃y like(x, y) versus ∃y ∀x like(x, y) Left: everyone likes something – possibly a different thing each. Right: there is one thing that everyone likes. The entailment goes one way only ∃y ∀x φ |= ∀x ∃y φ but ∀x ∃y φ ⊭ ∃y ∀x φ If there is one universally-liked thing, then certainly everyone likes something. The converse fails. A counter-model is easy to build – and worth building yourself before the next slide. 22 / 37 A Counter-Model Take D = {1, 2} and I(like) = {(1, 1), (2, 2)}. 1 2 ∀x ∃y like(x, y): 1 likes 1 ✓, 2 likes 2 ✓. ∃y ∀x like(x, y): is 1 liked by both? No. Is 2? No. True. False. Quantifier order is semantically significant, and the two orders are not interderivable. Two formulas, same atoms, same quantifiers – different truth conditions. 23 / 37 Why This Matters for Natural Language Every student read a book. One string. Two logical forms. Surface (∀ > ∃) ∀x [ student(x) → ∃y [ book(y) ∧ read(x, y) ] ] Inverse (∃ > ∀) ∃y [ book(y) ∧ ∀x [ student(x) → read(x, y) ] ] The problem for compositionality. The syntax gives us one structure. Composition, as we defined it in Session 2, is a function of the structure. So where does the second reading come from? This is the central puzzle of Session 5, and the capstone of Theme 1. You will derive both readings in Problem Set 1 – and Part E of that assignment asks you to say which entails which. 24 / 37 Satisfaction Is an Algorithm Look again at the ∀ clause: M, g |= ∀x φ ⇐⇒ for every d ∈ D : M, g[x 7→ d] |= φ If D is finite, this is a for loop. Logic Computation ∀x φ ∃x φ φ∧ψ P (t1 , . . . , tn ) check φ for every element of D check φ until one element succeeds conjunction of two Booleans membership test in a finite set Over a finite model, satisfaction is decidable – and the decision procedure is a direct transcription of the definition. Over infinite models it is not. First-order validity is undecidable (Church, Turing, 1936) – the same year as the lambda calculus, and not a coincidence. 25 / 37 A Model in Haskell The definitions you just saw, as code you can run. 26 / 37 Why Haskell, and Why Now Everything today has been a definition by recursion over structure. Haskell is a language in which such definitions are transcribed almost literally. Functions are values; you write them without naming them (λ becomes \). Types are checked; a semantic type mismatch becomes a compile error. No mutable state, so an expression’s value depends only on its parts – referential transparency is compositionality, enforced by the compiler. You are not being asked to learn Haskell as a language. You are being asked to read and write a few dozen lines of it as notation for the semantics you already know. Labs 1–3 cover the mechanics. Session 4 covers the notation properly. Today is a first look, so that the file you receive at the end of class is not a surprise. 27 / 37 The Domain data Entity = Alice | Bob | Carol | Fido deriving (Eq, Ord, Show, Enum, Bounded) domain :: [Entity] domain = [minBound .. maxBound] data Entity = ... declares the domain D by listing its members. domain is that set as a list – this is what quantifiers will range over. deriving asks the compiler to generate equality, ordering, and printing for free. This is D = {Alice, Bob, Carol, Fido}, in four lines. 28 / 37 Types, and the Interpretation Function type T type ET type TV = Bool = Entity -> T = Entity -> Entity -> T -- the type t -- the type <e,t> -- the type <e,<e,t>> studentSet, dogSet, sleepSet :: [Entity] studentSet = [Alice, Bob, Carol] dogSet = [Fido] sleepSet = [Carol, Fido] likePairs :: [(Entity, Entity)] likePairs = [(Alice,Bob), (Alice,Fido), (Bob,Fido)] The type declarations are the semantic types of Session 2, spelled in Haskell. The sets below are I – the interpretation function, written out as extensions. Compare the table three slides back. This is the same model, in a form a compiler can check. 29 / 37 From Sets to Predicates inSet :: [Entity] -> ET inSet xs = \x -> x ‘elem‘ xs inRel :: [(Entity,Entity)] -> TV inRel ps = \obj subj -> (subj, obj) ‘elem‘ ps student, dog, sleeps :: ET student = inSet studentSet dog = inSet dogSet sleeps = inSet sleepSet likes :: TV likes = inRel likePairs inSet is the characteristic function construction from Session 2: it turns a set into a function of type ⟨e, t⟩. Note \x -> ... – that backslash is λ. And note that inRel takes the object first, exactly as we argued in Session 2. 30 / 37 Quantifiers Are Loops The satisfaction clauses, transcribed: forAll :: ET -> T forAll p = all p domain -- for EVERY d in D: p(d) exists :: ET -> T exists p = any p domain -- for SOME d in D: p(d) Compare: M, g |= ∀x φ ⇐⇒ for every d ∈ D : M, g[x 7→ d] |= φ The assignment update g[x 7→ d] is Haskell’s function application: p d. Because p is a function of x, applying it to d is evaluating φ under the modified assignment. This works because domain is finite. An infinite domain would make all diverge – the computational shadow of undecidability. 31 / 37 Evaluating Sentences Now the two worked examples from earlier, as code: -- Every student sleeps. s1 :: T s1 = forAll (\x -> not (student x) || sleeps x) -- Some dog sleeps. s2 :: T s2 = exists (\x -> dog x && sleeps x) Logic Haskell Value ∀x[student(x) → sleep(x)] s1 False ∃x[dog(x) ∧ sleep(x)] s2 True Same answers we computed by hand – but now the computer checks them. That is what makes Problem Set 1 testable. Note not p || q for p → q: material implication, exactly as in the equivalence table. 32 / 37 What You Have Just Seen Session 2–3 concept Haskell In PS 1 domain D data Entity, domain given type e, t Entity, Bool given type ⟨e, t⟩ Entity -> Bool given interpretation I the sets and pair lists given characteristic function inSet, inRel given λx.φ \x -> ... you write these ∀, ∃ all, any over domain you write these composition rules function application you write these Everything in the “given” rows is already written for you. The assignment is the semantics, not the infrastructure. 33 / 37 Problem Set 1 Out today. Due Friday 25 September. A working Haskell file with roughly twenty holes marked -- TODO. You fill in: lexical denotations – nouns, verbs, and the determiners every, a, no; composition rules – function application and predicate modification; derivations for seven sentences; both scope readings of Every student read a book. Plus a short writeup: the scope reasoning, one type error you hit and what it told you, and one limitation of the fragment. Run runghc Fragment.hs at any point to see TODO / FAIL / PASS per sentence. Unfilled holes do not crash the run. Lab this week and next covers the Haskell you need. Session 4 covers the notation properly and builds the Fragment together. 34 / 37 Summary Concept Key point Two-level architecture Terms Formulas Scope Sentence Model ⟨D, I⟩ Assignment g Satisfaction Truth Entailment Quantifier duality Quantifier order Finite models English → logical form → model constants and variables; denote individuals recursive definition; atoms, connectives, quantifiers the formula a quantifier governs; bracket explicitly closed formula – only these have truth values domain plus extensions for each symbol interprets variables; g[x 7→ d] drives quantification recursive: ∀ checks all d, ∃ checks some d satisfaction under every assignment; well defined for sentences every model of the premises is a model of the conclusion ¬∀x φ ≡ ∃x ¬φ ∀∃ ̸≡ ∃∀; entailment runs one way only satisfaction becomes a decidable computation 35 / 37 Coming Up Session 4 (Tuesday): The Fragment of English The lexicon as a set of typed denotations Composition rules, stated generally Building and checking a fragment end to end Haskell notation, properly – enough to write, not just read Reading: EU Chapter 6. Then Session 5: Quantifiers and scope – where Every student read a book gets its two readings, and where composition stops being mechanical. Reminder: if your linear algebra self-assessment showed a weak section – especially Section E, determinants and orientation – Weeks 2–5 are when there is room to fix it. The review guide is on the course site. 36 / 37

title: The Fragment of English
text: Session 4: The Fragment of English Lexicon, Composition, and Model Checking James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics September 8, 2026 1 / 43 Where We Were Session 1. Meanings are functions; composition is β-reduction. Session 2. Types license composition and determine its direction. Session 3. Formulas are evaluated against a model by a recursive satisfaction relation – and over a finite domain, that relation is a program. Today we assemble all three into a working system. By the end of this session you will have seen a complete, executable fragment of English: a syntax, a lexicon, composition rules, and a model – with every sentence’s truth value computable. This is also the session that teaches the Haskell you need to write Problem Set 1, not merely read it. 2 / 43 Today 1 What a fragment is, and why the discipline matters 2 The syntax: categories and rules 3 The lexicon: form, category, type, denotation 4 Composition rules, and the rule-to-rule hypothesis 5 Haskell, properly – signatures, currying, higher-order functions, and how to read a type error 6 Building the fragment, entry by entry 7 Scope in the fragment: two readings, in code 8 What the fragment cannot do Technical session. Bring the scaffold up on a laptop if you have one. 3 / 43 What Is a Fragment? Definition A fragment of a natural language is an explicitly specified subset of it, given by four components: 1 a syntax – categories and phrase structure rules; 2 a lexicon – for each word, its category, semantic type, and denotation; 3 composition rules – one semantic operation for each syntactic rule; 4 a model – domain and interpretation. The methodology is Montague’s, from The Proper Treatment of Quantification in Ordinary English (1973). The essential move: do not attempt all of English. Take a small piece, specify it completely, and be exact about what is in and what is out. 4 / 43 Why Fragments? Testability. A fragment makes predictions. Feed it a sentence and a model, and it returns a truth value – which can be right or wrong. Honesty about coverage. “Our theory handles quantification” is unfalsifiable. “Our fragment derives both readings of Every student read a book and neither reading of Every student read every book they liked” is a claim. Compositional discipline. Every rule must pair with a semantic operation. You cannot quietly patch one sentence. Implementability. A fragment is a specification. If it is precise enough, it compiles. This is also the standard by which we will judge the geometric framework in Part IV. Problem Set 3 asks you to rebuild this fragment on a geometric substrate – so the comparison is between two implementations of the same specification. 5 / 43 The Rule-to-Rule Hypothesis Bach (1976) For every syntactic rule combining constituents, there is exactly one semantic rule that combines their meanings. S → NP VP Function Application VP → TV NP Function Application N→AN Predicate Modification Syntax and semantics run in parallel. The semantics is a homomorphic image of the syntax – which is compositionality, stated as an architectural constraint rather than a slogan. 6 / 43 Categories Our fragment uses eight categories: Cat. Name S NP VP N IV TV DET A sentence noun phrase verb phrase common noun intransitive verb transitive verb determiner adjective Type t e or ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ Examples Alice sleeps Alice, every student sleeps, likes Bob student, dog sleeps likes, read every, a, no tall, sleeping Note the NP row. Proper names and quantified NPs occupy the same syntactic category but different semantic types. We return to this – it is the fragment’s one real design tension. 7 / 43 Phrase Structure Rules (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) Rule Semantic operation Example S → NP VP VP → IV VP → TV NP NP → PN NP → DET N N→AN FA identity FA identity FA PM Alice sleeps sleeps likes Bob Alice every student sleeping student Six rules. Every one paired with exactly one semantic operation, as the rule-to-rule hypothesis demands. “Identity” means the semantics passes through unchanged – the rule is syntactically useful but semantically inert. Some presentations omit such rules entirely. 8 / 43 A Derivation Tree Every student likes Bob. S:t NP : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ DET every N student VP : ⟨e, t⟩ TV likes NP : e Bob Reading bottom-up, with the rule used at each step: 1 2 3 Rule (5), FA: [[every]]([[student]]) – gives a GQ Rule (3), FA: [[likes]]([[Bob]]) – gives a VP of type ⟨e, t⟩ Rule (1), FA: the GQ applies to the VP – gives t At step 3 the subject is the function and the VP is the argument. At step 2 the verb is the function. The types decide, not the tree geometry. 9 / 43 The NP Tension, Stated Rule (1) is S → NP VP. But NP has two possible types: NP Type Who applies to whom Alice e VP applies to NP every student ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ NP applies to VP So rule (1) corresponds to two composition paths, depending on the subject – violating the rule-to-rule hypothesis in letter, if not in spirit. Two responses: 1 Keep both paths. Simple, and what Problem Set 1 does. 2 Lift every NP to ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩, using Partee’s lift from Session 2. Then rule (1) is uniformly “NP applies to VP”. This is Montague’s choice. We take (1) today for clarity. Session 5 gives the argument for (2) – and it is scope that makes the argument. 10 / 43 What This Fragment Covers In: Out: Proper names Tense and aspect Common nouns Plurals Intransitive and transitive verbs Pronouns and anaphora Determiners: every, a/some, no Relative clauses Intersective adjectives Coordination Simple declarative sentences Negation of sentences Scope ambiguity (two quantifiers) Modality, attitude verbs Non-intersective adjectives The right-hand column is not a list of failures – it is the fragment being honest about its scope. Your PS 1 writeup asks you to name one item from it and say what would have to be added. 11 / 43 Anatomy of a Lexical Entry Each entry specifies four things: Form likes Category TV Type ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ Denotation λx.λy. like(y, x) The type is not an extra annotation – it is determined by the denotation, and constrains where the word may appear. In Haskell the type and the denotation are written on consecutive lines, and the compiler checks that they agree. That checking is the whole reason we are using it. 12 / 43 Names and Nouns Form Cat. Type Denotation Alice PN e a Bob PN e b student N ⟨e, t⟩ λx. student(x) dog N ⟨e, t⟩ λx. dog(x) sleeps IV ⟨e, t⟩ λx. sleep(x) Note again: student and sleeps have the same semantic type. Semantically, a common noun and an intransitive verb are the same kind of object – a one-place predicate. The syntax distinguishes them because they occur in different positions. The semantics does not need to. 13 / 43 Transitive Verbs, and Argument Order [[likes]] = λx.λy. like(y, x) : ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ The first argument is the object; the second is the subject. Three reasons this is right: 1 Constituency. English builds VP before S. Applying to the object first yields a VP. 2 Type uniformity. The result, λy.like(y, b), has type ⟨e, t⟩ – indistinguishable from an intransitive verb. Rule (1) then does not care how the VP was built. 3 Rule economy. One rule for S → NP VP covers both Alice sleeps and Alice likes Bob. This convention is a frequent source of bugs. In the scaffold, likes b a means a likes b – object first. Write it on a sticky note. 14 / 43 Determiners A determiner takes a restrictor (the noun) and a scope (the VP), and returns a truth value. DET : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ Form Denotation every λQ.λP. ∀x [ Q(x) → P (x) ] a, some λQ.λP. ∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] no λQ.λP. ¬∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] Two structural observations. The λQ.λP prefix is identical in all three. Only the logical skeleton differs. every pairs with →; some and no pair with ∧. This is the vacuous-satisfaction point from Session 3, and it is not interchangeable. 15 / 43 Applying a Determiner: every student [[every student]] = [[every]] [[student]]    = λQ.λP. ∀x [ Q(x) → P (x) ] λz. student(z) ⇝ λP. ∀x [ (λz. student(z))(x) → P (x) ] ⇝ λP. ∀x [ student(x) → P (x) ] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ A generalized quantifier: it is waiting for a predicate. Apply it to sleeps:   λP. ∀x[student(x) → P (x)] λw.sleep(w) ⇝ ∀x [ student(x) → sleep(x) ] : t Which is exactly the formula we evaluated by hand in Session 3 – and found false in our model. 16 / 43 Haskell, Properly Enough to write the fragment, not merely read it. Everything in this section is notation for something you already know. 17 / 43 Type Signatures Every definition gets a signature on the line above it. sleeps :: Entity -> Bool sleeps x = x ‘elem‘ [Carol, Fido] Haskell Semantic type Read as Entity Bool Entity -> Bool Entity -> Entity -> Bool (Entity -> Bool) -> Bool e t ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ an individual a truth value a one-place predicate a two-place predicate a generalized quantifier -> associates to the right: a -> b -> c means a -> (b -> c). Which is currying, spelled in the type. A two-argument function is a one-argument function returning a function. 18 / 43 Two Ways to Write a Function These are the same definition: -- equation style sleeps :: Entity -> Bool sleeps x = x ‘elem‘ [Carol, Fido] -- lambda style sleeps :: Entity -> Bool sleeps = \x -> x ‘elem‘ [Carol, Fido] \ is λ. The second form is literally λx. x ∈ {Carol, Fido}. Use whichever is clearer. In the scaffold you will often want lambda style, because a denotation is a lambda term and writing it that way keeps the correspondence visible. Backticks turn a two-argument function into an infix operator: x ‘elem‘ xs is elem x xs. Purely cosmetic, but it reads better. 19 / 43 Application Is Juxtaposition No parentheses needed for application. Application associates to the left. likes :: Entity -> Entity -> Bool likes Bob likes Bob Alice -- partial application: type Entity -> Bool -- means (likes Bob) Alice : type Bool Expression Type Meaning likes likes Bob likes Bob Alice Entity -> Entity -> Bool Entity -> Bool Bool the relation likes Bob – the VP! Alice likes Bob The middle row is the point: partial application produces the verb phrase, and its type is exactly that of an intransitive verb. Currying and constituency, lined up. Object first. likes Bob Alice is Alice likes Bob, not Bob likes Alice. 20 / 43 Higher-Order Functions Functions are ordinary values: they can be arguments and results. -- takes a predicate, returns a Bool: this is a GQ someDog :: (Entity -> Bool) -> Bool someDog p = any (\x -> dog x && p x) domain -- takes two predicates, returns a Bool: this is a determiner every :: (Entity -> Bool) -> (Entity -> Bool) -> Bool every q p = all (\x -> not (q x) || p x) domain all :: (a -> Bool) -> [a] -> Bool – true if the predicate holds of every element any :: (a -> Bool) -> [a] -> Bool – true if it holds of at least one These are ∀ and ∃ over the finite domain – the satisfaction clauses of Session 3, transcribed. And not (q x) || p x is material implication, Q(x) → P (x). 21 / 43 Type Synonyms Keep It Readable Writing (Entity -> Bool) -> (Entity -> Bool) -> Bool everywhere is unbearable. The scaffold defines synonyms: type T = Bool type ET = Entity -> T type TV = Entity -> Entity -> T type GQ = ET -> T type DET = ET -> GQ -- t -- <e,t> -- <e,<e,t>> -- <<e,t>,t> -- <<e,t>,<<e,t>,t>> Now signatures read like the semantics: student :: ET likes :: TV every :: DET type declares a synonym, not a new type – ET and Entity -> Bool are interchangeable everywhere. The compiler will sometimes report an error using one and sometimes the other. 22 / 43 Reading a Type Error, I Suppose you write: s :: T s = alice sleeps intending Alice sleeps. GHC replies: Fragment.hs:87:5: error: * Couldn’t match expected type: (Entity -> Bool) -> t0 with actual type: Entity * The function ‘alice’ is applied to one value argument, but its type ‘Entity’ has none In the expression: alice sleeps Decode it. actual type: Entity – alice is an individual, type e. applied to one value argument, but its type has none – individuals are not functions. They cannot be applied to anything. The fix is semantic, not syntactic: the predicate applies to the individual, so write sleeps alice. 23 / 43 Reading a Type Error, II Now a subtler one. You write: tallStudent :: ET tallStudent = tall student Fragment.hs:94:20: error: * Couldn’t match expected type: Entity with actual type: Entity -> Bool * In the first argument of ‘tall’, namely ‘student’ Decode it. tall has type ET, so it expects an Entity. You gave it student, which is itself an ET. This is exactly the mismatch from Session 2 – ⟨e, t⟩ applied to ⟨e, t⟩. The compiler has just rediscovered the argument for predicate modification. The fix is not to force the application through; it is to use the other composition rule: pm tall student. 24 / 43 The Errors Types Will Not Catch Type checking is a theory of what can combine. It is not a theory of what is correct. -- typechecks perfectly; means the wrong thing aliceLikesBob :: T aliceLikesBob = likes Alice Bob -- WRONG: this is "Bob likes Alice" Both arguments are Entity; the compiler is satisfied. But the object-first convention means this says Bob likes Alice. Types catch Types miss combining incompatible kinds wrong arity missing arguments swapped arguments of the same kind wrong logical connective (∧ for →) wrong quantifier This is why the scaffold ships a test suite. Types give you well-formedness; the model gives you truth. 25 / 43 Debugging Strategy 1 Read the type error top down. The first error is usually the real one; later errors are often cascade damage. 2 Compare expected against actual. The gap between them tells you which composition step is wrong. 3 Ask the compiler. Put a hole where you are stuck: myDenotation = _ GHC will tell you the type it expects there. 4 Test in GHCi. ghci Fragment.hs, then evaluate pieces: > :t likes Bob likes Bob :: Entity -> Bool > student Alice True 5 Run the suite often. runghc Fragment.hs reports TODO, FAIL, or PASS per sentence; unfilled holes never crash the run. 26 / 43 The Scaffold, Top to Bottom Part Contents Status A Domain, semantic types, extensions, inSet/inRel given B Lexicon – 2 worked, 7 holes yours C Composition rules – 4 holes yours D Sentences – 1 worked, 7 holes yours E Scope – 4 holes yours F Test harness given Work in order. Part C depends on B; D depends on both; E depends on all three. Twenty-two holes, and in the reference solution every single one is a single line. If a hole is taking you more than three or four lines, you are probably fighting the language rather than doing the semantics – come to office hours. 27 / 43 Writing a Noun The scaffold gives you one worked example: student :: ET student = inSet studentSet So the holes follow immediately: dog :: ET dog = inSet dogSet book :: ET book = inSet bookSet Why this works. inSet :: [Entity] -> ET turns a list into a characteristic function. Recall Session 2: a set and a function of type ⟨e, t⟩ are the same object, and inSet is the isomorphism. Equivalent, if you prefer to see the lambda: dog = \x -> x ‘elem‘ dogSet. 28 / 43 Writing a Transitive Verb read’ :: TV read’ = inRel readPairs where the scaffold defines inRel :: [(Entity,Entity)] -> TV inRel ps = \obj subj -> (subj, obj) ‘elem‘ ps Trace the argument order carefully. read’ Hamlet Alice Alice read Hamlet looks up (Alice, Hamlet) ‘elem‘ readPairs The name has a prime because read is already taken by the Prelude. Same for some’ and no’ – some and no clash with library names. 29 / 43 Writing a Determiner: every The mathematics: [[every]] = λQ.λP. ∀x [ Q(x) → P (x) ] The code, given to you as the worked example: every :: DET every restrictor scope = all (\x -> not (restrictor x) || scope x) domain Logic Haskell ∀x all (\x -> ...) Q(x) restrictor x → not (...) P (x) scope x domain || ... Line for line. That correspondence is the reason this course uses a functional language. 30 / 43 Writing some and no Your turn. The mathematics: [[some]] = λQ.λP. ∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] [[no]] = λQ.λP. ¬∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] 31 / 43 Writing some and no Your turn. The mathematics: [[some]] = λQ.λP. ∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] [[no]] = λQ.λP. ¬∃x [ Q(x) ∧ P (x) ] some’ :: DET some’ restrictor scope = any (\x -> restrictor x && scope x) domain no’ :: DET no’ restrictor scope = not (some’ restrictor scope) Note that no’ is defined in terms of some’. That is the quantifier duality from Session 3: ¬∃x φ ≡ ∀x ¬φ, put to work. And note ∧ for some, not →. Using implication here would make Some dog sleeps true whenever anything fails to be a dog. 31 / 43 Composition Rules in Code -- Function application fa :: (a -> b) -> a -> b fa f x = f x -- Predicate modification pm :: ET -> ET -> ET pm p q = \x -> p x && q x -- Subject-predicate, for a proper-name subject spName :: Entity -> ET -> T spName x vp = fa vp x -- Build a VP from a TV and a proper-name object vpName :: TV -> Entity -> ET vpName tv obj = fa tv obj fa looks trivial – it is just application. That is the point: in a functional language, the fundamental composition rule of semantics is the language’s own primitive. The polymorphic signature (a -> b) -> a -> b makes it a general rule rather than a special case. 32 / 43 Sentences With the lexicon and rules in place, sentences are one-liners. -- Carol sleeps. s1 :: T s1 = spName carol sleeps [worked example] -- Alice likes Bob. s3 :: T s3 = spName alice (vpName likes bob) -- Every student sleeps. s4 :: T s4 = every student sleeps -- Some student likes Fido. s8 :: T s8 = some’ student (vpName likes Fido) Read s4 aloud: “every student sleeps”. The code and the English have the same shape, because the determiner is a function of two predicates and English puts them in that order. 33 / 43 Model Checking The harness evaluates each sentence and compares against the expected value: tests :: [(String, Bool, Bool)] tests = [ ("D3 Every student sleeps , ("D4 Some dog sleeps ... ] ", False, s4) ", True, s5) Running it: $ runghc Fragment.hs CS 135 PS1 -- Fragment test suite --------------------------------PASS D0 Carol sleeps FAIL D3 Every student sleeps expected False, got True TODO D6 Every student read Hamlet TODO = hole unfilled (the harness catches undefined, so it never crashes). FAIL = filled and typechecks, but wrong against the model. PASS = correct. A FAIL means your denotation is well-formed but says something false about this model – a semantic bug, and the interesting kind. 34 / 43 Two Readings, One String Every student read a book. Surface (∀ > ∃) ∀x [ student(x) → ∃y [ book(y) ∧ read(x, y) ] ] Inverse (∃ > ∀) ∃y [ book(y) ∧ ∀x [ student(x) → read(x, y) ] ] Both use the same lexical items. What differs is which quantifier is applied first – equivalently, which one takes the other in its scope. And here is the useful fact for Problem Set 1: you do not need any new machinery. every, some’, and read’ are enough. You only need to nest them in the two possible orders. 35 / 43 Surface Scope, in Code ∀x [ student(x) → ∃y [ book(y) ∧ read(x, y) ] ] surface :: T surface = every student (\x -> some’ book (\y -> read’ y x)) Read it outside in. every student (...) – for each student x . . . some’ book (...) – . . . there is some book y . . . read’ y x – . . . such that x read y. (object first!) The lambda \x -> ... is the scope argument of every: a predicate, built on the fly, which is true of an individual just when that individual read some book. 36 / 43 Inverse Scope, in Code ∃y [ book(y) ∧ ∀x [ student(x) → read(x, y) ] ] inverse :: T inverse = some’ book (\y -> every student (\x -> read’ y x)) The only change: the two quantifiers swapped places. The innermost expression read’ y x is identical. every student (\x -> some’ book (\y -> ...)) surface some’ book (\y -> every student (\x -> ...)) inverse Nesting order is scope. This is the clearest possible demonstration of why the ∀∃ / ∃∀ asymmetry from Session 3 matters for natural language. 37 / 43 Why They Differ, in Our Model read = {(Alice,

title: Lecture 5 — Quantifier Scope
text: Session 5: Quantifiers and Scope Where Composition Stops Being Mechanical James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics September 11, 2026 1 / 35 Where We Were Sessions 1–4 built a working fragment. Types drive composition, function application does the work, and every sentence gets a truth value against a model. Three loose ends were left deliberately. 1 Session 2: proper names are type e, quantified NPs are ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩. Two types, one syntactic category. 2 Session 3: ∀∃ ̸≡ ∃∀, with a counter-model. What does that mean for English? 3 Session 4: rule (1), S → NP VP, has two composition paths. That violates rule-to-rule. All three are the same loose end. Today we tie it off — and in the process meet the phenomenon that makes semantic composition genuinely hard. 2 / 35 Today 1 Generalized quantifiers: NPs as sets of sets 2 What determiners can mean — conservativity, monotonicity 3 Why every NP should have the same type: the coordination argument 4 Scope ambiguity: one structure, two readings 5 Three mechanisms — QR, storage, continuations 6 Entailment between readings, and which readings actually occur 7 What this means for Problem Set 1 This is the capstone of Part I. It is also the session that Sessions 2, 3, and 4 have each been deferring to. 3 / 35 The Problem, Restated Alice sleeps. Every student sleeps. Same syntax: S → NP VP. If the semantics is compositional, the same rule must derive both. But every student cannot denote an individual: there is no one person it picks out; no student would have to pick out a non-existent individual; and Every student sleeps does not mean sleep(someone in particular). 4 / 35 The Problem, Restated Alice sleeps. Every student sleeps. Same syntax: S → NP VP. If the semantics is compositional, the same rule must derive both. But every student cannot denote an individual: there is no one person it picks out; no student would have to pick out a non-existent individual; and Every student sleeps does not mean sleep(someone in particular). Montague’s move: if the NP cannot be the argument, make it the function. This inverts the naive picture, in which predicates apply to things. Here a noun phrase applies to a predicate. It takes some getting used to, and it is correct. 4 / 35 A Quantifier Is a Set of Sets [[every student]] = λP. ∀x [ student(x) → P (x) ] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ Equivalently, and more revealingly: the set of all sets that contain every student. NP Denotes the set of sets X such that. . . every student student ⊆ X some student student ∩ X ̸= ∅ no student student ∩ X = ∅ most students |student ∩ X| > |student − X| Alice Alice ∈ X Note the last row. A proper name has a perfectly good reading as a set of sets: the properties Alice has. That is Partee’s lift from Session 2, and it is about to become important. 5 / 35 Determiners If every student is ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ and student is ⟨e, t⟩, the determiner must be: [[every]] = λQ.λP. ∀x [ Q(x) → P (x) ] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩ A relation between two sets — the restrictor Q and the scope P . Determiner Denotation Relation between Q and P every λQλP. ∀x[Q(x) → P (x)] Q⊆P some, a λQλP. ∃x[Q(x) ∧ P (x)] Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ no λQλP. ¬∃x[Q(x) ∧ P (x)] Q∩P =∅ at least two — |Q ∩ P | ≥ 2 Viewing determiners as relations between sets is what makes the next section possible: we can now ask which relations are possible determiner meanings, and the answer is surprisingly restrictive. 6 / 35 How Many Determiners Are There? A determiner is a relation between two subsets of D. With |D| = n: n n n possible determiner meanings = 2(2 ×2 ) = 24 For n = 2 that is already 216 = 65,536. But natural languages use almost none of them. No language has a determiner meaning, say, “Q and P have the same number of elements, or Alice is in P ” So: which relations are possible determiner meanings? This is one of the genuine empirical successes of formal semantics — the constraints are sharp, cross-linguistically robust, and have real consequences. Barwise & Cooper (1981); Keenan & Stavi (1986); van Benthem (1986). 7 / 35 Conservativity CONS D(Q)(P ) ⇐⇒ D(Q)(Q ∩ P ) Only the part of the scope inside the restrictor matters. Every student sleeps ≡ Every student is a student who sleeps Some student sleeps ≡ Some student is a student who sleeps No student sleeps ≡ No student is a student who sleeps These paraphrases are not merely true — they are trivially, boringly true. That triviality is the phenomenon. Every determiner in every language studied is conservative. It is the strongest candidate for a semantic universal we have. 8 / 35 The Test Case: only Only students sleep vs. Only students are students who sleep These are not equivalent. The first says: everyone who sleeps is a student. It constrains non-students. The second is trivially true — everything that is a student-who-sleeps is a student. So only is not conservative. The standard conclusion: only is not a determiner. It is a focus-sensitive adverbial that happens to appear in determiner position. Note the shape of the argument — a semantic universal is used to make a syntactic classification. That is the kind of leverage a good universal gives you. 9 / 35 Monotonicity Determiners also differ in how they behave under enlarging or shrinking their arguments. Upward and downward monotone (in the scope argument) MON ↑: D(Q)(P ) and P ⊆ P ′ =⇒ D(Q)(P ′ ) MON ↓: D(Q)(P ) and P ′ ⊆ P =⇒ D(Q)(P ′ ) Determiner Scope Example inference every some no exactly two MON↑ MON↑ MON↓ neither every student jogs ⇒ every student moves some student jogs ⇒ some student moves no student moves ⇒ no student jogs no inference either way Monotonicity is the engine of natural-language inference, and it is computable directly from the determiner’s denotation. 10 / 35 Why Monotonicity Matters Negative polarity items are licensed exactly in downward-monotone contexts. Sentence Determiner ok No student had any money MON↓ ∗ Every student had any money MON↑ (in scope) ok Every student who had any money left MON↓ in restrictor The third row is the striking one. Every is upward monotone in its scope but downward monotone in its restrictor — and any is licensed exactly there. A semantic property predicts a syntactic distribution, argument position by argument position. This is as good as evidence gets that the generalized-quantifier analysis is tracking something real, and not just a convenient encoding. 11 / 35 Worked Derivation: Every student sleeps Step 1 — determiner meets restrictor.   [[every student]] = λQ.λP. ∀x[Q(x) → P (x)] λz. student(z)   ⇝ λP. ∀x (λz.student(z))(x) → P (x) ⇝ λP. ∀x[student(x) → P (x)] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ Step 2 — quantifier meets scope.   [[Every student sleeps]] = λP. ∀x[student(x) → P (x)] λw. sleep(w)   ⇝ ∀x student(x) → (λw.sleep(w))(x) ⇝ ∀x[student(x) → sleep(x)] :t Four β-reductions, and the composition rule was function application throughout. Note step 2: the subject is the function and the VP is the argument. The types said so; we did not have to stipulate it. 12 / 35 Practice: Write the Quantifier Give the denotation, of type ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩, for each NP. 1 2 3 4 5 no dog some student Alice (lifted) every sleeping student at least two books 13 / 35 Practice: Write the Quantifier Give the denotation, of type ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩, for each NP. 1 2 3 4 5 no dog some student Alice (lifted) every sleeping student at least two books Answers. 1 λP. ¬∃x[dog(x) ∧ P (x)] 2 λP. ∃x[student(x) ∧ P (x)] 3 λP. P (a) 4 λP. ∀x[(student(x) ∧ sleep(x)) → P (x)] 5 λP. |{x : book(x) ∧ P (x)}| ≥ 2 Item 4 shows predicate modification feeding the restrictor. Item 5 is not first-order expressible with a single quantifier — counting genuinely needs the cardinality operator. 13 / 35 Two More Determiner Properties Symmetry D(Q)(P ) ⇐⇒ D(P )(Q) Determiner Sym.? Test some no every yes yes no some students are athletes ≡ some athletes are students no students are athletes ≡ no athletes are students every student is an athlete ̸≡ every athlete is a student Symmetric determiners are exactly those licensed in there-sentences: there are some/no/two students, but ∗there is every student. Existential import Every unicorn sleeps comes out true — vacuously, since there are no unicorns. Whether every presupposes a non-empty restrictor is contested, and goes back to Aristotle. 14 / 35 The Type Mismatch, Revisited Currently our fragment has two composition paths for one syntactic rule: Subject Type Direction of application Alice e VP applies to NP every student ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ NP applies to VP Session 4 called this the fragment’s one real design tension, and deferred the argument. Here it is. Two ways out: 1 Keep both paths, and let the rule be disjunctive. (What PS 1 does.) 2 Lift every NP to ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩, so one path suffices. Option 2 costs something — proper names get a more complicated denotation than they need. So we need a real argument for paying that cost. 15 / 35 The Coordination Argument Alice and every student left. Coordination requires its two conjuncts to have the same type. You cannot conjoin a truth value with an individual. Alice e every student ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ These cannot be conjoined as they stand. And yet the sentence is perfectly good English. 16 / 35 The Coordination Argument Alice and every student left. Coordination requires its two conjuncts to have the same type. You cannot conjoin a truth value with an individual. Alice e every student ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ These cannot be conjoined as they stand. And yet the sentence is perfectly good English. Lift the name using lift(x) = λP. P (x): [[Alice]] = λP. P (a) : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ Now both conjuncts are ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩, and conjunction proceeds: [[Alice and every student]] = λP. P (a) ∧ ∀x[student(x) → P (x)] 16 / 35 What Lifting Buys Two types Uniform lifting S → NP VP two paths one path Coordination of NPs fails works Rule-to-rule hypothesis violated respected Denotation of Alice a — simple λP.P (a) — baroque And nothing is lost semantically. Applying the lifted name to a predicate β-reduces straight back:  λP. P (a) ([[sleeps]]) ⇝ [[sleeps]](a) The lift is a repackaging, not a change of meaning. That is what makes it a legitimate move rather than a fudge — and it is why lift and lower are inverse where both are defined. Montague lifted everything. Most modern treatments lift only when forced, which is a practical compromise — and Problem Set 1 takes the simpler route. 17 / 35 Two Quantifiers, One Sentence Every student read a book. Surface (∀ > ∃) ∀x[student(x) → ∃y[book(y) ∧ read(x, y)]] each student read some book, possibly different ones Inverse (∃ > ∀) ∃y[book(y) ∧ ∀x[student(x) → read(x, y)]] one particular book was read by every student One string. One syntactic structure. Two meanings. This is a crisis for compositionality as we stated it. If meaning is a function of structure, and there is one structure, where does the second meaning come from? 18 / 35 Why Ordinary Composition Gives Only One Reading Build the sentence bottom-up with the rules we have. 1 a book = λP. ∃y[book(y) ∧ P (y)] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ 2 The VP needs read applied to its object. But read wants type e, and a book is ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩. Type mismatch. The standard repair: let the object quantifier take scope over the VP. [[read a book]] = λx. ∃y[book(y) ∧ read(x, y)] Then the subject quantifier applies to that. Result: ∀x[student(x) → ∃y[. . .]] — the surface reading. Composition builds inside-out, so the deeper quantifier ends up with narrower scope. The inverse reading requires the object to somehow escape and take scope above the subject. 19 / 35 The Object-Position Problem Subject quantifiers work because the NP applies to the VP. Object quantifiers do not have that option. Alice read every book. [[read]] : ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ wants an entity [[every book]] : ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩ is not an entity The verb cannot apply to its own object. This is the real source of the scope problem. Subject quantifiers are easy; object quantifiers are stuck. Every mechanism on the following slides exists to unstick them — and once a quantifier can move to fix a type mismatch, how far it moves becomes a question, and ambiguity follows. 20 / 35 Three Ways to Unstick It Lift the verb Give read the type ⟨⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ so it takes a quantifier directly. Works; every transitive verb gets a second, higher-typed entry. Type-shift in place Apply a general rule turning ⟨e, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ into the higher type. One rule instead of many entries — Hendriks’ flexible types. Move the quantifier Let it take scope over the whole clause, binding a trace. QR, storage, continuations — the three mechanisms. The first two fix the type mismatch but give only one reading each — whichever the rule builds in. The third fixes the mismatch and predicts ambiguity, because a moved quantifier can land in more than one place. That is why it is the standard treatment, despite being the most machinery. 21 / 35 Three Mechanisms Mechanism Idea Tradition Quantifier Raising move the NP at LF, leave a trace generative syntax Cooper storage set the quantifier aside, retrieve later Montague grammar Continuations give the NP access to its own context type-theoretic All three do the same job: let a quantifier take scope wider than its surface position. They differ in where the machinery lives. We will look at each briefly. None is the answer — this is a place where the field has several working proposals rather than one settled account, and it is worth seeing that clearly. 22 / 35 Mechanism 1: Quantifier Raising Posit a level of Logical Form at which the quantified NP has moved, leaving a coindexed trace. [ a book2 ] [ every student1 ] Surface order is every student read a book; at LF the object has raised above the subject. t1 read t2 Each raised NP binds its trace, and the LF is interpreted compositionally in the ordinary way.
