Gain Cost composition itself is untouched; ambiguity is structural an extra, unpronounced level of representation The strategy: keep the semantics simple by letting the syntax be more complicated. Whether the extra level is real is a long-running debate in syntax. 23 / 35 Mechanism 2: Cooper Storage Keep one level of structure. When you meet a quantified NP, put it in a store and leave a variable behind. Step Core meaning Store read a book read(x1 , y2 ) {⟨a book, 2⟩} + every student read(x1 , y2 ) {⟨a book, 2⟩, ⟨every student, 1⟩} retrieve in either order The ambiguity comes from the order of retrieval. Retrieve the subject last and you get surface scope; retrieve the object last and you get inverse scope. Gain Cost one syntactic structure; ambiguity is derivational meanings are now pairs (core, store) — not just denotations 24 / 35 Mechanism 3: Continuations Give each expression access to its own surrounding context — what happens to its value once it is computed. Instead of [[α]], we compute λk. . . . k([[α]]) . . ., where k is the continuation. A quantifier is then an expression that does something interesting with its continuation: [[a book]] = λk. ∃y[book(y) ∧ k(y)] Scope ambiguity becomes the order in which continuations are composed. Gain Cost one structure, one representation level, general mechanism every type gets more complicated; hard to read Note the family resemblance: a generalized quantifier λP. . . . P . . . already is a continuation-passing denotation. Type-lifting an NP and CPS-transforming it are the same operation. Barker (2002); Barker & Shan (2014). 25 / 35 Comparing the Three QR Storage Continuations yes no no Ambiguity located in structure derivation derivation Meanings are denotations pairs denotations Generalizes beyond scope no partly yes Ease of implementation moderate easy hard Extra representation level What they share, and this is the point: every one of them adds machinery beyond function application. Composition alone does not deliver scope ambiguity. Remember this when we reach Part IV. A proposal that “contraction implements function application” inherits exactly this problem. Getting application right is necessary and not sufficient — scope needs something more, in any framework. 26 / 35 Three Quantifiers, Six Readings Every student showed a book to some teacher. Three quantifiers means up to 3! = 6 scope orderings: ∀ > ∃bk > ∃tc ∀ > ∃tc > ∃bk ∃bk > ∀ > ∃tc ∃bk > ∃tc > ∀ ∃tc > ∀ > ∃bk ∃tc > ∃bk > ∀ each student, some book, some teacher each student, some teacher, some book one book, each student showed it to someone one book, one teacher, all students one teacher, each student showed some book one teacher, one book, all students In general, n quantifiers give up to n! readings. Two consequences. For theory: any mechanism must generate all and only the available readings. For parsing: the search space is factorial, which is why systems in practice generate one reading and move on. 27 / 35 Inverse Linking Some scope facts are more surprising than others. Someone from every city despises it. The preferred reading is: ∀x[city(x) → ∃y[from(y, x) ∧ despise(y, x)]] The embedded quantifier every city takes scope over the NP containing it — and binds the pronoun it in the object position. This is called inverse linking, and it is hard for every mechanism. The quantifier must escape its own NP, outscope the NP it is embedded in, and still be available to bind a pronoun downstream. Any account that gets the simple cases right still owes an explanation here. 28 / 35 Practice: Which Reading? For each sentence, give the logical form of the reading indicated. 1 Every student read a book — inverse 2 Some student read every book — surface 3 No student read a book — surface 29 / 35 Practice: Which Reading? For each sentence, give the logical form of the reading indicated. 1 Every student read a book — inverse 2 Some student read every book — surface 3 No student read a book — surface Answers. 1 ∃y[book(y) ∧ ∀x[student(x) → read(x, y)]] 2 ∃x[student(x) ∧ ∀y[book(y) → read(x, y)]] 3 ¬∃x[student(x) ∧ ∃y[book(y) ∧ read(x, y)]] Item 3 is worth a second look: with no in subject position, the two scope orderings happen to be equivalent. Not every sentence with two quantifiers is genuinely ambiguous — some ambiguities collapse, and which ones do is determined by the monotonicity properties of the determiners involved. 29 / 35 The Entailment Between Readings inverse |= surface surface ̸|= inverse If one book was read by every student, then certainly every student read some book. The converse fails. Proof sketch of the entailment. Assume ∃y[book(y) ∧ ∀x[. . . → read(x, y)]]. Fix such a y0 . For any student x, we have read(x, y0 ) and book(y0 ), so ∃y[book(y) ∧ read(x, y)] holds. Hence the surface reading. □ This is the ∃∀ |= ∀∃ result from Session 3, with the restrictor carried along. The counter-model for the converse is on the Session 3 slide. Problem Set 1’s writeup asks you for exactly this argument — and specifically whether it holds in general or only in our model. 30 / 35 Not Every Reading Is Available Scope is not free. Some configurations are systematically unavailable. Constraint Example Effect Clause boundedness Alice thinks every student left ∀ tends to stay in its clause Islands a man who saw every boy left ∀ cannot escape the relative clause Preference every student read a book surface reading strongly preferred A theory that generates all scope permutations overgenerates. The mechanisms on the previous slides must be constrained, and how to constrain them is an active research question — not a solved problem with an implementation detail left over. This is also why real semantic parsers often generate only surface scope: the inverse reading is rarer, harder to constrain, and for most applications not worth the search-space cost. We saw that decision made explicitly in the λ-DCS lecture. 31 / 35 What This Means for Problem Set 1 Part E asks for both readings. You now have everything you need. surface :: T surface = every student (\x -> some’ book (\y -> read’ y x)) inverse :: T inverse = some’ book (\y -> every student (\x -> read’ y x)

title: Lecture 5 Extra — Monotonicity
text: Monotonicity How Determiners Drive Inference James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 (Session 5A — supplement to Session 5) 1 / 36 Why This Deserves Its Own Session Session 5 introduced monotonicity in two slides and moved on. It carries more than that. It is the only property of determiners that directly predicts inference — and inference is what a semantic theory is ultimately for. It predicts a syntactic distribution (negative polarity items) with no syntactic stipulation. It supports a computational inference procedure — Natural Logic — that works directly on surface forms, without ever building a logical form. And it is the first property we will meet that a distributional representation straightforwardly destroys. Today: definitions done properly, derivations from denotations, polarity marking, NPI licensing, and where it all breaks. 2 / 36 Today 1 Two arguments, two monotonicities 2 The full classification, and how to derive it 3 Polarity marking: computing inference on the surface 4 Nested contexts and polarity flipping 5 Negative polarity items 6 Downward-entailing environments beyond determiners 7 Natural Logic as a computational system 8 What monotonicity needs, and what loses it 3 / 36 A Determiner Has Two Arguments Recall from Session 5: a determiner is a relation between two sets. D(Q)(P ) Q |{z} restrictor P |{z} scope every student | {z } sleeps | {z } Q P So there are two independent questions: What happens if we change the restrictor, holding the scope fixed? What happens if we change the scope, holding the restrictor fixed? Session 5 only looked at the second. Both matter, and for every they go in opposite directions. 4 / 36 Right Monotonicity (the Scope) Definitions D is MON ↑ (right upward) : D(Q)(P ) and P ⊆ P ′ =⇒ D(Q)(P ′ ) D is MON ↓ (right downward) : D(Q)(P ) and P ′ ⊆ P =⇒ D(Q)(P ′ ) In words. Upward: you may replace the scope by anything more general. Downward: you may replace the scope by anything more specific. Some student jogs ⇒ Some student moves MON ↑ No student moves ⇒ No student jogs MON ↓ Note that jog ⊆ move: jogging is a way of moving. The arrows in the two rows point in opposite directions. 5 / 36 Left Monotonicity (the Restrictor) Definitions D is ↑ MON (left upward) : D(Q)(P ) and Q ⊆ Q′ =⇒ D(Q′ )(P ) D is ↓ MON (left downward) : D(Q)(P ) and Q′ ⊆ Q =⇒ D(Q′ )(P ) Every student sleeps ⇒ Every first-year student sleeps ↓ MON Some first-year student sleeps ⇒ Some student sleeps ↑ MON Notice that every behaves oppositely in its two arguments. Narrowing the restrictor preserves truth; narrowing the scope does not. That asymmetry is not a curiosity. It is what makes the NPI facts come out right, as we will see. 6 / 36 The Notation Write the two together, left arrow first: ↓ MON ↑ means left downward, right upward — which is every. Pattern Restrictor Scope ↑ MON ↑ upward upward ↓ MON ↑ downward upward ↑ MON ↓ upward downward ↓ MON ↓ downward downward A determiner may also be non-monotone in one or both arguments — neither direction of inference holds. Exactly two is the standard example, and we prove it shortly. 7 / 36 The Full Classification Determiner Pattern Condition every, all ↓ MON ↑ Q⊆P some, a ↑ MON ↑ Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ no ↓ MON ↓ Q∩P =∅ not every ↑ MON ↓ Q ̸⊆ P at least two ↑ MON ↑ |Q ∩ P | ≥ 2 at most two ↓ MON ↓ |Q ∩ P | ≤ 2 few ↓ MON ↓ (roughly) |Q ∩ P | small most non-mon. MON ↑ |Q ∩ P | > |Q − P | exactly two non-mon. non-mon. |Q ∩ P | = 2 Every cell in this table is derivable from the condition in the third column. None of it is stipulated — which is the next section. 8 / 36 Deriving: some is ↑ MON ↑ [[some]](Q)(P ) = 1 ⇐⇒ Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ Right upward. Suppose Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ and P ⊆ P ′ . Take a ∈ Q ∩ P . Then a ∈ Q, and a ∈ P ⊆ P ′ , so a ∈ P ′ . Hence a ∈ Q ∩ P ′ , so Q ∩ P ′ ̸= ∅. MON ↑ ✓ Left upward. Suppose Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ and Q ⊆ Q′ . Take a ∈ Q ∩ P . Then a ∈ Q ⊆ Q′ and a ∈ P , so a ∈ Q′ ∩ P . ↑ MON ✓ The two proofs are the same proof with the roles swapped — which is exactly what you would expect, since some is symmetric: Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ is symmetric in Q and P . 9 / 36 Deriving: every is ↓ MON ↑ [[every]](Q)(P ) = 1 ⇐⇒ Q ⊆ P Right upward. Suppose Q ⊆ P and P ⊆ P ′ . Transitivity of ⊆ gives Q ⊆ P ′ . MON ↑ ✓ Left downward. Suppose Q ⊆ P and Q′ ⊆ Q. Transitivity again: Q′ ⊆ Q ⊆ P , so Q′ ⊆ P . ↓ MON ✓ Both directions are transitivity of ⊆, read from the two ends. The subset relation is the whole content of every, and monotonicity is just what transitivity looks like when you fix one argument and vary the other. 10 / 36 Deriving: no is ↓ MON ↓ [[no]](Q)(P ) = 1 ⇐⇒ Q ∩ P = ∅ Right downward. Suppose Q ∩ P = ∅ and P ′ ⊆ P . Then Q ∩ P ′ ⊆ Q ∩ P = ∅, so Q ∩ P ′ = ∅. MON ↓ ✓ Left downward. Symmetric, for the same reason as some: the condition is symmetric. Compare some and no. Their conditions differ only by a negation: some : Q ∩ P ̸= ∅ no : Q ∩ P = ∅ And their monotonicity patterns differ by flipping both arrows: ↑ MON ↑ becomes ↓ MON ↓. Negation reverses monotonicity — a fact we will use heavily in the next section. 11 / 36 Deriving: exactly two is Non-Monotone [[exactly two]](Q)(P ) = 1 ⇐⇒ |Q ∩ P | = 2 To show non-monotonicity we need a counterexample in each direction. Let student = {a, b, c}, jog = {a, b}, move = {a, b, c}, with jog ⊆ move. Sentence |Q ∩ P | Value Exactly two students jog |{a, b}| = 2 true Exactly two students move |{a, b, c}| = 3 false So not MON ↑. And going the other way, with sprint = {a}: Exactly two students sprint is false (|{a}| = 1), so not MON ↓ either. The reason is structural: exactly n is a conjunction of an upward condition (≥ n) and a downward one (≤ n). Conjoining opposite monotonicities gives none. 12 / 36 Practice: Classify These Give the monotonicity pattern, and justify with an inference or a counterexample. 1 2 3 4 at least three fewer than five both neither 13 / 36 Practice: Classify These Give the monotonicity pattern, and justify with an inference or a counterexample. 1 2 3 4 at least three fewer than five both neither Answers. 1 ↑ MON ↑ — |Q ∩ P | ≥ 3; enlarging either set can only grow the intersection. 2 ↓ MON ↓ — |Q ∩ P | < 5; shrinking either set can only shrink it. 3 MON ↑ in scope, and non-monotone in restrictor (it presupposes |Q| = 2, so changing Q breaks the presupposition). 4 ↓ MON ↓ in the same way no is, with the same presupposition caveat. Items 3 and 4 show that presuppositions interact with monotonicity — when changing an argument destroys a presupposition, the inference fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the monotonicity pattern itself. 13 / 36 From Property to Procedure So far monotonicity is a fact about individual determiners. Now make it a calculus. The idea Mark every position in a sentence with a polarity: + if it occurs in an upward-entailing position, − if downward. Then: at a + position you may substitute something more general; at a − position, something more specific. This turns inference into a local edit. No logical form, no theorem prover — just replace one word and check the polarity of its position. The system is van Benthem’s monotonicity calculus, developed by Sánchez Valencia as Natural Logic. 14 / 36 Marking a Simple Sentence Every student− jogs+ Every is ↓ MON ↑: restrictor gets −, scope gets +. Now read off the licensed inferences. Edit Position Result student → first-year student −, so narrow ✓ Every first-year student jogs jogs → moves +, so widen ✓ Every student moves student → person −, widening × not licensed jogs → sprints +, narrowing × not licensed And edits compose: Every first-year student moves follows, by making both licensed edits at once. 15 / 36 Marking with no No student− moves− No is ↓ MON ↓, so both arguments are negative. No student moves ⇒ No first-year student moves narrow the restrictor No student moves ⇒ No student jogs narrow the scope No student moves ⇒ No first-year student jogs both at once Compare with some, which is ↑ MON ↑ — both positions positive, and every inference runs the other way. One determiner choice flips the entire inferential behaviour of the sentence. That is a lot of work for one word, and it is why the classification table earns its keep. 16 / 36 Nested Contexts: Polarity Flips Polarity is computed by composing the operators a position sits under. The rule Start at + at the root. Each downward-entailing operator you pass through flips the polarity. One flip. No student who owns a car− is happy The restrictor of no is DE, so narrowing car to sports car is licensed. Two flips. Every student who doesn’t own a car+ is happy Operator Effect Running polarity — restrictor of every doesn’t start flip flip + − + Check: widening car to vehicle gives every student who doesn’t own a vehicle is happy. Non-vehicle-owners are a subset of non-car-owners, so the restrictor narrowed — licensed. ✓ 17 / 36 Double Negation No student failed to move+ Two downward operators stack: Operator Effect Running polarity — no (scope) failed to start flip flip + − + So the inference runs upward: No student failed to jog ⇒ No student failed to move Correct — it says every student jogged, hence every student moved. Polarity composes multiplicatively: two negatives make a positive, exactly as in arithmetic. An even number of DE operators restores upward entailment. 18 / 36 The Data Some expressions occur only in certain environments. Sentence Environment ok No student had any money scope of no ∗ Some student had any money scope of some ∗ Every student had any money scope of every ok Every student who had any money left restrictor of every ok Alice didn’t have any money under negation ok Few students had any money scope of few Any, ever, yet, lift a finger, budge an inch all pattern alike. Six environments, and the acceptable ones look unrelated at first glance. What do no, the restrictor of every, negation, and few have in common? 19 / 36 Ladusaw’s Generalization Ladusaw (1979) Negative polarity items are licensed exactly in downward-entailing environments. Check it against the data: Environment Polarity NPI? scope of no scope of some scope of every restrictor of every under negation scope of few − + + − − − ok ∗ ∗ ok ok ok Perfect correspondence. A semantic property — how a position behaves under set inclusion — predicts a syntactic fact about where a word may appear. Note the crucial case: every licenses NPIs in one argument and not the other. No account treating every as uniformly positive or negative could get that right. 20 / 36 Why It Might Be True The generalization is robust. Why would language work this way? One influential answer (Kadmon & Landman; Krifka; Chierchia). NPIs like any are domain wideners: they signal that even the most marginal cases are included. In a downward environment, widening the domain makes the statement stronger. I don’t have any money is stronger than I don’t have money. In an upward environment, widening makes it weaker — and asserting a gratuitously weakened claim is odd. So the licensing condition falls out of a pragmatic preference for strength, given the monotonicity of the position. This is a good example of the division of labour in semantics: the distribution is predicted by monotonicity, and the reason for it is pragmatic. 21 / 36 Where the Generalization Strains Only licenses NPIs — but is not downward entailing in the relevant argument. Only Alice had any money. ok And the restrictor of every is DE only under a presupposition. Consider: Every student left ⇒ Every student with a hat left Fine — unless the inference requires that there be students with hats. Von Fintel’s repair: Strawson downward entailment. Require the inference to go through only when the conclusion’s presuppositions are satisfied. Under that weakening, only is Strawson-DE and the generalization survives. Worth seeing: a clean generalization, a genuine counterexample, and a principled weakening that rescues it. That is how this field actually progresses. 22 / 36 Downward-Entailing Environments Determiners are not the only source of negative polarity. Environment Example NPI ok? sentential negation antecedent of a conditional before-clause without comparative rarely, seldom Alice didn’t ever call If you have any questions, ask She left before anyone arrived He left without any warning Taller than anyone here She rarely says anything yes yes yes yes yes yes after-clause often ∗She left after anyone arrived ∗She often says anything no no Check the DE claim on before: She left before anyone arrived entails She left before any student arrived — narrowing the scope preserves truth. After does not work this way, and correspondingly blocks NPIs. 23 / 36 A Minimal Pair Worth Knowing Few students passed. vs. A few students passed. Monotonicity NPI few ↓ MON ↓ Few students said anything ok a few ↑ MON ↑ ∗A few students said anything ∗ One indefinite article, and the entire inferential profile inverts. This is the cleanest available demonstration that NPI licensing tracks monotonicity rather than anything about negation, form, or lexical marking. The two expressions are nearly identical in shape and meaning; only the direction of entailment differs. Test it yourself: Few students moved ⇒ Few students jogged ✓; A few students jogged ⇒ A few students moved ✓. Opposite directions. 24 / 36 Inference Without Logical Forms Everything so far suggests a computational procedure. premise mark polarities apply edits conclusion Natural Logic (Sánchez Valencia; MacCartney & Manning) does inference by editing surface forms, using a lexical resource such as WordNet to know which words are more general than which. No logical form is ever built Edits are local Limited expressiveness no parsing to formulas, no theorem prover one word at a time, composable no arithmetic, no long chains of reasoning The trade: much less power than first-order inference, at a tiny fraction of the cost — and it covers a surprising share of the entailments in natural text. 25 / 36 A Natural Logic Derivation Premise: No student who owns a car commutes by bus. Question: does it entail No first-year student who owns a sports car commutes by school bus? Edit Direction Position Licensed? student → first-year student car → sports car bus → school bus narrow narrow narrow restrictor of no, − inside restrictor, − scope of no, − yes yes yes All three licensed — the entailment holds. Every position in this sentence is negative, because no is ↓ MON ↓ and both of its arguments therefore narrow. Now change one edit. Replace the second with car → vehicle — a widening at a − position. Not licensed, and the counterexample is easy: a student who owns a motorcycle but no car, and commutes by bus. The premise is silent about her; the conclusion is not. 26 / 36 Monotonicity Requires an Order Look at what every definition today had in common. P ⊆ P′ =⇒ ... Every statement of monotonicity is a claim about ⊆. The sets of individuals form a partial order under inclusion, and a determiner is a map between orders that either preserves or reverses it. Monotone increasing Monotone decreasing Non-monotone order-preserving order-reversing neither This is the same notion of monotonicity as in analysis or order theory. Nothing about it is linguistic — what is linguistic is the empirical claim that determiner meanings are almost always monotone in each argument. 27 / 36 And Orders Are Exactly What Vectors Lose Session 6B encodes a predicate as an indicator vector p ∈ {0, 1}n . Sets Indicator vectors Order P ⊆ P′ p ≤ p′ componentwise Monotonicity well defined well defined In the exact regime, everything survives. Componentwise ≤ on indicator vectors is exactly ⊆, so today’s results transfer unchanged. In the approximate regime, it does not. Dense embeddings have no natural partial order — vjog is not “≤” vmove in any sense the geometry provides. And with no order, there is no monotonicity, and therefore no natural-logic inference. So the loss we described abstractly in Session 6B has a concrete casualty: this entire session’s inference machinery. 28 / 36 Case Study: few vs. a few Take the minimal pair from earlier and ask what each framework does with it. In the exact encoding (Session 6B), with a the restrictor and b the scope: few(Q)(P ) ⇐⇒ a · b < k Condition a few(Q)(P ) ⇐⇒ a · b ≥ k Shrink either set few a·b<k intersection shrinks, still < k ↓ MON ↓ a few a·b≥k needs growth, not shrinkage ↑ MON ↑ Both compute the same inner product. They differ only in the comparison operator: < versus ≥. One bit, in the decision boundary — and the entire inferential profile follows from it. 29 / 36 Why Dense Distributions Fail Here Three independent problems, any one of which is fatal. 1 Distributional near-identity. Few and a few occur in the same slots, with the same nouns, in the same registers. Their co-occurrence profiles are about as similar as two English expressions get. The distributional hypothesis therefore predicts they mean nearly the same thing — and it is confidently wrong. 2 The distinguishing token is a stopword. The whole contrast is carried by a. Any pipeline with stopword removal makes the two expressions literally identical — standard practice in distributional semantics for decades. 3 No order, so nowhere to put the flip. Even granting the model distinguishes them, ↓ MON ↓ versus ↑ MON ↑ is a fact about how an operator transforms ⊆. With no partial order on meanings, there is no structure for “reverses the order” to be a property of. Note that (1) is worse than having no opinion: the framework makes a prediction, and the prediction is inverted. 30 / 36 Can a Transformer Do It? In principle, yes. Contextual embeddings compose a and few into a distinct representation, so the two phrases are not forced to be identical the way a bag-of-words model forces them to be. But notice what has to be learned. Not that they are different words — that their entailment direction is opposite. That is a functional property, acquirable only from enough downward- versus upward-entailing contrasts. Working against it downward-entailing contexts are comparatively rare in text the cue is one high-frequency function word the correct inference reverses, rather than weakening Empirically this pair appears in monotonicity NLI datasets — HELP, MED — precisely because it is handled unevenly, with the downward direction weaker. Which is the honest verdict: not impossible, not reliable, and expensive to get right. 31 / 36 What Would Actually Be Required 1 A partial order on predicate meanings. Solved — order embeddings, box embeddings, hyperbolic embeddings all supply one. 2 Determiners as monotone maps between ordered spaces, with a provable direction in each argument. Open. 3 A mechanism for the flip. Order-reversal is discrete — a sign change — and continuous machinery does not produce discrete decisions naturally. Compare what the symbolic account needed: a single comparison operator. The difference between < and ≥ is not something a continuous representation has a natural home for — and that, rather than any lack of expressive power, is why this minimal pair is hard. It is also a good test to run yourself. Take any embedding model, and check whether it distinguishes the two in a way that supports the right inferences. The answer is informative either way. 32 / 36 An Open Question Can a distributional representation support monotonicity? Attempts exist. Order embeddings (Vendrov et al.): embed so that p ≤ p′ componentwise encodes hyponymy. Imposes an order by construction. Box embeddings: represent concepts as axis-aligned regions, with containment as the order. Hyperbolic embeddings: exploit the tree-like geometry of hyperbolic space to encode hierarchy. All three work by putting the order back in — choosing a geometry in which inclusion has a meaning. None of them gets it for free. A candidate final project: take a monotonicity-marked inference dataset, and measure whether any of these representa

title: Lecture 5 Extra — Negative Polarity Items (NPIs)
text: Negative Polarity Items A Semantic Property That Predicts a Syntactic Distribution James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 (Session 5B — supplement to Session 5A) 1 / 19 The Phenomenon Some expressions are picky about where they occur. ok Alice didn’t see anyone. ∗ Alice saw anyone. ok Nobody has ever been to Mars. ∗ Somebody has ever been to Mars. ok Bob didn’t lift a finger to help. ∗ Bob lifted a finger to help. (on the idiomatic reading) These are negative polarity items (NPIs). The obvious first hypothesis — they need a negation — is close, and wrong. Today: what actually licenses them, why it is a monotonicity fact, and how far the generalization holds. 2 / 19 The Inventory English has a large and heterogeneous NPI vocabulary. Kind Examples Note Determiners any, a single Adverbs ever, yet, at all, anymore Minimizers a red cent, a wink, a drop literal small quantities Idioms lift a finger, budge an inch idiomatic reading only Durative in years, in weeks stricter licensing Aspectual until (punctual), either stricter licensing Note the last two rows. Not all NPIs are licensed in the same environments — some need a stronger licensor. That is the strength hierarchy, and we return to it. Minimizers are revealing: he didn’t drink a drop means he drank nothing at all. The literal smallness is doing semantic work. 3 / 19 The Mirror Image: Positive Polarity Some expressions are picky in the opposite direction. ok Alice saw someone. ∗ Alice didn’t see someone. ok Bob would rather stay. ∗ Bob wouldn’t rather stay. (narrow-scope reading) Positive polarity items (PPIs) are anti-licensed in the very environments that license NPIs. Alice didn’t see someone is not ungrammatical — it has a wide-scope reading: ∃x ¬see(a, x), “there is someone she didn’t see”. What is blocked is the narrow-scope reading, where someone sits inside the negation. So NPIs and PPIs partition environments between them — which is already evidence that a single semantic property is doing the work. 4 / 19 The Licensing Data Environment Example sentential negation no (scope) every (restrictor) every (scope) some (scope) few a few conditional antecedent conditional consequent before after without comparative Alice didn’t ever call No student had any money Every student who had any money left Every student had any money Some student had any money Few students said anything A few students said anything If you have any questions, ask If you ask, I have any answers She left before anyone arrived She left after anyone arrived He left without any warning Taller than anyone here ok ok ok ∗ ∗ ok ∗ ok ∗ ok ∗ ok ok Thirteen environments. What do the seven acceptable ones share? Not negation — only two of them contain a negative word. 5 / 19 Ladusaw’s Generalization Ladusaw (1979) An NPI is licensed exactly in a downward-entailing position. Environment Polarity NPI sentential negation no (scope) every (restrictor) every (scope) some (scope) few a few conditional antecedent before after − − − + + − + − − + ok ok ok ∗ ∗ ok ∗ ok ok ∗ A perfect match. A semantic property — behaviour under set inclusion — predicts a syntactic distribution, with no syntactic stipulation anywhere. 6 / 19 The Crucial Case ok Every student who had any money left ∗ Every student had any money Same determiner. Same NPI. Different argument. Recall that every is ↓ MON ↑ — downward in its restrictor, upward in its scope. The NPI is licensed in the first and only the first. No theory that treats every as uniformly “positive” or “negative” can get this right. The licensing condition has to be stated per argument position, which is exactly what monotonicity does and what a lexical feature like [±neg] cannot. This single contrast is the strongest evidence for Ladusaw’s generalization, and it is why we spent Session 5A separating left from right monotonicity. 7 / 19 How to Test a Position for DE A procedure you can apply to any environment. 1 2 3 4 Find a pair of predicates where one is more specific: jog ⊆ move, poodle ⊆ dog. Put the general one in the position and check the sentence is true. Substitute the specific one. If truth is preserved, the position is downward entailing. Worked: the before-clause. She left before anyone arrived Test: She left before a student arrived — does She left before a first-year student arrived follow? Yes. If she left before any arrival at all, she left before the more specific ones too. DE ✓ Now try after: She left after a student arrived does not entail She left after a first-year student arrived. Not DE — and correspondingly it blocks NPIs. 8 / 19 Not All Downward Contexts Are Equal Ladusaw’s generalization is not quite the whole story. Consider: ok At most three students have ever been to Paris. ? At most three students have been to Paris in years. ok No student has ever been to Paris. ok No student has been to Paris in years. Both at most three and no are downward entailing. But only no licenses in years. So NPIs come in strengths, and DE-ness comes in strengths to match. The rest of this session is about that correspondence. Ever and any are weak NPIs; in years, until, and either are strong. 9 / 19 Anti-Additivity A strictly stronger property than downward entailment. Anti-additive f is anti-additive iff f (A ∨ B) ≡ f (A) ∧ f (B) Test it on no: No student sang or danced ≡ No student sang and no student danced ✓ Test it on at most three: At most three students sang or danced Not equivalent to at most three sang and at most three danced. Suppose two sang and two others danced: both conjuncts hold, but four students sang-or-danced. ∗ So no is anti-additive and at most three is merely DE — exactly tracking which one licenses in years. 10 / 19 The Zwarts Hierarchy Three nested classes of negative strength, with NPI classes to match. Class Condition Licensors Licenses Downward entailing Anti-additive Antimorphic A ⊆ B ⇒ f (B) ⊆ f (A) + f (A ∨ B) = f (A) ∧ f (B) + f (A ∧ B) = f (A) ∨ f (B) few, at most three no, without not (sentential) weak: any, ever strong: in years superstrong antimorphic ⊊ anti-additive ⊊ downward entailing A graded licensing condition. The stronger the NPI, the stronger the licensor it demands — and the classes line up exactly. 11 / 19 Structure Matters, Not Word Order Linear precedence is not enough. The licensor must be structurally superior to the NPI. ok No one who has any money is here. ∗ Someone who has no money has any friends. In the second, no precedes any linearly — but it is buried inside a relative clause modifying the subject, and does not take scope over the main predicate. The licensor must c-command the NPI — equivalently, the NPI must lie inside the licensor’s semantic scope. Which is just to say: polarity is computed over the derivation, not over the string. This matters computationally. A model that keys on the presence of a negative word nearby will get these wrong, and the minimal pairs to catch it are easy to construct. 12 / 19 Cases That Strain the Generalization 1. Only. Licenses NPIs, but is not DE in the relevant argument. Only Alice had any money. ok 2. Questions. License NPIs with no DE operator in sight. Did anyone call? ok 3. Comparatives. Alice is taller than anyone here. ok 4. The restrictor of every is DE only if the conclusion’s presupposition is met. Four genuine counterexamples. The generalization is too good to abandon and too leaky to leave as it stands — so the literature repaired it. 13 / 19 Von Fintel’s Repair: Strawson-DE Strawson downward entailment (von Fintel 1999) A position is Strawson-DE if the inference goes through whenever the conclusion’s presuppositions are satisfied. Apply it to only. Only Alice sings. ⇒ Only Alice sings loudly. This fails in general — but only Alice sings loudly presupposes that Alice sings loudly. Grant that presupposition, and the inference goes through. So only is Strawson-DE, and Ladusaw’s generalization survives — restated with Strawson-DE in place of plain DE. Worth noticing the shape of this episode: a clean generalization, real counterexamples, and a principled weakening that keeps the predictive content. That is what progress looks like here. 14 / 19 Why Would Language Work This Way? Ladusaw’s generalization describes. It does not explain. The domain-widening account (Kadmon & Landman 1993; Krifka; Chierchia). An NPI like any widens the domain of quantification — it signals that even marginal cases are included. Context Widening makes the claim Result downward stronger informative, licensed upward weaker gratuitously weak, blocked Check it. I don’t have any money is stronger than I don’t have money — it rules out even a penny. But I have any money would be weaker than I have money, and asserting a deliberately weakened claim is odd. So the distribution is predicted by monotonicity, and the reason is pragmatic. A nice division of labour. 15 / 19 NPIs as a Probe for Neural Models NPI licensing is an unusually good diagnostic, and it is used as one. Minimal pairs are easy to build automatically, differing in one word. Acceptability is sharp, and native judgements agree. Getting it right requires hierarchical structure, not surface cues — the c-command slide. The strength hierarchy gives graded difficulty for free. BLiMP and the NPI-licensing probes of Warstadt et al. are built on exactly this. Models do well on the easy cases and less well where the licensor is structurally embedded — consistent with keying on surface proximity. And notice what building such a benchmark requires: the DE classification, the strength hierarchy, and the c-command condition. You cannot test a model for this without first having the theory. 16 / 19 Summary Point Detail NPIs PPIs Ladusaw The crucial case Testing DE Strength Anti-additive c-command Strawson-DE Domain widening As a probe any, ever, lift a finger, in years, . . . the mirror image: some, would rather licensed exactly in downward-entailing positions every licenses in its restrictor, not its scope substitute a more specific predicate; check truth survives weak (DE), strong (anti-additive), superstrong (antimorphic) f (A ∨ B) = f (A) ∧ f (B); no yes, at most three no structure, not linear order von Fintel’s repair; rescues only why: widening strengthens in DE, weakens in UE sharp judgements, automatic minimal pairs, needs structure 17 / 19 Reading and Exercises Reading: Ladusaw (1979), Polarity Sensitivity as Inherent Scope Relations Zwarts (1998), Three Types of Polarity von Fintel (1999), NPI Licensing, Strawson Entailment, and Context Dependency Chierchia (2013), Logic in Grammar — the pragmatic derivation Warstadt et al. (2019) on NPI licensing as a probe Exercises: 1 Classify seldom, rarely, hardly for DE, anti-additivity, antimorphism. 2 Construct a minimal pair distinguishing linear precedence from c-command. 3 Nobody who didn’t bring any money was admitted — is any licensed? Compute the polarity and check against your judgement. 4 Find an environment where your judgement and Ladusaw’s generalization disagree. Then decide which one is wrong. 18 / 19

title: Lecture 5 Extra — Taking Stock
text: Where We Are, and Where We Are Going A Positioning Note James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 1 / 22 A Fair Question We have spent six sessions on lambda calculus, types, models, quantifiers, monotonicity, and possible worlds. Meanwhile, a large language model answers all of these questions. So: why are we doing this? Today’s answer, in one line: Because the structure we have been building is what those systems are spending enormous resources to approximate — and it is not clear they have it. 2 / 22 What We Have Built Session Machinery Guarantees 1–2 typed lambda calculus composition is exact and total 3 models, satisfaction truth is defined, and computable 4 the fragment the whole thing runs 5 generalized quantifiers scope, and what determiners can mean 5A monotonicity inference falls out of the denotations 6 worlds, context change belief, modality, discourse The word to notice is guarantees. These are not tendencies or high-probability behaviors. Given the lexicon, the entailments follow — always, for every sentence, including ones nobody has written down. That is an unusual property for a system to have, and worth knowing the price of. 3 / 22 Monotonicity, Concretely Today’s material is the sharpest example. No student who owns a car commutes by bus. From no being ↓ MON ↓, it follows — with no training, no data, no examples — that this entails: No first-year student who owns a car commutes by bus No student who owns a sports car commutes by school bus and every other narrowing of either argument, without bound One lexical fact licenses an infinite family of inferences. The generalization is not learned from examples; it is a consequence of what no means. A system that learns these one at a time is doing something fundamentally different — and paying for it. 4 / 22 How a Transformer Does This Instead Attention computes, for each pair of positions, a learned compatibility:   QK ⊤ Attn(Q, K, V ) = softmax √ V d What it is a learned, soft, weighted mixture over positions What it is not a typed operation with a determinate result Relations are encoded in the learned matrices WQ , WK , WV — one set per head, per layer. Whatever structure the model has is distributed across them. This is genuinely powerful, and it is how every deployed system works. The question is not whether it works. The question is what it costs, and what it guarantees. 5 / 22 Three Things Attention Does Not Give You 1 Typing. Nothing prevents combining two representations that should not compose. Every pair of positions gets a score; there is no undefined. 2 An order on meanings. Monotonicity needs ⊆. Dense vectors have no partial order — so nothing in the representation makes jog ⊆ move. 3 Exactness. Softmax returns a distribution. There is no step at which a derivation is complete and a result determined. These are not bugs. They are the price of a representation that is continuous, learnable, and differentiable — which is exactly what buys similarity, robustness, and coverage. But they are the three properties Sessions 1–6 spent their time establishing. 6 / 22 Can a Distributional Model Get Monotonicity? People have tried. It helps to see that two different things are being asked for. What is needed Example Lexical an order on concepts jog ⊑ move Functional how an operator transforms that order no reverses it These are separable problems, and the literature has made much more progress on the first. But today’s session was entirely about the second. Knowing that jogging is a way of moving tells you nothing about whether No student jogs follows from No student moves. 7 / 22 Approach 1: Polarity as an Input Feature The most direct route: mark each token with its polarity and hand that to the model. A determiner contributes a two-bit signature — one bit per argument: Determiner Restrictor Scope every some no not every − + − + + + − − Propagate those bits over the spans and you get a token-level annotation: No student− who owns− a car− commutes− by bus− Every student− who owns− a car− commutes+ by bus+ Then add a learned polarity embedding: xi = ei + p± . The model now has the information. 8 / 22 Does the Markup Work? Yes — and that is exactly the problem. Systems given polarity features improve substantially on downward-entailing inference. (Hu, Chen & Moss and related work on monotonicity marking from CCG or UD parses.) But ask where the bits came from. They were computed by a symbolic procedure — the polarity calculus from Session 5A, run over a parse. So the pipeline is: parse → determiner lookup → polarity composition → neural model. The theory does the monotonicity; the network does everything else. Three costs follow. You need a parser, and errors propagate. You need a lexicon of determiner signatures — written by hand. The model has not learned monotonicity. It has been told. 9 / 22 Approach 2: Put the Order Into the Geometry Rather than annotating, change the representation so that inclusion means something. Scheme Entailment is Idea Order embeddings u ≤ v componentwise train in the positive orthant Box embeddings box containment concepts as axis-aligned regions Hyperbolic (Poincaré) position in the hierarchy trees embed with low distortion Density embeddings KL divergence concepts as Gaussians These genuinely solve the lexical problem. They give a partial order on concepts, learned from data, in a continuous space — which is precisely what plain dense embeddings lack. Note what they have in common: each chooses a geometry in which containment is expressible. None of them gets an order for free from the vectors. 10 / 22 The Gap That Remains Order embeddings tell you jog ⊑ move. They do not tell you what no does to ⊑. Problem Status Solved by Lexical order Functional monotonicity largely solved open order / box / hyperbolic embeddings no standard account What would be needed: a determiner represented as an operator that is provably order-preserving or order-reversing in each argument — a monotone map between ordered spaces, not merely a learned matrix. Monotone networks exist: constrain weights to be non-negative and the function is increasing. But decreasing needs a sign flip, and choosing when to flip is a discrete decision the continuous machinery does not naturally make. 11 / 22 Why This Is a Good Example for This Course 1 The property is precisely stated. Not “does it understand negation” but: is this operator order-reversing in its second argument? That is checkable. 2 The symbolic account is complete. Session 5A derived every case from the denotations, in a few lines each. 3 The distributional account is partial, and we can say exactly which part. Lexical order, yes. Functional behaviour, not yet. 4 And the repair attempts all do the same thing: choose a richer geometry so that the structure has somewhere to live. That last point is the whole argument for Parts III and IV. Order embeddings choose a cone; box embeddings choose regions; geometric algebra chooses grades and an invertible product. Each is a bet that the right geometry makes the structure expressible. 12 / 22 The Cost, in Resources What does it take to approximate structure statistically? Resource Symbolic Learned Lexicon written once inferred from billions of tokens A new entailment derived must appear, or be generalized to Inference at test time one substitution a full forward pass Chained reasoning free, by transitivity often needs explicit steps in context Guarantee by construction empirical, per-input Note the fourth row. A monotonicity chain of ten steps is ten substitutions and costs nothing extra. In a generative system it becomes ten reasoning steps, emitted as tokens, each an opportunity for error. Chain-of-thought is, among other things, a way of buying back compositionality at inference time — by the token. 13 / 22 The Empirical Question Do learned models actually acquire the structure? Benchmark Tests Design SCAN compositional generalization train on parts, test on combinations COGS sentence → logical form novel structures at test time CFQ question → query maximum compound divergence Monotonicity NLI today’s material DE/UE contexts, systematically varied The construction is always the same. Train on jump, walk twice, run left; test on jump twice. A compositional system generalizes for free. Results have improved a great deal and remain uneven — particularly on downward-entailing contexts, where the correct inference reverses. That is a natural place for a statistical learner to fail: DE contexts are rarer in text, and the 14 / 22 surface cue is a single word. What These Benchmarks Presuppose To ask whether a model composes, you need a theory of what composing is. Every benchmark on the previous slide is built by someone who: wrote a grammar to generate the items; used a compositional semantics to compute the gold answers; and chose the train/test split by a structural criterion. Sessions 1–6 are the machinery those people used. You are not learning an alternative to modern NLP; you are learning the standard against which it is measured. The same holds for evaluation more broadly: an entailment dataset is only as good as the semantics used to label it. 15 / 22 The Honest Position Two overclaims to avoid, in both directions. Wrong: “Neural models don’t really understand; symbols are needed.” They work, at a scale and robustness no symbolic system approaches. Also wrong: “Scale solved it; this material is history.” The guarantees are not there, and the benchmarks that test for them say so. The defensible position: each tradition has exactly what the other lacks. Logic has structure without similarity; distribution has similarity without structure. Whether one substrate can carry both is an open research question — and it is the question this course is organized around. 16 / 22 The Arc, Restated no similarity 1. Logic exact composition no composition 2. Distribution similarity, learning not closed 3. Linear algebra the geometry underneath no semantics 4. Geometric alg. one invertible product 5. FGA semantics on that substrate We are finishing Theme 1. Everything from Session 1 to today has been building the left-hand box — and establishing, precisely, what is missing from it. Next week Theme 2 begins, and the red label above the first arrow becomes the subject. 17 / 22 What Happens to Today’s Material Today In Part II In Parts III–IV types lost candidate: grade composition lossy candidate: contraction monotonicity no order, so gone open binding approximate candidate: wedge product worlds, discourse no counterpart open The middle column is why Part II is not the end of the course. Everything we built gets lost on the way into vector space. The right column is the bet. Geometric algebra has operations with the right formal shape — graded, invertible, order-sensitive. Whether they can carry a semantics is what Sessions 17–24 examine, and what Problem Set 3 asks you to test. 18 / 22 Why You Are Learning Both If you build systems you will write evaluation sets, and the gold labels come from a compositional semantics. If you do research the open questions in this area are stated in the vocabulary of Sessions 1–6. If you do neither you will still need to judge claims about what models understand — and that requires a standard. The skill this course is actually teaching is knowing what a representation guarantees. That is a question you can ask of a lambda term, a knowledge graph, an embedding, an attention head, or a multivector. The answer differs, and the difference is what determines what you can safely build on it. 19 / 22 Two Questions to Carry Forward 1 What does this representation guarantee? Not: what does it usually do. What follows, by construction, for inputs nobody has seen? 2 What does it cost to get that guarantee some other way? In parameters, in tokens, in training data, in inference-time compute — and in confidence that it will hold next time. Ask both of every framework in the rest of this course — including the one I am proposing in Part IV. Problem Set 3 explicitly asks you what the geometric account cannot do, and a well-argued negative result earns full marks. 20 / 22 Back to Work Today: monotonicity in depth, then modality, intensionality, and dynamics. Then: λ-DCS — the symbolic tradition at Freebase scale — and semantic types as vectors, which is the bridge. Next week: Part II. Meaning from data. Keep the monotonicity material in view when we get to Session 10. When we show that vector composition loses structure, you will already know one precise thing it loses — and you will be able to say exactly which inferences go with it. 21 / 22 Questions? Now: monotonicity 22 / 22

title: Lecture 6 — Beyond the Sentence
text: Session 6: Beyond the Sentence Modality, Intensionality, and Dynamics James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics September 15, 2026 1 / 32 Where We Are Sessions 1–5 built a semantics that works. It is: compositional — meanings built from parts by typed application; truth-conditional — every sentence gets a value in a model; computable — over a finite domain, satisfaction is a program. It is also, in two specific ways, too small. Extensional a predicate is its extension Sentence-level each sentence is evaluated on its own Today: what each restriction costs, and what the standard repairs look like. This is a survey — we will see the shape of two large literatures rather than work through either. 2 / 32 Today 1 The extensionality problem 2 Possible worlds; intensional types 3 Modality: must, might, necessarily 4 Propositional attitudes; de re and de dicto 5 The anaphora problem 6 Dynamic semantics: meaning as context change 7 Discourse Representation Theory 8 What carries into Part II Nothing today is on Problem Set 1, and Sessions 12–24 do not use it. It is here because a semantics course that never mentions these boundaries would be misrepresenting the field. 3 / 32 A Predicate Is Its Extension In our fragment, [[dog]] is the set of dogs. That is the whole story. Now suppose, as a matter of biological fact, that exactly the same creatures have hearts and kidneys. Then [[creature with a heart]] = [[creature with a kidney]] Our semantics says these two predicates mean the same thing. That is wrong, and demonstrably so. Alice is looking for a creature with a heart and Alice is looking for a creature with a kidney can differ in truth value — so meaning must be finer-grained than extension. The example is Quine’s. It is the standard demonstration that coextensive is not cosignificant. 4 / 32 Three Symptoms of the Same Disease Phenomenon What breaks Coextensive predicates identified, though they differ in meaning Attitude reports Alice believes Bob left gets no truth conditions Modal claims Bob might have left is about how things could be All three want the same thing: a way to talk about how things are not, but could be. Our model has one world. Everything true in it is settled, and everything false is simply false. There is no room for alternatives — and every phenomenon above requires alternatives. The repair is to add them. 5 / 32 Possible Worlds The move Replace the single model with a set of worlds W. Each w ∈ W is a complete way things might be — its own interpretation function Iw . Denotation becomes world-relative: [[α]]w . w1 Bob left w2 Bob stayed w3 Bob left, Alice too . . . and so on Extension of φ at w its truth value in that world Intension of φ the function from worlds to truth values A proposition is an intension of a sentence: equivalently, the set of worlds where it is true. 6 / 32 Intensional Types Add a new basic type s for worlds. Then for any type τ , the type ⟨s, τ ⟩ is an intension. Type Denotes Called t ⟨s, t⟩ ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨s, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ e ⟨s, e⟩ a truth value worlds → truth values a set of individuals worlds → sets an individual worlds → individuals extension of a sentence a proposition extension of a predicate a property an individual concept Now creature with a heart and creature with a kidney can differ: same set in our world, different sets in some other — so their intensions differ, and meaning is intension. The Queen of England is the standard individual concept: a different person depending on the world, and on the time. 7 / 32 The Cost Extensional Intensional Basic types e, t e, t, s Type of a sentence t ⟨s, t⟩ Type of a noun ⟨e, t⟩ ⟨s, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ Every denotation as written wrapped in a world argument Every type in the fragment gains an s. Montague’s PTQ does this uniformly, and the denotations become considerably harder to read. This is why most working systems stay extensional. The intensional apparatus is well understood and expensive, and for question answering over a database there is only one world anyway. Knowing when you can afford to ignore it is part of the skill. 8 / 32 Frege’s Puzzle The oldest form of the problem, and still the cleanest. The Morning Star is the Evening Star. Both expressions refer to Venus. So extensionally, the sentence says venus = venus — a triviality, knowable a priori. But the identity was an astronomical discovery. Someone can competently understand both terms and not know they corefer. Frege (1892): expressions have both a Bedeutung (reference) and a Sinn (sense) — a “mode of presentation”. Possible-worlds intensions make sense precise: two terms differ in sense if they pick out different things in some world. It is not the only way, and arguably not a fully satisfying one — see the next slide. 9 / 32 Where Possible Worlds Are Still Too Coarse Intensions fix coextension. They do not fix everything. Alice believes that 2 + 2 = 4. Alice believes that every group of prime order is cyclic. Both complements are necessarily true — true at every possible world. So both denote the same proposition: the set of all worlds. Our semantics therefore predicts that anyone who believes one believes the other. That is false: mathematical ignorance is possible. The problem of logical omniscience. A possible-worlds account makes every agent believe all the consequences of what they believe. This is a genuine open problem, not a detail — and proposals to fix it (impossible worlds, structured propositions, hyperintensions) are all live. 10 / 32 Intensional Verbs Some verbs create intensional contexts, and some do not. The difference is testable. Verb Example Entails existence? find Alice found a unicorn yes — extensional seek Alice sought a unicorn no — intensional own Alice owns a unicorn yes want Alice wants a unicorn no Two further diagnostics for intensionality: Substitution failure. If the morning star is the evening star, Alice seeks the morning star does not entail Alice seeks the evening star. Scope ambiguity. Intensional verbs give de re/de dicto readings; extensional ones do not. The type of seek must take a quantifier intension rather than an entity: ⟨⟨s, ⟨⟨e, t⟩, t⟩⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩. Montague’s PTQ is largely an argument about getting this type right. 11 / 32 Modal Operators With worlds in hand, modality is quantification over them. Operator Reading Truth at w □φ necessarily φ φ true at all worlds accessible from w ♢φ possibly φ φ true at some world accessible from w □ is ∀ over worlds; ♢ is ∃ over worlds. The duality is the same one from Session 3: ¬□φ ≡ ♢¬φ ¬♢φ ≡ □¬φ Accessibility R ⊆ W × W says which worlds count as alternatives from where you stand. Different choices of R give different flavors of modality. 12 / 32 flavors of Modality The same words express different modalities, distinguished by what R is. flavor Accessible worlds Example Epistemic compatible with what is known Bob might be home Deontic compatible with the rules You must file by Friday Alethic metaphysically possible 2 + 2 must equal 4 Bouletic compatible with someone’s wishes I want it to rain Bob must be home is ambiguous between epistemic (I infer it) and deontic (he is required to be). One semantics, parameterized. The modal operator is fixed; the accessibility relation varies with context. That is Kratzer’s analysis, and it is the standard treatment. 13 / 32 Properties of R Become Logical Laws Constraints on accessibility correspond exactly to modal axioms. Property of R Axiom Reads reflexive □φ → φ what is necessary is true transitive □φ → □□φ necessity iterates symmetric φ → □♢φ what is true is necessarily possible serial □φ → ♢φ necessity implies possibility The empirical payoff. Epistemic modality is not reflexive in general — Bob must be home does not entail that he is. Deontic modality is not either: you must file does not entail that you will. So a semantic framework can be tested against which entailments speakers accept. This is one of the cleaner places where formal semantics makes checkable predictions. 14 / 32 Propositional Attitudes Alice believes that Bob left. The problem. If Bob left denotes a truth value, then believe takes a truth value as argument — and every true complement would be interchangeable: Alice believes 2 + 2 = 4 ≡ Alice believes Bob left whenever both complements are true. Plainly wrong. The repair. Believe takes a proposition — an intension — not a truth value: [[believe]] : ⟨⟨s, t⟩, ⟨e, t⟩⟩ [[Alice believes Bob left]]w = 1 ⇐⇒ Bob left is true at every world compatible with Alice’s beliefs An attitude verb is a modal operator with a subject-relative accessibility relation. 15 / 32 De Re and De Dicto Alice is looking for a unicorn. De dicto there is a unicorn-seeking going on no particular unicorn; consistent with there being none De re there is a particular unicorn she seeks commits us to a unicorn existing This is scope ambiguity again — but the quantifier now scopes over an intensional operator rather than another quantifier. de dicto de re seek(a,ˆλP ∃x[unicorn(x) ∧ P (x)]) quantifier inside ∃x[unicorn(x) ∧ seek(a, x)] quantifier outside Session 5’s machinery — QR, storage, continuations — handles this too. The mechanisms 16 / 32 were not built only for quantifier–quantifier interaction. The Second Boundary So far: one sentence at a time. 17 / 32 Pronouns Across Sentences A student walked in. She sat down. Interpret each sentence separately, as our fragment does: A student walked in. ⇝ ∃x[student(x) ∧ walk-in(x)] She sat down. ⇝ sit-down(y) y free! The pronoun cannot reach the quantifier. The ∃x closed off at the end of the first sentence; y in the second is unbound, so the second sentence is not even a sentence in the Session 3 sense — it has no truth value. And gluing them together does not help: ∃x[student(x) ∧ walk-in(x)] ∧ sit-down(y) y is still outside the scope of ∃x. Conjunction does not extend a quantifier’s scope. 18 / 32 The Donkey Sentence The same problem, inside a single sentence. If a farmer owns a donkey, he beats it. What it means: every farmer who owns a donkey beats every donkey he owns. What compositional translation gives: ∃x[farmer(x) ∧ ∃y[donkey(y) ∧ own(x, y)]] → beat(x, y) with x and y free in the consequent. The puzzle. The indefinites are existential in isolation, but come out universal here. And the pronouns need to be bound from inside the antecedent, where the quantifier’s scope does not reach. Geach’s example, 1962, and the problem that launched dynamic semantics. 19 / 32 The Dynamic Turn The idea A sentence does not denote a truth value. It denotes a function from contexts to contexts — an instruction for updating what the discourse has established so far. Static Dynamic A sentence denotes a truth value a context change Meaning is truth conditions context change potential Composition is function application sequencing of updates Truth does not disappear — a sentence is true if updating with it does not empty the context. But truth is now derived from something more basic. Kamp (1981); Heim (1982); Groenendijk & Stokhof (1991). 20 / 32 Why This Solves the Problem The key move: an indefinite introduces a discourse referent that persists. Step Update Context after — — {} A student walked in. add x; require student, walked-in {x} She sat down. require x sat down {x} The referent x introduced by the first sentence is still available when the second arrives. The pronoun picks it up. In static semantics, ∃x has a scope that closes. In dynamic semantics, the existential extends its scope rightward across the discourse. That single change is what the framework buys. 21 / 32 Discourse Representation Theory DRT gives this a notation: the DRS box. x student(x) walk-in(x) sit-down(x) The top compartment lists discourse referents — the variables in play. The bottom lists conditions on them. Processing a new sentence adds to the box rather than building a separate formula. The pronoun in the third condition simply reuses the x already present. No scope problem, because there is no scope to escape. 22 / 32 Donkeys, Resolved If a farmer owns a donkey, he beats it. x, y farmer(x) donkey(y) own(x, y) ⇒ beat(x, y) The truth condition for a conditional DRS: every way of satisfying the left box must extend to a way of satisfying the right. That is where the universal force comes from. The indefinites are not universal quantifiers — they introduce referents, and the conditional quantifies universally over ways of assigning them. The pronouns are bound because x and y in the left box are accessible from the right. Accessibility is structural, not scopal. 23 / 32 What Dynamic Semantics Costs Gains cross-sentential anaphora; donkey sentences; presupposition projection; a natural account of discourse structure Costs meanings are no longer truth conditions composition is no longer function application the elegant type system of Sessions 2–5 must be rebuilt There is a reconciliation. Dynamic meanings can be given as functions in a suitably rich type system — and in the functional-programming presentation, context-change potential is naturally expressed with a state monad. We are not pursuing that here; it is a substantial topic, and EU Chapter 8 does it properly if you want it. The point for today is that the dynamic turn is a real change of framework, not a patch. 24 / 32 Tense, in Passing Worlds are not the only extra parameter a sentence needs. Alice was a student. This is not about how things are, but how they were. The standard treatment mirrors modality: add a set of times T with an ordering, and evaluate relative to a time as well as a world — [[α]]w, t . Operator Reads True at t iff PAST φ FUT φ it was the case that φ it will be the case that φ φ true at some t′ < t φ true at some t′ > t Same shape as □ and ♢: quantification over an index set, with an accessibility relation — here, temporal precedence. Aspect and its interaction with quantification are a large literature; TimeML is one computational descendant. 25 / 32 Presupposition A third thing sentences do beyond asserting. Alice stopped smoking. Asserts Alice does not smoke now Presupposes Alice smoked before The diagnostic: presuppositions survive negation. Alice did not stop smoking still conveys that she smoked before. Assertions do not survive; presuppositions do. Why this belongs in a dynamic framework. A presupposition is a requirement on the input context — the update is defined only if the context already contains the presupposed material. Natural when meanings are context-change operations; awkward otherwise. Heim’s dissertation (1982) treats presupposition and anaphora with the same machinery, which is the main argument that the dynamic turn earns its cost. 26 / 32 A Worked Update A student walked in. She sat down. Every professor noticed her. After processing Referents Conditions — ∅ — A student walked in. x student(x), walk-in(x) She sat down. x + sit-down(x) Every professor noticed her. x + ∀y[prof(y) → notice(y, x)] Note that x persists across all three sentences — introduced once, referred to twice. And note what did not happen. The universal quantifier in the third sentence introduces y, but y does not persist: ∗Every professor noticed her. He frowned. is bad. Indefinites introduce accessible referents; universals do not. That asymmetry is data, and a dynamic theory has to predict it — which it does, because the universal’s referent is introduced inside a subordinate box. 27 / 32 Part I, Complete Session Added Still missing 1 composition as application types 2 types; what can combine truth 3 models; satisfaction a working fragment 4 the fragment, executable quantifiers 5 generalized quantifiers; scope intensions, discourse 6 worlds; context change similarity Each row closed the previous row’s gap. The last one does not get closed inside Part I. Add worlds, add discourse referents, add whatever you like — in every framework today, a word is still an arbitrary symbol. dog and wolf remain as unrelated as dog and Tuesday. That is what Part II is about. 28 / 32 What Carries Forward Idea Returns in As Intension as a function — not used again in this course Modality as quantification Session 24 epistemic states, alignment Discourse referents Session 11 role–filler binding Variable reuse Part IV the copying problem The last row is the one to remember. Donkey anaphora needs a variable used twice — once in the antecedent, once in the consequent. In Part IV we will meet a framework where binding is the wedge product, and where a ∧ a = 0. A structure that cannot bind the same thing twice cannot do donkey anaphora. Whether that is repairable is open. You have now seen the same limitation three times: as mu-abstraction in λ-DCS, as shadowing in the lambda calculus, and as donkey sentences here. 29 / 32 Summary Concept Key point Extensionality Possible worlds Intension Proposition Type s □, ♢ Accessibility Attitudes de re / de dicto Anaphora problem Dynamic semantics DRT a predicate is its extension; coextensive becomes identical a set W; denotation is world-relative a function from worlds; this is meaning intension of a sentence; a set of worlds added to the inventory; every type gains an s ∀ and ∃ over accessible worlds its properties are modal axioms; flavors of modality take propositions, not truth values scope over an intensional operator ∃ closes; the pronoun cannot reach it meaning is context change potential boxes; referents persist; accessibility is structural 30 / 32 Coming Up Session 6A: λ-DCS — the logical tradition at Freebase scale, and what it still cannot do. Session 6B: Semantic types as vectors — the bridge into Part II. Session 7: The distributional hypothesis. Part II begins. Reading: course slides. EU Chapter 8 if you want dynamic semantics properly; Portner’s Modality is the standard short introduction to the first half. Problem Set 1 is due Friday 25 September. Distributional Semantics (Studies in Natural Language Processing) (Hard cover). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2023. 452 pp. 1. Introduction It has been 70 years since the publication in this journal of Harris’s article “Distributional Structure”, a work which has become one of the foundational documents for contemporary computational linguistics. The present article reviews what could be viewed as Harris’s legacy, as presented in Distributional Semantics by Alessandro Lenci and Magnus Sahlgren (henceforth LS). That work is a comprehensive and compelling exploration of the theoretical and computational underpinnings of distributional semantics. It is a significant contribution to both linguistic theory and computational linguistics in its own right, providing a bridge between semantic theories and practical applications in natural language processing (NLP). As both a linguist and computational linguist, I found this book relevant to current computational as well as formal semantic research, which increasingly employs distributional methods to understand and model language meaning. Distributional semantics relies on the principle that words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings, a technique that has become a cornerstone of modern NLP. This book addresses the growing need for a comprehensive understanding of this paradigm, offering insights that are crucial for both theoretical developments and practical applications. My review aims to highlight the importance of this book for ongoing research in both linguistics and computational linguistics, examining its major sections and topics while providing a critical analysis of its contributions in the context of linguistic research over the past 70 years. I begin by making some general observations regarding the book’s aim and scope, followed by a detailed review and examination of the themes covered in each of the three major sections of the book. I emphasize throughout how the topics and their treatment are related and relevant to contemporary research in linguistics and computational linguistics. I conclude with some general observations on the nature and use of data in linguistics. *Email: pustejovsky@gmail.com; jamesp@cs.brandeis.edu © 2024 The Author(s).
