The honest statement: text co-occurrence is a narrow, mechanizable proxy for use. That it works as well as it does is a striking empirical fact, not a consequence of Wittgenstein. 8 / 51 The Distributional Hypothesis, Stated The working hypothesis for Part II Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. Therefore: represent a word by a summary of the contexts it occurs in, and measure meaning similarity by similarity of those summaries. Three things are being asserted, and they are independent: 1 Contexts are informative. The environments of a word carry signal about it. 2 The signal is summarizable. A single fixed-length object suffices; we need not keep the contexts themselves. 3 Similarity transfers. Geometric closeness of summaries tracks semantic closeness of words. (1) is close to uncontroversial. (2) is an engineering bet — Session 9 revisits it. (3) is where the trouble is, and we will spend the last quarter of today on it. 9 / 51 The Classic Demonstration Here are six sentences containing a word you do not know. 1 A bottle of tezgüino is on the table. 2 Everyone likes tezgüino. 3 Tezgüino makes you drunk. 4 We make tezgüino out of corn. 5 Don’t have any more tezgüino before you drive. 6 The tezgüino had gone sour. 10 / 51 The Classic Demonstration Here are six sentences containing a word you do not know. 1 A bottle of tezgüino is on the table. 2 Everyone likes tezgüino. 3 Tezgüino makes you drunk. 4 We make tezgüino out of corn. 5 Don’t have any more tezgüino before you drive. 6 The tezgüino had gone sour. You now know, with some confidence, that it is an alcoholic beverage, probably fermented rather than distilled, made from maize, and drinkable in quantity. No definition was given. No entry was consulted. The contexts did all of it. The example is Nida’s (1975), made famous in this form by Lin (1998). 10 / 51 Why That Worked Look at what each sentence actually contributed. Sentence Context element Inference licensed 1 2 3 4 5 6 a bottle of likes makes you drunk make out of corn don’t have more had gone sour mass noun, liquid, containerizable consumable or enjoyable alcoholic manufactured, from maize dosed, consumed repeatedly perishable, fermentable Crucially, no single context is decisive. Sentence 1 alone is consistent with ink. The inference comes from the intersection of many weak constraints. That is the shape of the whole method: many individually uninformative observations, aggregated. 11 / 51 Practice: Two Unknown Words Word A: The A was flush against the rafter. · Drive the A in at an angle. · a box of galvanized As · bent the A with a bad swing Word B: She was elected B in March. · the outgoing B · B of the finance committee · report to the B by Friday 12 / 51 Practice: Two Unknown Words Word A: The A was flush against the rafter. · Drive the A in at an angle. · a box of galvanized As · bent the A with a bad swing Word B: She was elected B in March. · the outgoing B · B of the finance committee · report to the B by Friday What you inferred, and how: Type Cue Nearest neighbors A B concrete count noun, small artifact pluralizes, boxed, driven, bent nail, screw, brad, spike human role elected, outgoing, reports chair, president, director Note what you did not recover: whether A is a nail or a screw. Those two have near-identical distributions in this sample. Hold that thought — it returns at the end of the lecture as the central limitation. 12 / 51 What the Hypothesis Does Not Say Not claimed Why it matters That distribution determines reference That distribution determines truth That similar means synonymous That the relation is symmetric in strength That it works for function words Nothing in a corpus fixes which individual Alice denotes Corpora contain false sentences, at scale hot/cold are distributionally near-identical Entailment is directional; cosine is not the, of, not occur everywhere Every row here is a place where Part I’s machinery is strictly better. That is why this is a course about both, and why Part IV asks whether a single algebra can host both. We are not replacing the logic. We are adding a second source of information, with different strengths and a different failure profile. 13 / 51 Three Decisions To turn the hypothesis into something you can run, you must fix three things. Every distributional model — including, in a disguised form, every language model — makes these three choices. Decision Options we will consider 1 What is a context? 2 What is a count? 3 What is a comparison? document, paragraph, ±k window, dependency relation raw frequency, PMI, PPMI, tf–idf, smoothed variants Euclidean, Jaccard, cosine, Kullback– Leibler These are not tuning knobs of equal weight. Decision 1 determines what kind of similarity you get. Decision 2 determines whether you get any signal at all. Decision 3 is the most constrained — there is a clear right answer, and a clear reason for it. 14 / 51 Decision 1, First Option: The Term–Document Matrix The oldest form, from information retrieval. Rows are words, columns are documents, cell (w, d) is the count of w in d. ship sail proof lemma Doc 1 Doc 2 Doc 3 Doc 4 14 9 0 0 0 0 23 18 21 17 0 0 1 0 19 24 Two ways to read this matrix, and both are used: By column — each document is a vector over words. This is retrieval: match a query vector against document vectors. By row — each word is a vector over documents. This is lexical semantics: ship and sail are similar because they share documents. The row reading, with dimensionality reduction applied, is Latent Semantic Analysis (Deerwester et al. 1990); we return to it in Session 8. 15 / 51 Decision 1, Second Option: The Term–Term Matrix Rows are words; columns are also words. Cell (w, c) counts how often c occurred in the context of w. This requires saying what “in the context of” means. The standard choice: a symmetric window of ±k tokens. they drank the hot coffee in the morning window, k = 2 This single position contributes four increments to row coffee: to columns the (twice), hot, and in. Slide the window over every token of the corpus and accumulate. That is the entire algorithm. It is one pass, and it parallelizes trivially — which is exactly why it scaled in the 1990s on hardware that could not have trained anything. 16 / 51 Building a Row by Hand Corpus fragment (three sentences), target coffee, window k = 2, stopwords kept: 1 they drank the hot coffee in the morning 2 pour the coffee into a cup 3 she brews coffee every morning Occurrence Left 2 Right 2 Increments 1 2 3 the, hot pour, the she, brews in, the into, a every, morning the+2, hot+1, in+1 pour+1, the+1, into+1, a+1 she+1, brews+1, every+1, morning+1 Row coffee so far: the=3, hot=1, in=1, pour=1, into=1, a=1, she=1, brews=1, every=1, morning=1. Already the largest entry is the, and it tells us nothing. That observation is the whole of Decision 2. 17 / 51 Window Size Changes What You Measure This is the single most consequential knob, and it is routinely set without comment. Window Similarity you get Top neighbors of dog ±1 to ±2 ±5 to ±10 whole document paradigmatic / substitutional mixed topical / associative cat, horse, rabbit, puppy cat, pet, bark, leash veterinarian, kennel, walk, owner Why: a narrow window sees mostly syntactic neighbors, so words that can occupy the same slot look alike. A wide window sees the topic, so words that belong to the same activity look alike. The terms are Saussure’s, and they are worth having Paradigmatic: relation between items that can substitute for one another (dog/cat). Syntagmatic: relation between items that combine (dog/bark). Window size is the dial between them. Choose it according to the task, not the default. 18 / 51 Beyond Windows: Syntactic Contexts A window is a crude proxy for “related to.” With a parser, you can use the dependency relation itself as the context. dobj nsubj she brews strong coffee every morning amod Contexts for coffee become typed: ⟨brew, dobj−1 ⟩ and ⟨strong, amod⟩, instead of untyped adjacency. Range Precision Neighbors produced Cost Window Dependency bounded by k includes accidental adjacency topical one pass unbounded, but structurally local only genuine relations sharply paradigmatic requires a parser, and inherits its errors Padó & Lapata (2007); Levy & Goldberg (2014), who showed the same effect for word2vec. 19 / 51 Decision 1: Summary Context type Dimensions Captures Cost Document Paragraph Window ±k, large k Window ±k, small k Dependency |D| |D| large |V | |V | |V | × |R| topic topic, narrower topic + association substitutability typed relations one pass one pass one pass one pass parsing There is no neutral choice here. “Similar” is not one relation, and the context definition picks which one you are measuring. Keep this in mind when you read a paper reporting that some model “captures semantic similarity.” The first question is always: which similarity, and what was the context window? For the rest of today we fix the choice: term–term, ±4 window, so that the arithmetic is concrete. 20 / 51 The Counts Are Wrong Here is a small term–term matrix, raw counts, from a corpus of technology and beverage text. Window ±4. coffee tea laptop tablet the cup brew screen battery morning 300 240 260 220 48 44 3 1 32 28 0 0 2 1 52 44 1 0 41 39 38 24 6 4 Your intuition says: two clusters, {coffee, tea} and {laptop, tablet}, and the columns cup/brew versus screen/battery separate them cleanly. Your intuition is reading the small numbers. The arithmetic will read the large ones. 21 / 51 Raw Counts: The Disaster Compute cosine similarity on the raw rows. (Cosine is defined properly in a few slides; for now, the standard angle-based similarity, 1 for identical direction.) Pair Cosine on raw counts coffee / tea laptop / tablet 0.999 1.000 coffee / laptop coffee / tablet tea / laptop 0.950 0.946 0.947 Everything is similar to everything, at around 0.95. The measure has almost no discriminative power. And note: the two correct pairs do score highest. The problem is not the ranking — it is that the margin is 0.05, which will not survive noise. 22 / 51 The Diagnosis One column is responsible. Column Total count Share of all counts the screen cup battery morning brew 1020 99 96 81 72 60 71.4% 6.9% 6.7% 5.7% 5.0% 4.2% Every row has a large the entry, so every pair of rows shares a large component in the the direction, and the angle between any two rows is small. The principle Frequency is not informativeness. A context occurring with everything distinguishes nothing. We want not how often w and c co-occur, but how much more often than chance. 23 / 51 Pointwise Mutual Information Definition PMI(w, c) = log2 P (w, c) P (w) P (c) where, with #(w, c) the cell count and N the sum of all cells: P P ′ ′ #(w, c) ′ #(w , c) c′ #(w, c ) P (w, c) = , P (w) = , P (c) = w . N N N Read the formula as a ratio of observed to expected. The denominator P (w)P (c) is what the joint probability would be if w and c were independent; the numerator is what it is. PMI > 0 PMI = 0 PMI < 0 observed > expected observed = expected observed < expected c is attracted to w c is independent of w c avoids w 24 / 51 Where PMI Comes From It is not an arbitrary formula. Mutual information between two random variables is I(W ; C) = XX w c P (w, c) log2 P (w, c) , P (w)P (c) the expected number of bits that observing one variable saves you when coding the other. PMI is the pointwise version: the summand, before taking the expectation. It is the number of bits of information that this particular c gives you about this particular w.   I(W ; C) = E(w,c) PMI(w, c) So the units are meaningful: PMI(w, c) = 1 means seeing c halves your uncertainty about w relative to chance — one bit. Church & Hanks (1990) introduced PMI to computational lexicography for exactly Firth’s problem: finding collocations. 25 / 51 PMI Worked: coffee and cup Using the six-column matrix. N = 1428. 48 P (coffee, cup) = 1428 = 0.0336 421 P (coffee) = 300+48+32+2+1+38 = 1428 = 0.2948 1428 96 P (cup) = 48+44+3+1 = 1428 = 0.0672 1428 0.0336 0.0336 P (w, c) = = = 1.697 P (w)P (c) 0.2948 × 0.0672 0.01981 PMI(coffee, cup) = log2 1.697 = 0.76 cup occurs with coffee about 1.7 times more often than chance would predict — worth about three quarters of a bit. 26 / 51 PMI Worked: Three Contrasting Cells Cell (coffee, cup) (coffee, brew) (laptop, cup) (coffee, screen) (coffee, the) attracted attracted repelled repelled indifferent Count obs/exp PMI 48 32 3 2 300 1.70 1.80 0.12 0.07 0.99 +0.76 +0.85 −3.02 −3.87 −0.01 Look at the last row. The largest count in the entire matrix — 300 — receives a PMI of essentially zero. That is not a bug being papered over. It is the formula doing precisely what it was designed to do: the occurs with coffee exactly as often as it occurs with everything, so it carries zero bits about coffee. Stopword removal, which you have probably done as a preprocessing hack, falls out of PMI as a theorem rather than a heuristic. 27 / 51 The Full PMI Matrix coffee tea laptop tablet the cup brew screen battery morning −0.00 −0.00 0.01 0.00 0.76 0.96 −3.02 −4.37 0.85 0.98 −∞ −∞ −3.87 −4.55 1.05 1.04 −4.58 −∞ 1.00 1.16 0.83 0.50 −1.60 −1.95 The structure is now visible to the eye: a positive block at upper-left, a positive block at lower-right, negatives off the diagonal blocks, and a column of zeros where the used to dominate. Two cells are −∞. Those are the zero counts: log2 0 is undefined. This is not a numerical inconvenience — it is the first symptom of a real problem. 28 / 51 The Trouble Below Zero Negative PMI is a claim that two words co-occur less than chance. Estimating that reliably is much harder than estimating attraction. 1 2 Unbounded below. A count of zero gives −∞. The value depends entirely on whether you happened to observe the pair. Statistically fragile. To establish that P (w, c) is, say, 10−6 rather than 10−5 — one bit of negative PMI — you need on the order of 106 observations of w. For most of the vocabulary you do not have them. 3 Psychologically dubious. Do speakers represent the fact that coffee and battery are mutually avoidant? There are |V |2 such facts and almost all of them are uninformative. 4 Computationally costly. A matrix with meaningful negatives is dense. A matrix with negatives clipped is sparse, and sparsity is what makes 50,000 × 50,000 tractable. All four arguments point the same way, and the fix is the crudest possible one. 29 / 51 Positive PMI Definition  PPMI(w, c) = max PMI(w, c), 0 Clip everything negative to zero. Undefined cells become zero. Done. What this costs you: the distinction between “independent” and “strongly repelled” is erased. coffee/battery and coffee/the now look the same. What this buys you: a sparse, non-negative matrix with no infinities, on which every similarity measure is well behaved — and, empirically, better neighbors than PMI on essentially every benchmark. This is your first example of a pattern that recurs for the rest of the course: a theoretically motivated quantity, modified by a theoretically unmotivated clip, because the clipped version works better. Be neither

title: Lecture 8 — Reduction and Prediction
text: Reduction and Prediction From Fifty Thousand Dimensions to Three Hundred James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 1 / 58 Where We Left Off Session 7 built a word vector in three decisions: choose a context, weight the counts, compare with cosine. It worked — the margin between correct and incorrect pairs went from 0.05 to 0.96. It also left three problems, all consequences of the matrix being |V | × |C| and mostly zero. Problem Symptom Sparsity as blindness espresso and cappuccino share no context ⇒ cosine exactly 0 columns car and automobile are unrelated coordinates 50,000 features where downstream models want a few hundred No generalization Dimensionality And one promise: that all three are addressed by a single move — find a low-dimensional space in which the observed matrix is approximately recoverable. 2 / 58 Today: Three Routes, One Destination Count and factorize SVD / LSA Predict word2vec, SGNS Dense vectors vw ∈ Rd d ≈ 100–500 Count and fit GloVe The three routes were developed a quarter-century apart, in different communities, with different justifications — and the middle one was widely described as having replaced the first. The result we will prove today: the middle route is the first route, with a particular weighting and a particular objective. Session 7 already put the clue on the board — the shifted PMI row in the weighting table. 3 / 58 The Fourth Reason to Reduce Three of the reasons are practical. The fourth is the interesting one, and it is not about size at all. Generalization Two words with no shared context have cosine exactly zero, no matter how similar they are. Reduction can give them a nonzero similarity — by forcing both to be expressed in terms of a small set of shared latent directions. This is a genuinely different kind of claim from “the matrix is too big.” It says the reduced representation can assert something the data did not contain. Is that inference, or invention? The answer: reduction adds an inductive bias — the assumption that the true matrix is approximately low rank. That is information only if the assumption is right. We will test it on a case where we know the answer. 4 / 58 The Tool: Singular Value Decomposition Theorem Every real matrix M ∈ Rm×n factors as M = U ΣV ⊤ with U ∈ Rm×m and V ∈ Rn×n orthogonal, and Σ diagonal with entries σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ · · · ≥ 0. Read the three factors as a change of coordinates, a scaling, and a change of coordinates back: V⊤ Σ U rotate the context space to a new orthogonal basis scale each new direction by its importance σi rotate into the word space The new basis directions are not contexts. They are linear combinations of contexts, ordered by how much of the matrix they explain. 5 / 58 First: What Does “Rank” Mean? The theorem we are heading for is about rank-k approximation, so we need that word. The simplest case A matrix has rank 1 when every row is a multiple of one single row — one pattern, rescaled.  3 6 0  1 2 0 rows are 1 · (3, 1), 2 · (3, 1), 0 · (3, 1) There is only one thing going on here. Knowing the pattern (3, 1) and the three scale factors (1, 2, 0) is knowing the whole matrix: five numbers instead of six, and the saving grows with the size. Rank k then means: the matrix is a sum of k such patterns, and no fewer. Equivalently, the row space has dimension k. We will use the sum-of-patterns reading throughout, because it is the one that makes the theorem obvious. 6 / 58 The Outer Product Builds Those Patterns Given a column u ∈ Rm and a row v ∈ Rn , the outer product uv⊤ is the m × n matrix (uv⊤ )ij = ui vj   1  u = 2 , 0 v u  v⊤ = (3, 1) =⇒  3 1 uv⊤ = 6 2 0 0 the pattern — what the rows all look like the weights — how much of the pattern each row gets Every rank-1 matrix is an outer product, and every outer product is rank 1. The two notions are the same. Contrast the inner product u · v, which sums the index away and returns a scalar. The outer product sums nothing and raises the order from 1 to 2. 7 / 58 The SVD, Rewritten Now read M = U ΣV ⊤ one column at a time. It is a sum of rank-1 pieces: M = σ1 u1 v1⊤ + σ2 u2 v2⊤ + · · · + σr ur vr⊤ vi ui σi the ith pattern over contexts how much each word uses that pattern how important the pattern is, and they are sorted This is the same factorization as before, written so you can see what it is for. The matrix is decomposed into named patterns, ordered by how much of the data each one explains. And now truncation has an obvious meaning: keep the big terms, drop the small ones. 8 / 58 The Three Factors, For Our Matrix  0  0  0.01 0 | 0.76 0.96 0 0 0.86 0 0 0.98 0 0 0 1.05 1.00 0 1.04 1.16 {z M (4×6)  0.84 0.50  0  0 } =  0.00 0.00  0.68 0.73 |   0.70 −0.72 0.00 2.13 0 0 0 0.00  0   0.00 0.72 0.70 0.00  2.02 0 0   0.00 0.00 −0.73  0 0 0.29 0   0.00 0.00 0.00 0.68 0 0 0 0.08 −0.07 {z }| {z }| U (4×4) Σ (4×4) 0.00 0.60 0.41 0.00 0.00 0.70 0.65 0.00 0.25 0.00 0.00 −0.72 {z V ⊤ (4×6)  0.72 0.00 0.00 0.47   0.00 −0.88 0.69 0.00 } How to read it: column i of U , the ith entry of Σ, and row i of V ⊤ belong together — they are the ith term. The first and second are picked out above. 9 / 58 Three Things to Notice Σ is diagonal every off-diagonal entry is 0. All Σ does is scale — it mixes nothing. The content is in U and V ⊤ . and sorted 2.13 > 2.02 > 0.29 > 0.08, always descending. That ordering is what makes “keep the top k” well defined. U and V are orthonormal columns of U are unit length and mutually perpendicular, likewise rows of V ⊤ . This is the property that makes truncation optimal. A note on shapes. V ⊤ is 4 × 6, not 6 × 6. This is the economy (or thin) SVD: the last two rows of the full V ⊤ would multiply zero singular values and contribute nothing, so they are dropped. In general, an m × n matrix of rank r has at most min(m, n) nonzero singular values. Here min(4, 6) = 4, which is why there are four terms and not six. 10 / 58 Our Matrix: the First Two Patterns Run it on the Session 7 matrix. σ1 = 2.127: u1 = (0, 0, 0.681, 0.733), v1 = (0, 0, 0, 0.696, 0.719, 0) Weights on laptop and tablet; pattern on screen and battery. This term is “device-ness”. σ2 = 2.016: u2 = (0.697, 0.717, 0, 0), v2 = (0, 0.604, 0.645, 0, 0, 0.467) Weights on coffee and tea; pattern on cup, brew, morning. This term is “beverage-ness”. Nobody supplied those two categories. They are what the factorization found, and they are the two largest terms because they explain the most. All four entries of u1 are non-negative, and likewise u2 — these terms add structure. The next two will not. 11 / 58 Our Matrix: the Last Two Patterns σ3 = 0.292, an order of magnitude smaller: u3 = (−0.717, +0.697, 0, 0), v3 = (0, 0.414, 0.247, 0, 0, −0.876) Look at the signs. coffee gets − and tea gets + — this term does not describe a topic, it describes a difference within one: mostly that coffee leans on morning more than tea does. σ4 = 0.084: u4 = (0, 0, −0.733, +0.681) Same shape, separating laptop from tablet. The structure of the spectrum The large terms are the topics. The small terms are the distinctions within a topic, and they are the ones carrying opposite signs. Keep that in view. It tells you in advance what truncation will cost. 12 / 58 Truncation Is Just Dropping Terms M = 2.127 u1 v1⊤ + 2.016 u2 v2⊤ + 0.292 u3 v3⊤ + 0.084 u4 v4⊤ | {z } | {z } keep: the two topics discard: the within-topic detail Setting k = 2 does not “compress” in any mysterious sense. It deletes the last two summands. What you keep What you lose the structure shared across a group of words what distinguishes members of that group So the smoothing we are about to observe is not a side effect. It is the definition of what we did. And you can already predict the antonym problem from here: hot and cold differ in a low-σ direction, and low-σ directions are what truncation removes. 13 / 58 How Wrong Is the Result? The Frobenius Norm To say “closest” we need to measure the distance between two matrices. The simplest way: flatten each one into a long vector and take the ordinary length of the difference. ∥A∥F = sX a2ij i,j No new ideas — the Euclidean norm, applied to a matrix that has been unrolled. Worked.  A= 2 2  √ √ 1 −→ (2, 1, 2, 0) −→ ∥A∥F = 4 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 9 = 3 0 For a distance, subtract first and then measure: ∥A − B∥F is the length of the vector of cell-by-cell differences. That is the quantity Eckart–Young minimizes. 14 / 58 Each Singular Value Is Itself a Size Before the identity, one step that is easy to miss. ui and vi are unit vectors, and for unit vectors the outer product has Frobenius norm exactly 1:  X  X  X ∥ui vi⊤ ∥2F = u2j vk2 = u2j vk2 = 1 · 1 = 1 j j,k σi ui vi⊤ k F = σi σi is the Frobenius size of the ith term. Not a score attached to it — its actual measured size. Note the direction. The norm does not rank the singular values — the SVD produces them already sorted, and each one is a measurement of its own piece. Changing the norm would not reshuffle them; it would change which truncation is optimal. On our matrix the four terms measure 2.127, 2.016, 0.292, 0.084 — the singular values, exactly. 15 / 58 The Singular Values Are the Size of the Matrix A useful identity ∥M ∥F = qP 2 i σi √ √ Check on our matrix: 2.1272 + 2.0162 + 0.2922 + 0.0842 = 8.681 = 2.946 — and squaring all twenty-four entries of M and adding gives 8.681 too. So the singular values are not just importance scores — squared and summed, they are the size of the matrix. Why it is true. The SVD writes M as a sum of rank-1 pieces that are mutually orthogonal — the property we noted about U and V . For orthogonal pieces, squared lengths add: X X ∥M ∥2F = ∥σi ui vi⊤ ∥2F = σi2 i i That is Pythagoras, in a space whose points are matrices — each term contributes its own σi2 and nothing else, with no cross terms, because orthogonal pieces do not interfere. Which is also why dropping a term costs you exactly σi2 and not more. That is the next slide. 16 / 58 Why This Is the Right Tool: Eckart–Young Keep only the top k directions: Mk = Uk Σk Vk⊤ , rank(Mk ) = k. Eckart–Young–Mirsky Mk is the best rank-k approximation to M in Frobenius norm: ∥M − Mk ∥F = min rank(X)≤k ∥M − X∥F = qP 2 i>k σi . Read the right-hand side against the previous slides: the error is exactly the terms you discarded, √ squared and summed. On our matrix, 0.2922 + 0.0842 = 0.304, and computing ∥M − M2 ∥F directly gives 0.304. So the singular values are the error budget: before truncating you know what it will cost. This is where the “retain 90% of the variance” heuristic comes from. “In Frobenius norm” is a choice, and not obviously the right loss for a co-occurrence matrix. We return to this at GloVe’s weighting function. 17 / 58 Why That Theorem Is Not Obvious It is easy to hear Eckart–Young as a restatement of the definition. It is not. What we did What was claimed sorted the terms by σ and kept the first k no other rank-k matrix, however constructed, is closer Truncation is a greedy procedure: take the biggest piece, then the next, never reconsidering. Greedy algorithms are usually not optimal — the field of dynamic programming exists because planning ahead normally beats them. Here greedy is optimal, provably. The rank-1 pieces are mutually orthogonal, so each contribution is independent of the others — nothing is gained by trading a large term for two small ones. That orthogonality is what U and V are for, and it is why this factorization gets a theorem when others do not. The result holds for any unitarily invariant norm, not just Frobenius — Mirsky’s extension of Eckart and Young’s 1936 theorem. 18 / 58 Quick Check Before we run the recipe — three questions on what we just built.   2 4 1 The matrix — what is its rank? Write it as an outer product uv⊤ . 3 6 2 Our matrix had σ3 = 0.292 and σ4 = 0.084. What is the relative error ∥M − M3 ∥F /∥M ∥F if we truncate at k = 3 instead of 2? 3 u3 had entries of opposite sign on coffee and tea. What would it have meant if u3 had been all non-negative? 19 / 58 Quick Check Before we run the recipe — three questions on what we just built.   2 4 1 The matrix — what is its rank? Write it as an outer product uv⊤ . 3 6 2 Our matrix had σ3 = 0.292 and σ4 = 0.084. What is the relative error ∥M − M3 ∥F /∥M ∥F if we truncate at k = 3 instead of 2? 3 u3 had entries of opposite sign on coffee and tea. What would it have meant if u3 had been all non-negative? Answers. 1 Rank 1 — the second column is twice the first, and the second row is 1.5× the first. u = (2, 3)⊤ , v = (1, 2). 2 0.084/2.946 = 0.029, under 3%. At k = 2 it was 0.304/2.946 = 10.3%. 3 It would have been a third topic — another group of words sharing a pattern — rather than a distinction drawn inside an existing group. Sign structure in u is how you tell the two apart. 19 / 58 The Recipe 1 2 3 4 Build the PPMI matrix M , size |V | × |C|. Compute M = U ΣV ⊤ . Choose k. Take the word vectors to be the rows of W = Uk Σαk , α=1 α = 0.5 α=0 W = Uk Σk 1/2 W = Uk Σk W = Uk α ∈ [0, 1]. the “natural” choice; preserves distances in M symmetric between words and contexts discards the singular values entirely Empirically, α = 0 often wins — throwing away the very quantities that told you which directions mattered. That is the third instance of the pattern Session 7 named: a principled quantity, modified by an unprincipled exponent, because the modification works. Keep counting them. 20 / 58 Worked: the Session 7 Matrix Take the PPMI matrix you computed by hand last session. Four words, six contexts. coffee tea laptop tablet the cup brew screen battery morning 0 0 0.01 0 0.76 0.96 0 0 0.85 0.98 0 0 0 0 1.05 1.04 0 0 1.00 1.16 0.84 0.50 0 0 Its singular values: σ1 = 2.127, Fraction of σ2 = 2.016, P σi2 retained σ3 = 0.292, σ4 = 0.084. k=1 k=2 k=3 52.1% 98.9% 99.9% There is a visible gap between σ2 and σ3 — a factor of seven. The matrix is telling us it is essentially two-dimensional. 21 / 58 The Two-Dimensional Word Vectors Taking k = 2 and α = 1: coffee tea laptop tablet dim 1 dim 2 0.000 0.000 1.448 1.558 1.405 1.447 0.000 0.000 Six numbers per word became two, and the two clusters landed on separate axes. Pair coffee/tea laptop/tablet coffee/laptop Cosine, 6 dims Cosine, 2 dims 0.959 0.997 0.000 1.000 1.000 0.000 Two-thirds of the coordinates discarded, and every similarity judgment preserved or sharpened. 22 / 58 What Do the Latent Dimensions Mean? The rows of V ⊤ say which contexts each latent direction is built from. Direction Loads on Weight dim 1 battery screen everything else 0.719 0.696 ≈0 dim 2 brew cup morning 0.645 0.604 0.467 You would be forgiven for calling these “device-ness” and “beverage-ness.” Nobody supplied those categories; they fell out of the factorization. But do not generalize from this. On a real matrix the latent directions are not interpretable: they are arbitrary orthogonal combinations of tens of thousands of contexts. This example is interpretable because it was built to be. 23 / 58 The Reconstruction, and What It Changed Multiply the pieces back: M2 = U2 Σ2 V2⊤ . coffee tea laptop tablet the cup brew screen battery morning 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.85 0.87 0.00 0.00 0.91 0.93 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00 1.01 1.08 0.00 0.00 1.04 1.12 0.66 0.68 0.00 0.00 Relative error ∥M − M2 ∥F /∥M ∥F = 10.3%. But look at which entries moved: Cell (coffee, cup) (coffee, morning) (tea, morning) Observed Reconstructed 0.76 0.84 0.50 0.85 0.66 0.68 pulled up toward tea pulled down toward tea pulled up toward coffee Reduction did not merely compress — it smoothed. Each profile moved toward the profiles of the words it resembles. That is the inductive bias, doing its work in plain sight. 24 / 58 The Demonstration That Matters Smoothing is nice. The real claim was generalization: similarity between words that share no context at all. Here is a corpus built to test it. coffee tea espresso cappuccino laptop tablet phone cup brew morn. shot foam roast screen batt. charg. app boot 32 27 0 25 0 0 0 31 0 20 0 0 0 0 27 23 0 20 0 0 0 0 16 16 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 11 0 0 0 21 0 22 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 32 36 0 0 0 0 0 31 0 32 0 0 0 0 0 20 20 0 0 0 0 25 25 0 0 0 0 0 20 0 27 Check the two red rows. espresso was seen with brew, shot, roast. cappuccino was seen with cup, morning, foam. They share no context whatsoever. The counts were generated from two latent topics and then sparsified, which is a reasonable caricature of what a real corpus does to a real lexicon. 25 / 58 Before: Full PPMI, Eleven Dimensions Pair Cosine espresso / cappuccino espresso / coffee coffee / tea laptop / phone tablet / phone no shared context shares brew, roast shares cup, morning shares battery, boot shares charger 0.000 0.656 0.383 0.565 0.315 espresso / laptop different topics 0.000 Two words from the same small semantic field, both plainly beverages, score exactly zero — the same score as a beverage against a computer. This is the sparsity problem in its purest form. The cosine is not low because the evidence says they differ. It is zero because the evidence is silent. 26 / 58 After: Two Dimensions Pair 11 dims k=2 espresso / cappuccino espresso / coffee coffee / tea laptop / phone tablet / phone 0.000 0.656 0.383 0.565 0.315 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 espresso / laptop cappuccino / phone 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.000 Every within-topic pair goes to 1. Every cross-topic pair stays at 0. The model has asserted that espresso and cappuccino are similar on the basis of evidence that never mentioned them together. It reached that through coffee, which overlaps with both — transitivity through a shared latent direction. 27 / 58 And Now the Uncomfortable Part Run the same computation at k = 3. Pair 11 dims k=2 k=3 espresso / cappuccino espresso / coffee coffee / tea 0.000 0.656 0.383 1.000 1.000 1.000 −0.036 0.914 0.940 One extra dimension destroys the result. The reason is exactly the mechanism that produced it. At k = 2 the model has no room to represent anything but the two topics, so it must explain espresso and cappuccino with the same direction. At k = 3 it has room to re-fit the accident of which contexts each word happened to be observed with — and that accident is precisely what made them disjoint. The generalization was not free. It was bought by denying the model the capacity to fit the sparsity pattern. 28 / 58 How Should You Choose k? The standard heuristic is to retain some fixed fraction of k=2 k=3 P σi2 . Apply it here: Variance retained espresso/cappuccino 55.4% 76.7% 1.000 −0.036 A “retain 75% of the variance” rule picks k = 3 and throws away the effect we wanted. Why the heuristic fails Frobenius norm measures reconstruction of the observed matrix. But the observed matrix is not the target — its zeros are missing data, not evidence of dissimilarity. We are asking the model to be wrong about the observations in a particular useful way, and a criterion that rewards fidelity to observations cannot express that. In practice k is chosen by downstream evaluation — not a failure of rigor, but the admission that we have no intrinsic criterion for what the latent space should contain. 29 / 58 A Word on Cost Method Complexity Full SVD Truncated (Lanczos) Randomized SVD O(mn min(m, n)) O(nnz · k) O(nnz · k + (m+n)k 2 ) |V | = 50,000 infeasible hours minutes Two practical facts worth carrying: The methods that make this tractable exploit sparsity — which is why PPMI’s clip is load-bearing twice over, once for quality and once for feasibility. SVD is a batch method. Adding a new document means recomputing. This turns out to be one of the real practical advantages of the methods we meet next, and it is rarely the one cited. Halko, Martinsson & Tropp (2011) for randomized methods; the relevant point for us is that “count-based methods do not scale” was an overstatement even in 2013. 30 / 58 LSA: the First Version of This Argument Deerwester, Dumais, Furnas, Landauer & Harshman (1990) Apply truncated SVD to a term–document matrix. title: Reduction II: What the SVD Actually Does
text: Reduction II: What the SVD Actually Does A matrix, a circle, and three programs James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 1 / 43 Where We Left Off Session 8 used the SVD as a tool. We wrote M = U ΣV ⊤ , read off the singular values, dropped the small ones, and the word vectors got better. We never asked what the factorization is. Today One 2 × 2 matrix, one circle. We apply the matrix directly, then apply the three factors one at a time, and check that the two agree. By the end, U , Σ and V ⊤ each have a geometric job description. This also sets up the geometric algebra thread. Two of the three factors turn out to be rotors, which is the object we build the second half of the course on. 2 / 43 Factoring Exposes Structure Writing 12 = 3 × 4 does not change the number. It exposes what the number is built from, and it lets you answer questions you could not answer before: is it divisible by 6, how many divisors does it have. 12 = 3 × 4 A = U ΣV ⊤ exposes the arithmetic factors exposes the geometric factors A matrix is a single sudden transformation: numbers in, numbers out. The factorization separates that one action into three actions of three different kinds, applied in order. The claim to test today: running the three in sequence gives exactly what A gives in one stroke. 3 / 43 The Running Matrix  A = 2 3 0 2  Small enough to compute by hand, and not symmetric, which matters: for a symmetric matrix the first and last factors coincide and the interesting asymmetry disappears. det A = 4 ∥A∥F = √ 17 ≈ 4.123 A is invertible We will keep this matrix for the whole session, including the degenerate cases at the end, so that every picture is comparable to every other picture. 4 / 43 The Input: the Unit Circle The unit circle is the set of all vectors of length one: S 1 = { x ∈ R2 : ∥x∥ = 1 } = { (cos t, sin t) : 0 ≤ t < 2π } v1 v2 The twelve colored dots are placed every 30◦ . They carry no mathematics; they are there so that a transformation which does not change the shape is still visible. The two arrows are marked now and explained later. 5 / 43 Applying A Means Applying It Pointwise There is no special ”circle” operation. A acts on vectors, and the image of the circle is just the set of images of its points: A · S 1 = { Ax : ∥x∥ = 1 } For x = (x1 , x2 ):  Ax = 2 3 0 2     x1 2x1 + 3x2 = x2 2x2 Every point moves independently, by the same rule. Nothing in that rule mentions circles, ellipses, axes or angles. Whatever structure appears in the output was already implicit in the four numbers. 6 / 43 Four Points, By Hand t 0◦ 90 ◦ 63.43 ◦ 153.43◦ x = (cos t, sin t) Ax = (2x1 + 3x2 , 2x2 ) ∥Ax∥ (1, 0) (2, 0) 2.000 (0, 1) (3, 2) 3.606 (0.447, 0.894) (3.578, 1.789) 4.000 (−0.894, 0.447) (−0.447, 0.894) 1.000 Check the third row: 2(0.447) + 3(0.894) = 0.894 + 2.683 = 3.578, and 2(0.894) = 1.789. Unit vectors go in. Vectors of four different lengths come out. The transformation stretches some directions more than others, and that is the entire subject of this lecture. 7 / 43 The Whole Circle at Once dashed: the input circle A · S1 The fact this lecture explains The image of the unit circle under any 2 × 2 matrix is an ellipse centered at the origin. Not sometimes. Always. 8 / 43 Why It Has to Be an Ellipse A quick argument, before the machinery. A linear map sends the circle to some closed curve, and the curve satisfies y = Ax, ∥x∥ = 1 =⇒ x = A−1 y, ∥A−1 y∥ = 1 Squaring the second condition gives y⊤ (A−1 )⊤ A−1 y = 1 which is y⊤ Qy = 1 for a symmetric positive definite Q. That is the defining equation of an ellipse. The argument assumes A is invertible. When it is not, the ellipse degenerates to a segment or a point, which is the last section of today. 9 / 43 First Guess: Are the Columns the Axes? The columns of A are the images of the standard basis vectors:     2 3 Ae1 = , Ae2 = 0 2 Both are on the ellipse, since e1 and e2 are on the circle. So it is tempting to read them as the axes. √ ∥Ae1 ∥ = 2 ∥Ae2 ∥ = 13 ≈ 3.606 Ae1 · Ae2 = (2)(3) + (0)(2) = 6 They are not perpendicular, so they cannot be the two axes of an ellipse. And neither length is right: the true major semi-axis is 4, which is longer than both. 10 / 43 Seeing the Near Miss Ae2 true major axis, length 4 Ae1 Ae2 points near the long direction but overshoots the angle and undershoots the length. The standard basis is simply not aligned with anything A cares about. So the question becomes: which input directions do land on the axes? That question is what the SVD answers. 11 / 43 What We Can and Cannot Read Off Quantity From A directly? Value area scale factor yes, | det A| total size yes, ∥A∥F 4 √ length of major axis no 4 length of minor axis no 1 direction of the axes no 26.57◦ , 116.57◦ which inputs map there no 63.43◦ , 153.43◦ 17 ≈ 4.123 Everything in the lower block requires factoring A. Note the top block is consistent with the bottom: det A = 4 = 4 × 1 = σ1 σ2 , and ∥A∥2F = 17 = 16 + 1 = σ12 + σ22 . 12 / 43 The Factorization Theorem Every real matrix A ∈ Rm×n can be written A = U ΣV ⊤ with U and V orthogonal and Σ diagonal with non-negative entries σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ · · · ≥ 0. Factor Kind of matrix Freedom it has V⊤ Σ U orthogonal diagonal, non-negative orthogonal rotation or reflection only independent scaling per axis rotation or reflection only Two of the three factors are rigid. All of the shape change in A has been forced into the middle one. 13 / 43 Our Matrix, Factored        1 2 −1 2 3 4 0 1 1 2 √ =√ 0 2 0 1 5 1 2 5 −2 1 | {z } | {z } | {z } | {z } A U V⊤ Σ In decimals:   0.894 −0.447 U≈ , 0.447 0.894  Σ=  4 0 , 0 1 V ⊤  ≈ 0.447 0.894 −0.894 0.447  √ Everything is exact: the singular values are 4 and 1, and every entry of U and V is ±1/ 5 or √ ±2/ 5. This matrix was chosen so that nothing rounds. 14 / 43 Checking the Factorization Multiply the right-hand side back out. First ΣV ⊤ :       1 1 4 0 1 2 4 8 ·√ =√ 0 1 5 −2 1 5 −2 1 √ Then U times that, with the two 5 factors combining to 5:          1 2 −1 1 8 + 2 16 − 1 1 10 15 4 8 2 3 = = = −2 1 0 2 5 1 2 5 4−4 8+2 5 0 10 The factorization is an identity, not an approximation. Nothing has been lost or rounded away. 15 / 43 Three Programs Read Ax = U (Σ(V ⊤ x)) right to left, as a pipeline. Each factor is a program with an input shape and an output shape. Program Signature Changes the shape? 1 V⊤ circle → circle no 2 Σ circle → axis-aligned ellipse yes 3 U ellipse → ellipse no Exactly one of the three changes the shape. The other two only decide orientation. 16 / 43 Program 1: V ⊤ , Computationally V ⊤ 1 =√ 5  1 2 −2 1   ≈ 0.447 0.894 −0.894 0.447  Two checks that this is a rotation: Columns are unit length: 15 (1 + 4) = 1. ✓  Columns are perpendicular: 15 (1)(2) + (−2)(1) = 0. ✓ det V ⊤ = 15 (1 + 4) = +1, so it is a rotation and not a reflection. ✓   cos θ − sin θ gives cos θ = 0.447, sin θ = −0.894, so Matching against sin θ cos θ θ = −63.43◦ −63.43◦ is − arctan 2. The rotation is clockwise. 17 / 43 Program 1: the Arithmetic x V ⊤x (1, 0) (0.447, −0.894) (0, 1) (0.894, 0.447) v1 = (0.447, 0.894) (1, 0) = e1 lands on the x axis v2 = (−0.894, 0.447) (0, 1) = e2 lands on the y axis Row three, worked out: (0.447)(0.447) + (0.894)(0.894) = 0.2 + 0.8 = 1, and (−0.894)(0.447) + (0.447)(0.894) = −0.4 + 0.4 = 0. Every output has length one, as it must. The last two rows are the whole point of this program. 18 / 43 Program 1: the Picture V⊤ −→ in out The outline is identical. Only the dots moved, clockwise by 63.43◦ . The purple and green arrows have come to rest exactly on the axes. 19 / 43 Program 1: What It Is Doing Computationally Geometrically Rewrites each input vector in the basis {v1 , v2 }. Row i of V ⊤ is vi⊤ , so entry i of the output is vi ·x: the component of x along vi . Turns the plane so that the direction about to be stretched most lies along x, and the direction about to be stretched least lies along y. Lengths and angles are preserved, so the circle is untouched as a set. The same sentence twice ”Express x in the v coordinate system” and ”rotate the space until the v directions are the axes” describe one operation. A change of basis to an orthonormal basis is a rotation. 20 / 43 Program 2: Σ, Computationally  Σ=  4 0 , 0 1     y 4y1 Σ 1 = y2 1y2 There is no mixing. Coordinate one is multiplied by 4 and coordinate two by 1, and neither consults the other. y Σy (0.447, −0.894) (1.789, −0.894) (0.894, 0.447) (3.578, 0.447) (1, 0) (4, 0) (0, 1) (0, 1) The second singular value is 1 here, so the y coordinate happens to be left alone. That is a property of this matrix, not of Σ in general. 21 / 43 Program 2: the Picture Σ −→ in out This is the step where the circle stops being a circle. The semi-axes of the result are σ1 = 4 horizontally and σ2 = 1 vertically, read straight off the diagonal. 22 / 43 Program 2: What It Is Doing Computationally Geometrically Scales each coordinate independently. In the v coordinate system installed by program 1, this is a percoordinate multiply: no additions, no cross terms. Stretches the plane along the two axes by σ1 and σ2 . The unit circle becomes an axis-aligned ellipse whose semi-axis lengths are the singular values. The only factor that is not orthogonal Σ does not preserve lengths, does not preserve angles, and is the only one of the three that can be non-invertible. All three facts are the same fact. It is also the only factor that can destroy information, which is why truncation is always an operation on Σ. 23 / 43 Program 3: U , Computationally 1 U=√ 5     2 −1 0.894 −0.447 ≈ 1 2 0.447 0.894 Same three checks: columns of unit length, columns perpendicular, det U = 51 (4 + 1) = +1. Another rotation. Matching the rotation template gives cos θ = 0.894, sin θ = 0.447, so θ = +26.57◦ , which is arctan 12 , counterclockwise. z Uz (1.789, −0.894) (3.578, 0.447) (4, 0) (0, 1) (2, 0) (3, 2) (3.578, 1.789) (−0.447, 0.894) 24 / 43 Program 3: the Picture U −→ in out The axis lengths were fixed by Σ and are untouched here. This program decides only which way the finished ellipse points. 25 / 43 Program 3: What It Is Doing Computationally Geometrically Reads the stretched coordinates as coefficients in the basis {u1 , u2 }. Column i of U is ui , so U z = z1 u1 + z2 u2 . Rotates the axis-aligned ellipse into the orientation A actually produces, carrying the x axis to u1 and the y axis to u2 . Program 1 took the input out of the standard basis. Program 3 puts the output back into it. They are the two ends of a sandwich, and Σ is the filling. Note V ⊤ reads components off with dot products, while U builds a vector up from coefficients. That is the difference between a matrix acting by rows and by columns. 26 / 43 The Whole Pipeline V⊤ → S1 Σ → rotated U → stretched A · S1 Rotate, stretch, rotate. The first and last panels are the two sides of the identity A = U ΣV ⊤ . 27 / 43 One Point, All the Way Through Take x = e1 = (1, 0), the red dot. Stage Vector Length What changed input (1, 0) 1.000 – after V ⊤ (0.447, −0.894) 1.000 direction only after Σ (1.789, −0.894) 2.000 first coordinate ×4 after U (2, 0) 2.000 direction only Ax directly (2, 0) 2.000 same The vector leaves at the same place it would have gone in one step, having visited two positions no one would have predicted from A alone. 28 / 43 A Second Point Take x = e2 = (0, 1). Stage Vector Length input (0, 1) 1.000 after V ⊤ (0.894, 0.447) 1.000 after Σ (3.578, 0.447) 3.606 after U (3, 2) 3.606 Ax directly (3, 2) 3.606 √ 3.606 = 13, the length we computed on the columns slide. The stretch factor for this particular input is 3.606, which sits between σ2 = 1 and σ1 = 4, as every stretch factor must. 29 / 43 The Point That Explains Everything Now take x = v1 = (0.447, 0.894). Stage Vector Note input after V ⊤ after Σ after U v1 = (0.447, 0.894) (1, 0) = e1 (4, 0) = σ1 e1 (3.578, 1.789) = σ1 u1 on the circle exactly the first axis scaled by σ1 and nothing else the end of the major axis The fundamental relation Avi = σi ui vi is the input direction; ui is where it comes out; σi is how much longer it got. The middle program is a plain multiplication because program 1 put the vector on an axis first. 30 / 43 Reading the Relation Off the Original Matrix The relation can be checked against A with no factorization in sight:           1 2+6 1 8 1 2 1 1 2 3 =√ =√ =4· √ ·√ 0 2 5 2 5 0+4 5 4 5 1 and for the second pair,         1 −2 1 −4 + 3 1 −1 2 3 ·√ =√ =1· √ 0 2 5 1 5 0+2 5 2 Two special input directions come out pointing along perpendicular output directions, scaled and not rotated relative to each other. Finding those directions is what computing an SVD means. 31 / 43 Answering the Question From Earlier We asked: which input directions land on the axes of the ellipse? Input direction Output major axis v1 at 63.43◦ σ1 u1 , length 4, at 26.57◦ minor axis v2 at 153.43◦ σ2 u2 , length 1, at 116.57◦ The two input directions are 90◦ apart. So are the two output directions. But the pair has been turned: the inputs sit at 63.43◦ and the outputs at 26.57◦ . A perpendicular pair goes in and a perpendicular pair comes out, but it is a different perpendicular pair. That gap between V ⊤ and U is exactly why a single rotation could never have described A. 32 / 43 What Survives Each Stage Preserved? V⊤ Σ U lengths yes no yes angles yes no yes area yes no, ×4 yes orientation yes yes yes information all all, here all The area column multiplies out as 1 × 4 × 1 = 4 = det A. The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants, and the two rotations contribute 1 each. The last row says ”here” because σ2 = 1 ̸= 0. The next slides change that. 33 / 43 Where the Numbers Live Question about A Answered by Value here How much does it stretch, at most? σ1 4 How much, at least? σ2 1 Which input achieves the most? v1 , column 1 of V 63.43◦ Where does that input land? u1 , column 1 of U 26.57◦ By how much does area grow? σ1 σ2 4 Is it invertible? is σ2 > 0? yes How close to singular? σ1 /σ2 4 Every one of these is a question about A. None of them can be read off the four entries of A, and all of them are immediate once it is factored. That is what ”exposing the structure” means in practice. 34 / 43 Degenerate Case: a Small σ2 Keep U and V and shrink the second singular value. σ2 = 1 σ2 = 0.25 σ2 = 0 As σ2 → 0 the ellipse flattens onto the line through u1 . At σ2 = 0 the matrix has rank 1 and the whole plane is crushed onto that single line. The map stops being invertible exactly when σ2 reaches zero, and the ratio σ1 /σ2 measures how close it is to that. This is the condition number. 35 / 43 Degenerate Case: a Reflection Flip one sign: A′ =   2 3 , so det A′ = −4. 0 −2 The singular values are unchanged: σ1 = 4, σ2 = 1. The output ellipse is the same ellipse, the same shape in the same place. What differs is the traversal. Under A the colored dots run counterclockwise; under A′ they run clockwise. det σ1 , σ2 det U A A′ +4 4, 1 +1, a rotation −4 4, 1 −1, a reflection Σ is non-negative by convention and V is taken to be a rotation, so when the map reverses orientation the reflection has to be carried by U . It cannot be hidden anywhere else. 36 / 43 Singular Values Cannot See Orientation This is worth stating on its own, because it will matter later. σ1 and σ2 describe the shape of the image and nothing else. Two matrices with the same singular values produce the same ellipse, and may still differ by a reflection. Orientation lives in the sign of det, and det A = det U · det Σ · det V ⊤ with the two rotations contributing ±1. In the semantic setting this is the reason a reduced space can be right about similarity and wrong about direction. Cosine sees Σ; it does not see the sign. 37 / 43 Truncation, in This Picture Session 8 truncated by keeping the k largest singular values. Geometrically that is: Algebra Geometry set σk+1 = · · · = σr = 0 flatten the ellipsoid along those axes keep σ1 , . . . , σk keep the k longest axes at full length ∥M − Mk ∥2F = 2 i>k σi P the total length that was flattened away Eckart–Young says: of all the ways to flatten an ellipsoid down to k dimensions, flattening the shortest axes is the one that moves the surface least. Stated that way it is close to obvious. The content of the theorem is that no cleverer, non-axis-aligned flattening does better. And the loss is always inflicted on Σ, because Σ is the only factor that has any information to lose. 38 / 43 Two of the Three Are Rotors An orthogonal matrix with determinant +1 is a rotation. In geometric algebra a rotation is carried by a rotor  R = exp − 12 θ e12 = cos 2θ − sin 2θ e12 applied by the sandwich x 7→ R x R̃. For our two factors: V⊤ U angle θ half-angle in the rotor −63.43◦ +26.57◦ −31.72◦ +13.28◦ The half-angle is not a convenience of notation. It is forced by the two-sided sandwich, and it is the first real structural difference between rotors and rotation matrices. 39 / 43 Versors, and What Σ Is Not Reflections and rotations together are the versors: the transformations a geometric algebra implements by sandwiching. Every orthogonal map is a versor. Factor Orthogonal? A versor? V⊤ yes yes, a rotor Σ no no U yes yes, a rotor or a reflection The factorization, restated Every linear map is a versor, then a stretch along a frame, then another versor. Everything that is not length-preserving has been collected into the middle, and that middle is where reduction does its work. 40 / 43 Why This Matters for the Rest of the Course When we move to geometric algebra we stop writing transformations as arrays of numbers and start writing them as elements of the algebra itself. Matrix language Geometric algebra language orthogonal matrix, det = +1 rotor R, applied as RxR̃ composing two rotations multiplying two rotors the plane of rotation the bivector e12 the angle the magnitude of the bivector The advantage is not notational economy. It is that the plane of rotation becomes a first-class object you can name, add and compose, rather than something recovered after the fact from a matrix. In R2 there is only one plane, so the benefit is invisible. It appears the moment we go to three dimensions and beyond. 41 / 43 Summary Factor Computationally Geometrically V⊤ take dot products with the vi rotate so the extreme directions become the axes Σ multiply coordinate i by σi stretch the circle into an axisaligned ellipse U build the output from the ui rotate the ellipse to its final orientation Every matrix maps the unit circle to an ellipse. σ1 , σ2 are the semi-axis lengths; u1 , u2 their directions; v1 , v2 the inputs that get there. Avi = σi ui is the whole factorization in one line. The columns of A are on the ellipse but are not its axes. Only Σ changes shape, and only Σ can lose information. 42 / 43 Exercises 1 For B =   3 0 , write down U , Σ, V ⊤ without computing anything. What are v1 and 0 1 u1 ? 2 3 4   0 −2 For C = , the image of the unit circle is a circle of radius 2. What does that 2 0 say about σ1 and σ2 ? Are v1 and u1 determined? √ Our A has ∥Ae2 ∥ = 13 ≈ 3.606, between σ2 = 1 and σ1 = 4. Explain why no unit vector can have ∥Ax∥ outside [σ2 , σ1 ]. Take A and set σ2 to 0, keeping U and V . Write out the resulting rank-1 matrix as σ1 u1 v1⊤ and check that its columns are multiples of u1 . 43 / 43

title: Count‑Based NLP
text: What Counting Built Fifty years of count-based NLP, before we stop counting James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 1 / 29 Where We Are Session 7 built word vectors by counting. Session 8 compressed them with the SVD, and then began a sentence that ends badly for counting: stop counting, start predicting. Before we finish that sentence, it is worth asking what the counting tradition actually produced, because the answer is not “a first attempt”. Today Four places where counting became working technology: information retrieval, corpus linguistics and lexicography, question answering, and language modeling. Each one contributes a technique we will meet again. 2 / 29 The Claim Worth Resisting The standard story runs: first people counted words, which was crude; then people learned to predict them, which was not. That story is wrong in a specific way. Counting was not a preliminary stage that prediction replaced. It was, and in places still is, the substrate of deployed systems. Built on counts Still true Web search ranking Corpus lexicography Statistical MT and ASR BM25 remains a standard baseline and first-stage retriever Dictionary entries are still built from concordances n-gram models ran production systems for two decades The interesting question is not whether counting works. It does. The question is exactly which problem it cannot solve, and that is what the prediction methods were built to attack. 3 / 29 The Retrieval Problem Given a query and a collection of documents, return the documents in order of usefulness. Stated that way it is not obviously a counting problem. Salton’s move, in the SMART system from the 1960s onward, was to make it one: The vector space model Represent each document as a vector of term counts. Represent the query the same way. Rank by the similarity of the two vectors. You have already built this object. The term-document matrix from Session 7 is exactly an index: rows are words, columns are documents, and the entry is how often the word occurs in the document. What changes is the question asked of it. Session 7 compared rows to find similar words. Retrieval compares columns to find relevant documents. 4 / 29 Two Intuitions, Fifteen Years Apart Luhn, 1958 A word that occurs often in a document is probably what the document is about. Term frequency. Spärck Jones, 1972 A word that occurs in nearly every document tells you nothing about which one you want. Inverse document frequency. Put together: tf-idf(w, d) = tf(w, d) × log N df(w) where N is the number of documents and df(w) the number containing w. The second factor is the one worth noticing. It is a statement about the collection, not the document – the same weighting idea that PMI applies to word-context pairs. A term earns weight by being unevenly distributed. 5 / 29 A Collection of Six Documents D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6 brew coffee filter best morning coffee espresso machine review espresso coffee compared laptop battery life screen brightness review tablet screen battery comparison review perfect morning cup coffee brew guide coffee coffee coffee coffee coffee coffee brew shop menu prices hours location parking directions staff seating wifi music decor opening closing weekend Query: coffee brew df(coffee) = 4, so idf = log10 (6/4) = 0.176. df(brew) = 3, so idf = log10 (6/3) = 0.301. D6 is the interesting one. It is a real kind of document: a café page that mentions coffee constantly and answers no question at all. 6 / 29 Three Scorers, Three Answers D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6 len tf(coffee) tf(brew) raw tf tf-idf cos BM25 6 6 6 5 6 22 2 1 0 0 1 6 1 0 0 0 1 1 3 1 0 0 2 7 0.340 0.046 0.000 0.000 0.237 0.247 1.450 0.502 0.000 0.000 1.290 1.096 raw tf tf-idf cosine BM25 D6 > D1 > D5 > D2 D1 > D6 > D5 > D2 D1 > D5 > D6 > D2 Raw counting hands the top slot to the café page. Every refinement after Luhn is, in one way or another, a defense against D6. 7 / 29 What the Cosine Fixes, and What It Misses The cosine denominator normalizes by document length, which is why D6 falls to second. But the cosine still treats six occurrences as three times the evidence of two. The intuition BM25 adds The first occurrence of a term is strong evidence the document is about it. The sixth is nearly worthless. Relevance should saturate. BM25(w, d) = idf(w) · tf(w, d) (k1 + 1) |d| tf(w, d) + k1 1 − b + b avgdl  typically k1 ≈ 1.2 and b = 0.75 BM is Best Matching; the 25 is the twenty-fifth variant the group tried and means nothing else. From the Okapi system at City University London – Robertson, Spärck Jones and colleagues – established through the TREC evaluations of the 1990s. Unlike tf-idf it is derived from a probabilistic model of relevance rather than assembled from intuitions. 8 / 29 BM25: the Two Knobs k1 sets how fast relevance saturates. b sets the length penalty. tf multiplier gain |d|/avgdl multiplier at tf = 2 1 2 3 5 10 1.000 1.375 1.571 1.774 1.964 – +0.375 +0.196 +0.203 +0.190 0.5 1.0 2.0 4.0 1.600 1.375 1.073 0.746 ∞ 2.200 b = 0 turns it off. b = 1 divides fully by relative length. b = 0.75 concedes that some documents are long because k1 = 0 makes the term binary, present or absent. Large k1 they are thorough. makes it nearly linear, like raw tf. The whole per-term contribution is bounded by idf(w) · (k1 + 1). The first occurrence earns a full unit, the second a third of that, and everything past ten is rounding error. 9 / 29 Saturation, in One Comparison The contribution of coffee alone, under BM25: tf(coffee) length term score D1 2 6 0.662 D6 6 22 0.676 Three times the term frequency buys an improvement of 0.014. Saturation and length normalization together have almost exactly cancelled the repetition. That is the design working as intended: the function is asking is this document about coffee, and after two mentions it has already decided. BM25 is thirty years old and remains a standard first-stage retriever, including in front of neural rankers. It is not a historical curiosity. 10 / 29 The Concordance: the Oldest Tool Long before anything was computed, lexicographers read words in context by listing every occurrence with its neighbors. Keyword in context, KWIC. left context node right context a number to each individual, a indexed by one thing and a a two-place relation becomes a the shortcut worth memorizing: multiplying a a one-hot row vector by a the entry is what the matrix matrix matrix matrix matrix matrix assigns a number to each ordered by two, which is why a The pattern continues: three places would by a one-hot vector selects selects a row. Nothing else happens assigns to that pair of These are real lines, from a concordance of matrix over the text of this course’s own slides – 159 occurrences in 41,860 tokens. Read the node column downward and a pattern appears that no single sentence states: a matrix assigns, is indexed by, is what a relation becomes. Sinclair’s argument for the COBUILD dictionary was that this is how word meaning should be described – from attested use, not from introspection. 11 / 29 Collocation: Firth’s Question “You shall know a word by the company it keeps.” – Firth, 1957 Session 7 used that as a claim about meaning. Corpus linguistics uses it as a claim about word combinations: which pairs occur together more than chance allows? The canonical pair: strong tea powerful tea fine not English, though the words mean nearly the same No semantic theory predicts this. It is a fact about usage, recoverable only from counts, and it is exactly the kind of fact a learner of English needs and a dictionary should record. 12 / 29 Log-Likelihood, Defined Build the 2 × 2 table for a bigram, over N bigram tokens: w1 ¬w1 w2 ¬w2 a = c(w1 , w2 ) c = c(w2 ) − a b = c(w1 ) − a d = N − c(w1 ) − c(w2 ) + a Compare two hypotheses: that w2 ’s probability does not depend on whether w1 preceded it, against that it does. Twice the log of the likelihood ratio is G2 = 2 X ij Oij ln Oij , Eij Eij = (row total)(column total) N G2 is asymptotically χ2 with one degree of freedom, so it reads against a table: 3.84 at p = .05, 10.83 at p = .001. powerful tea scores 1.01 and fails; every other pair we will see passes. Dunning, 1993. The point of the paper was that Pearson’s χ2 , which divides by E, becomes unreliable exactly where language data lives – cells with tiny expected counts. The likelihood ratio does not. 13 / 29 Two Statistics on the Same Counts Take a corpus of 106 bigram tokens. bigram c(w1 ) c(w2 ) c(w1 , w2 ) PMI LLR of the 30000 60000 8000 2.15 13669.5 morning coffee 1200 900 55 5.67 330.3 strong tea 800 600 40 6.38 279.4 powerful tea 500 600 1 1.74 1.0 3 5 3 17.61 75.6 kumquat marmalade by PMI by LLR kumquat marmalade > strong tea > morning coffee > of the of the > morning coffee > strong tea > kumquat marmalade powerful tea scores near zero on both, which is the result we wanted. 14 / 29 Why They Disagree PMI (Church & Hanks, 1990) Log-likelihood (Dunning, 1993) Asks How surprising is this pairing, if the words were independent? How much evidence is there that they are not independent? Maximized by Rare words that always co-occur Frequent pairs, many observations Fails on Low counts: three occurrences of two rare words outscore any real collocation Little, though it ranks of the first, rarely what a lexicographer wants PMI = 17.61 for kumquat marmalade is computed from three observations. The statistic is not wrong; it answers a question about effect size with no regard for sample size. Sparsity again – the same problem PPMI had with its zeros. 15 / 29 They Are One Quantity, Scaled G2 is not merely similar to mutual information. It is mutual information, times 2N : X X Oij pij G2 = 2 Oij ln = 2N pij ln = 2N · I(w1 ; w2 ) Eij pi· p·j ij of the morning coffee strong tea kumquat marmalade ij LLR 2N × I I (nats) 13669.51 330.27 279.44 75.57 13669.51 330.27 279.44 75.57 0.006835 0.000165 0.000140 0.000038 So PMI and LLR are the pointwise and the expected mutual information of the same table, the second multiplied by the sample size. That is the entire difference between them. Multiply every count and N by ten: kumquat marmalade goes from LLR 75.6 to 755.7 while its PMI stays at 17.61; strong tea goes from 279.4 to 2794.4 with PMI fixed at 6.38. PMI cannot see how many observations produced it; LLR is linear in them, which is also why LLR values do not compare across corpora of different sizes. 16 / 29 Word Sketches: Collocation by Relation Raw collocation ignores structure. coffee near drink tells you less than knowing that coffee is the object of drink. Kilgarriff’s Word Sketches parse the corpus first, then count per grammatical relation: object of modifier subject of drink, brew, sip black, strong, iced spill, cool, taste This is a word profile a lexicographer can write an entry from, and it is still counting – counting over typed relations instead of over a window. Note the shape of the move. Adding linguistic structure to the definition of “context” made the counts more informative. That is the same knob you turned in Session 7 when you chose a context window, and it is the knob prediction methods largely stopped turning. 17 / 29 Zipf, on This Course’s Own Slides r word f r×f 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 the is and of it in to that 2913 1431 1046 746 590 496 457 454 2913 2862 3138 2984 2950 2976 3199 3632 log10 f 41,860 tokens, 3,951 types. Fitted slope over ranks 1–2000: −1.042. 3 2 slope −1.042 1 log10 r 0 0 1 2 3 The r × f column is nearly constant, which is Zipf’s law stated as arithmetic rather than as a curve. 18 / 29 Why Sparsity Is Permanent From the same corpus: types occurring exactly once (hapax legomena) as a share of the vocabulary as a share of the tokens 1,389 35.2% 3.3% share of tokens covered by the top 10 types by the top 100 by the top 1000 21.4% 48.0% 84.9% A third of the vocabulary was seen once. Heaps’s law says this does not improve with scale: vocabulary grows as roughly T β with β near 0.5, so a corpus ten times larger has a larger absolute hapax count, not a smaller one. This is the structural reason the PPMI matrix was mostly zeros, and why no amount of additional data makes the zeros go away. It is the problem every technique in this course is, in some sense, about. 19 / 29 Question Answering by Counting Who invented the telephone? The hard approach parses the question, parses candidate documents, and reasons over the result. The AskMSR system (Brill, Dumais and Banko, 2002) did almost none of that. The redundancy argument On a large enough collection, the answer is stated somewhere in an easy form. Do not parse the hard sentence; find the easy one, and use counting to decide which candidate keeps appearing. The procedure: 1 2 3 4 5 Rewrite the question into declarative patterns: “the telephone was invented by” Send those as queries; collect the retrieved snippets Harvest the n-grams adjacent to the matched pattern Filter by expected answer type (here, a person name) Rank by frequency 20 / 29 The Tally candidate n-gram count Alexander Graham Bell 14 returned as the answer Antonio Meucci 3 Elisha Gray 2 Bell Labs 2 wrong type, filtered the telephone 9 in the question, filtered Illustrative counts over a set of retrieved snippets. Nothing here understands the question. There is no parse, no inference, no representation of inventing or of telephones. There is a pattern, a filter, and a tally. And on factoid questions it was competitive with systems that did all of those things. That result is genuinely uncomfortable, and it is worth sitting with rather than explaining away. 21 / 29 Where Redundancy Runs Out Works when the answer is a short string, stated often, in predictable phrasings Fails when the answer appears once, or must be assembled from several documents, or the question is not factoid Fails badly when the frequent string is not the true answer – popularity is not correctness The Antonio Meucci row is the honest case. He has a real claim to the invention, and counting will never surface it, because counting measures how often something is said. Note that this failure is not fixed by predicting instead of counting. A model trained on the same corpus inherits the same distribution of assertions. It is a property of the evidence, not of the method. 22 / 29 Language Models Were Counting Too An n-gram language model estimates the next word from counts and nothing else: P (wi | wi−1 ) = c(wi−1 , wi ) c(wi−1 ) Take a three-sentence corpus: | the dog sat on the rug | the cat ate the fish bigram c(w1 , w2 ) c(w1 ) MLE add-one the cat cat sat dog sat dog ate 2 1 1 0 6 2 1 1 0.333 0.500 1.000 0.000 0.176 0.154 0.167 0.083 the cat sat on the mat Vocabulary size 11, including sentence boundaries. 23 / 29 The Zero Problem, Again the dog ate the fish is grammatical, and every word in it was observed. Its probability under the model is exactly zero, and its perplexity is infinite. This is the espresso and cappuccino problem in a different costume. A count of zero means “not observed”, and the model reads it as “impossible”. Add-one Fixes the zero and wrecks the estimates: P (sat | dog) falls from 1.000 to 0.167 Good–Turing Reallocate mass using the count of things seen exactly once – the hapax count again Kneser–Ney Back off to how many distinct contexts a word appears in, not how often Two decades of smoothing research is one long attempt at a single question: what should a model believe about something it has never seen? The prediction methods answer it differently; they do not escape it. 24 / 29 The Lesson That Should Have Been a Warning Brants and colleagues, at Google in 2007, trained n-gram models on two trillion tokens for machine translation. Their smoothing method, stupid backoff, is close to the crudest thing that could work: if the n-gram is unseen, back off to the shorter one and multiply by a fixed constant. No normalization, not a probability distribution. The finding At sufficient scale, stupid backoff matched carefully engineered Kneser–Ney smoothing. The data mattered more than the estimator. Read one way, this is a vindication of counting: just count more things. Read another way, it is the first clear signal that the returns were coming from scale rather than from linguistic insight. Both readings turned out to be right, which is the uncomfortable part. 25 / 29 What Counting Does Well Transparent Every score decomposes into observations you can point at. When BM25 ranks a document first, you can say which terms did it Cheap One pass over the corpus, no training loop, no hyperparameter search worth the name Incremental Add a document, update the counts. No retraining Well understood Significance tests, confidence intervals, and known failure modes Strong BM25 is still a first-stage retriever; concordances still underlie dictionaries Nothing in this list is true of a learned embedding, and some of it we will miss. 26 / 29 Where It Runs Out Every method today shares one limitation, and it is the one Session 8 already showed you. The limitation A count-based method can only relate two things that were observed in the same place. If espresso and cappuccino never share a context, no counting statistic over those counts will relate them – because there is nothing there to count. tf-idf, BM25 PMI, LLR n-gram models a query term missing from a document contributes nothing a pair never observed has no statistic an unseen bigram has probability zero The SVD was the first serious answer: use the structure of the whole matrix to fill in what was never observed. It worked, and Session 8 showed exactly how fragile the result was. 27 / 29 The Pivot The next move is to stop asking how often did these co-occur and start asking how well can I predict one from the other. Object Zeros Counting Predicting a matrix of observations absence of evidence parameters of a classifier training signal, by sampling Generalization bolted on afterward, via the SVD built into the objective Dimensions chosen by truncation chosen in advance Keep one question open as we go: word2vec looks like a different kind of object entirely. We will see later that, under a specific analysis, it is implicitly factoring a matrix of shifted PMI values – a matrix built from exactly the counts we have been discussing all along. Levy and Goldberg, 2014. We will come back to it. 28 / 29 Exercises 1 D6 mentions coffee six times and still loses to D5, which mentions it once. Using the BM25 formula, identify which of the two mechanisms – saturation or length normalization – contributes more to that outcome. 2 kumquat marmalade has PMI = 17.61 from three observations. Compute what its PMI would be if all three counts were multiplied by 1000 and the corpus size were also multiplied by 1000. What does the answer tell you about what PMI measures? 3 A corpus has 35% hapax legomena. You double its size. Argue from Heaps’s law whether the proportion of hapax types should rise, fall, or stay roughly constant. 4 The redundancy argument says the answer appears somewhere in an easy form. Name a question type for which this is false by construction, and say what a system would need instead. 29 / 29

title: What the Inner Product Left Out
text: What the Inner Product Left Out From factorization to binding James Pustejovsky Brandeis University Department of Computer Science CS 135: Computational Semantics Fall 2026 1 / 27 Where We Are Three routes to a word vector, all landing in the same place: vw · vc approximates some monotone function of PMI(w, c). That table settled what the routes have in common. It left two things unexplained, and both turn out to matter for where this course is going. The two questions 1 The table says SVD is solved by eigendecomposition and the other two by gradient descent. Why? Not as an engineering fact – as a mathematical one. 2 Every method so far compares meanings with an inner product. Why that operation, and what does it cost? The first question has a sharp answer involving a theorem you already know. The second one opens onto the second half of the course. 2 / 27 Two Rows That Are Really One Row From the comparison table: Cell weighting Solved by SVD on PPMI SGNS GloVe uniform eigendecomposition by frequency SGD f (x), capped SGD These read as two independent facts about three systems. They are not independent. The second row is a consequence of the first. Gradient descent is not what makes the predict models neural. It is what is left once you give up uniform weighting. 3 / 27 What Eckart–Young Promised, Exactly The theorem, stated carefully Among all matrices of rank at most k, the truncated SVD Mk minimizes X 2 Mij − Xij ∥M − X∥2F = ij Look at what the sum does. Every cell contributes equally. A cell resting on 48 observations and a cell resting on two are weighted the same, because the Frobenius norm has no idea how the numbers got there. That is not a limitation of the proof technique. Uniform weighting is a premise of the theorem. The spectral decomposition is the answer to that specific question and to no other. Session 8b put this geometrically: the SVD finds the axes of the ellipsoid, and truncation flattens the shortest ones. Nothing in that picture asks how much evidence each direction rests on. 4 / 27 Why Anyone Would Weight the Cells Return to the Session 7 counts behind the PPMI matrix: cell (coffee, cup) (laptop, the) count 48 2 a solid estimate essentially noise Both become a PPMI value, and the Frobenius norm then treats them as equally worth fitting. Given Zipf, most of the matrix is the second kind. The obvious fix, and its price P Weight each cell by how much evidence it rests on: minrank(X)≤k ij Wij (Mij − Xij )2 . There is no spectral solution to this problem, and weighted low-rank approximation is NP-hard in general. Srebro & Jaakkola 2003 for the algorithms; Gillis & Glineur 2011 for the hardness. 5 / 27 The Experiment Same matrix, same rank. Two factorizations, each optimizing a different loss. A B rank-2 truncated SVD of the Session 7 PPMI matrix rank-2 factorization found by alternating least squares, with each cell weighted by its raw co-occurrence count Score both on both objectives: unweighted loss weighted loss A: rank-2 SVD 0.0923 2.3264 B: rank-2 weighted ALS 0.8989 1.2294 6 / 27 Reading the Result unweighted weighted rank-2 SVD 0.0923 2.3264 rank-2 weighted ALS 0.8989 1.2294 Each wins its own column and loses the other. The SVD is nearly ten times better on the unweighted objective, exactly as Eckart–Young guarantees it must be, and 47% worse on the weighted one. Neither factorization is better. They are answers to different questions. And the second question has no closed form, which is why B had to be found by iteration. Nothing about B is neural, probabilistic, or predictive. It is least squares with weights, and that alone was enough to leave linear algebra behind. 7 / 27 What This Settles About “Count versus Predict” The usual framing Counting methods use linear algebra; predicting methods use neural networks and gradient descent. A change of paradigm. What is actually true All three methods factor a matrix of association scores. They differ in which cells they trust. Uniform trust admits a spectral solution; non-uniform trust does not. Levy and Goldberg made this point algebraically: SGNS is implicitly factoring shifted PMI. The weighting argument makes it geometrically concrete – SGNS is factoring roughly the same matrix the SVD does, in roughly the same way, while caring more about the cells it has seen often. That is a real difference and it does help. It is not a different theory of what a word is. 8 / 27 Three Routes, and a Fourth There is a fourth way to get from a large sparse count matrix to a small dense one. It is older than word2vec, and it is the door into the second half of this course. SVD SGNS, GloVe Random indexing How the dimensions are chosen Cost computed from the data learned from the data chosen in advance, at random factor the whole matrix many passes of SGD one pass, no factorization Kanerva and Sahlgren, from the late 1990s. Incremental, streaming, never materializes the co-occurrence matrix – every property word2vec was praised for in 2013, fifteen years earlier. It is also, though nobody called it that at the time, a vector symbolic architecture. 9 / 27 Random Indexing 1 Give every context a random sparse vector of dimension d: mostly zeros, a handful of ±1 entries in random positions. Call it the context’s index vector. 2 Give every word a zero vector of dimension d. 3 Walk the corpus. Each time word w occurs with context c, add c’s index vector to w’s. That is the entire algorithm. The result is P R where P is the count matrix and R is the random nC × d index matrix, computed without ever building P . Why it could possibly work Johnson–Lindenstrauss (1984). Any n points in any dimension can be projected onto O(log n/ϵ2 ) random dimensions with all pairwise distances preserved to within a factor 1 ± ϵ. The bound depends on the number of points, not on the dimension they started in. 10 / 27 Does It Work? 300 words, 3000 contexts, PPMI, 3.8% dense. Compare each reduction’s cosines against the full-dimensional cosines. SVD Gaussian proj.
